en: Source: AVS11-20.noacc [The Buddha said: “Ānanda, if a bhikṣu, having accepted a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife, should go to another village or town and, while there, should not wear it nor give it away, but should instead store it until the robe season has ended, that bhikṣu incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). “Ānanda, if a bhikṣu, having accepted a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife, should go to another village or town and, while there, should not wear it nor give it away, but should instead store it for more than one month, that bhikṣu incurs an offense of wrong-doing. “Ānanda, if a bhikṣu, having accepted a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife, should go to another village or town and, while there, should not wear it nor give it away, but should instead store it for more than two months, that bhikṣu incurs an offense of wrong-doing. “Ānanda, if a bhikṣu, having accepted a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife, should go to another village or town and, while there, should not wear it nor give it away, but should instead store it for more than three months, that bhikṣu incurs an offense of wrong-doing. “Ānanda, if a bhikṣu, having accepted a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife, should go to another village or town and, while there, should not wear it nor give it away, but should instead store it for more than four months, that bhikṣu incurs an offense of wrong-doing. “Ānanda, if a bhikṣu, having accepted a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife, should go to another village or town and, while there, should not wear it nor give it away, but should instead store it for more than five months, that bhikṣu incurs an offense of wrong-doing. “Ānanda, if a bhikṣu, having accepted a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife, should go to another village or town and, while there, should not wear it nor give it away, but should instead store it for more than six months, that bhikṣu incurs an offense of wrong-doing. “Ānanda, if a bhikṣu, having accepted a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife, should go to another village or town and, while there, should not wear it nor give it away, but should instead store it for more than seven months, that bhikṣu incurs an offense of wrong-doing. “Ānanda, if a bhikṣu, having accepted a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife, should go to another village or town and, while there, should not wear it nor give it away, but should instead store it for more than eight months, that bhikṣu incurs an offense of wrong-doing. “Ānanda, if a bhikṣu, having accepted a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife, should go to another village or town and, while there, should not wear it nor give it away, but should instead store it for more than nine months, that bhikṣu incurs an offense of wrong-doing. “Ānanda, if a bhikṣu, having accepted a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife, should go to another village or town and, while there, should not wear it nor give it away, but should instead store it for more than ten months, that bhikṣu incurs an offense of wrong-doing. “Ānanda, if a bhikṣu, having accepted a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife, should go to another village or town and, while there, should not wear it nor give it away, but should instead store it for more than eleven months, that bhikṣu incurs an offense of wrong-doing. “Ānanda, if a bhikṣu, having accepted a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife, should go to another village or town and, while there, should not wear it nor give it away, but should instead store it for more than twelve months, that bhikṣu incurs an offense of wrong-doing. “Ānanda, if a bhikṣu, having accepted a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife, should go to another village or town and, while there, should not wear it nor give it away, but should instead store it for more than thirteen months, that bhikṣu incurs an offense of wrong-doing. “Ānanda, if a bhikṣu, having accepted a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife, should go to another village or town and, while there, should not wear it nor give it away, but should instead store it for more than fourteen months, that bhikṣu incurs an offense of wrong-doing. “Ānanda, if a bhikṣu, having accepted a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife, should go to another village or town and, while there, should not wear it nor give it away, but should instead store it for more than fifteen months, that bhikṣu incurs an offense of wrong-doing. “Ānanda, if a bhikṣu, having accepted a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife, should go to another village or town and, while there, should not wear it nor give it away, but should instead store it for more than sixteen months, that bhikṣu incurs an offense of wrong-doing. “Ānanda, if a bhikṣu, having accepted a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife, should go to another village or town and, while there, should not wear it nor give it away, but should instead store it for more than seventeen months, that bhikṣu incurs an offense of wrong-doing. “Ānanda, if a bhikṣu, having accepted a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife, should go to another village or town and, while there, should not wear it nor give it away, but should instead store it for more than eighteen months, that bhikṣu incurs an offense of wrong-doing. “Ānanda, if a bhikṣu, having accepted a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife, should go to another village or town and, while there, should not wear it nor give it away, but should instead store it for more than nineteen months, that bhikṣu incurs an offense of wrong-doing. “Ānanda, if a bhikṣu, having accepted a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife, should go to another village or town and, while there, should not wear it nor give it away, but should instead store it for more than twenty months, that bhikṣu incurs an offense of wrong-doing. “Ānanda, if a bhikṣu, having accepted a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife, should go to another village or town and, while there, should not wear it nor give it away, but should instead store it for more than twenty-one months, that bhikṣu incurs an offense of wrong-doing. “Ānanda, if a bhikṣu, having accepted a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife, should go to another village or town and, while there, should not wear it nor give it away, but should instead store it for more than twenty-two months, that bhikṣu incurs an offense of wrong-doing. “Ānanda, if a bhikṣu, having accepted a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife, should go to another village or town and, while there, should not wear it nor give it away, but should instead store it for more than twenty-three months, that bhikṣu incurs an offense of wrong-doing. “Ānanda, if a bhikṣu, having accepted a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife, should go to another village or town and, while there, should not wear it nor give it away, but should instead store it for more than twenty-four months, that bhikṣu incurs an offense of wrong-doing. “Ānanda, if a bhikṣu, having accepted a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife, should go to another village or town and, while there, should
(11.1.1’) O Agni, be born; this Aditi here has made her plea. She cooks the *brahmaudana* desiring sons.
May the Seven Seers, the creators of beings, churn you forth here together with progeny.
(11.1.2’) Produce smoke, O bull-like friends; you who are free from guile, direct your speech toward the protection.
(11.1.2.c) This Agni is the conqueror of hostile armies and possesses excellent heroes, he by whom the gods overcame the Dasyus.
2 (11.1.3’) O Agni Jātavedas, you have been born for great heroic power, for the cooking of the *brahmaudana*.
(11.1.3.c) The seven Ṛṣis, the makers of beings, have generated you; bestow upon this woman wealth consisting of all-heroic sons. 3
(11.1.4’) Kindled with fuel, O Agni, be well-kindled; as one who knows, bring the gods worthy of sacrifice here.
(11.1.4.c) Cooking the oblation for them, O Jātavedas, cause this man to ascend to the highest firmament.
(11.1.5’) The portion that was formerly assigned to you threefold—belonging to the gods, the ancestors, and mortals—[that portion...]
(11.1.5.c) "Recognize the portions; I shall divide them among you. He who is the [foremost] of the gods shall carry this across for you.
(11.1.6’) "O Agni, you are powerful, victorious, and overwhelming; bend down the hateful rivals.
This is the measure being measured and already measured; let it make your kinsmen bringers of tribute."
(11.1.7’) Together with thy kinsmen, swell with milk; turn this [skin] upward for great heroic power.
(11.1.7.c) Standing erect, ascend the vault of the firmament, that which they call the heavenly world.
(11.1.8’) May this great earth receive the skin, the goddess Pṛthivī, being well-disposed.
(11.1.8.c) Then may we go to the world of the well-done.
‖8‖ (11.1.9’) Yoke these two pressing-stones as a pair upon the hide; extract the stalks skillfully for the sacrificer.
(11.1.9.c) Striking them out, strike down those who attack us here; lift up the offspring and carry it upward. ‖9‖
(11.1.10’) Take the two stones, O hero, ready in your hand; the gods worthy of sacrifice have come to your sacrifice.
(11.1.10.c) Whatever three boons you choose—those prosperities I shall grant to you here.
{1} (11.1.11’) This is your wisdom, and this is your place of birth; may Aditi, mother of heroes, accept you.
(11.1.11.c) Purify [them] away! Drive off those who attack this [sacrifice]; bestow upon her wealth consisting of all heroic sons.
(11.1.12’) Sit down upon the wooden vessel, O you who are worthy of sacrifice; separate yourselves from the husks.
(11.1.12.c) Through glory, may I surpass all my equals; I cast the feet of the hater beneath my own feet.
(11.1.13’) “O woman, come back quickly from the others! The stall of the waters has mounted you for the sake of bearing [the seed].

Of those [waters], take hold of whichever ones are worthy of sacrifice; having distinguished them, let the wise one leave the others behind. (11.1.14’) “These women have come here, adorning themselves. Arise, O woman, and seize the vigorous [seed]!”
(11.1.14.c) With a good husband and with offspring, O woman rich in progeny, the sacrifice has come to you; take hold of the jar!

(11.1.15’) The portion of strength that was placed for you of old—bring these waters, instructed by the seers! May this sacrifice be for you a finder of the path, a finder of protection, a finder of progeny, fierce, a finder of cattle, and a finder of heroes!
O Agni, the sacrificial pap has mounted thee, the pure and most fervent one; do thou consume it with thy heat.
Let the seers and the gods, having gathered together, partake of this portion; let the most fervent ones consume it according to the seasons.
Let these pure, purified, and bright waters, worthy of sacrifice, flow down upon the pap.
(11.1.17.c) May it grant us offspring and many cattle; may the cooked rice of the well-doer go to the world of the righteous.
(11.1.18’) These grains of rice, the stalks of Soma, are pure through the sacred word (*brahman*), purified by ghee, and worthy of sacrifice.
(11.1.18.c) Enter the waters; let the porridge (*caru*) receive you. Having been cooked, may this [porridge] go to the world of the well-doers. (11.1.18)
Spread wide with great majesty in the world of the well-performed deed, O thousand-backed one!
Grandfathers, fathers, progeny, and offspring—of these fifteen, I am the cooker.
The thousand-backed, hundred-streamed, inexhaustible *brahmaudana* is the path to the gods, leading to heaven.
(11.1.20.c) These I entrust to you; harm them with their offspring, but be gracious to me for the sake of receiving offerings.
(11.1.21’) Rise up upon the altar; increase it with offspring; drive away the demon; grant it long life.
(11.1.21.c) May I surpass all my equals in glory; I cast the feet of my enemies beneath my feet.
Turn back with cattle; turn toward her together with the deities.
Let not the curse nor sorcery reach you; reign without disease in your own field.
Fashioned by the *ṛta*, prepared by the mind, this altar for the *brahmaudana* has been laid out first.
(11.1.23.c) O woman, place the pure shoulder-bone upon it; set the rice-offering there for the gods.

(11.1.24’) This second ladle with handles, which the seven seers, the creators of beings, fashioned from the hands of Aditi—may that ladle, knowing the limbs of the rice-offering, arrange it upon the sacrificial altar.
(11.1.25’) Let the gods sit down near you, the cooked oblation; having emerged from the fire, sit down again with them.

(11.1.25.c) Purified by Soma, sit in the belly; may those of the seers among the Brahmins who consume you not come to harm. ‖25‖ (11.1.26’) O King Soma, bestow recognition upon these men, so that they may sit near you as excellent Brahmins.
(11.1.26.c) I invoke with a favorable call the seers, the descendants of seers, born from austerity, at the *brahmaudana* offering.
(11.1.27’) These pure, purified, and worthy-of-sacrifice women, I set down separately in the hands of the Brahmins.
(11.1.27.c) With whatever desire I sprinkle you here, may Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, grant that for me.
This light of mine is immortal and golden; it is ripe, and this cow of plenty is mine from the field.
This wealth I deposit among the Brahmins; I prepare the path to heaven that leads to the Fathers.
(28) Cast the husks into the fire, into Jātavedas; cast the chaff far away! (29)

(11.1.29.c) We have heard this: such is the portion of the King of the House; and thus we know the allotted share of Nirṛti. (11.1.30’) Know him who exerts himself, who cooks, and who presses the soma; lead him upward onto the path to heaven.
(11.1.30.c) By which he may ascend, reaching that which is supreme—the highest age, the firmament, the loftiest sky. (30) {3}
(11.1.31’) O Adhvaryu, cleanse this face of Babhru; being well-acquainted, prepare a space for the clarified butter.
(11.1.31.c) Anoint all his limbs with ghee; I shall prepare for him the path to heaven that leads among the Fathers.
(11.1.32’) O Babhru, cast away the demon and the strife from these [grains], whoever non-Brahmin sits down near you.
(11.1.32.c) May those who possess the soil, who expand in the east, the descendants of seers, the consumers, not harm me!
32 (11.1.33’) O Odana, I place you among the descendants of seers; there is also a place here for those who are not descendants of seers.
(11.1.33.c) May Agni be my protector, and all the Maruts; may the All-Gods guard the cooked offering! 33
Milking the sacrifice that is ever swelling—the male, the cow, the abode of riches—may we sit beside you with offspring, immortality, long life, and the increase of wealth.
(34) You are the bull; go to heaven and to the seers, the descendants of seers. (35)
(11.1.35.c) Sit in the world of the doers of good deeds; there let our prepared offering be.
(11.1.36’) Gather them together, follow along, O Agni; prepare the paths that lead to the gods.
(11.1.36.c) By means of these good deeds may we follow after the sacrifice standing in the vault of heaven upon the seven-rayed [sun].

(11.1.37’) By that light with which the gods ascended to heaven after cooking the *brahmaudana* for the world of the well-done— (11.1.37.c) by that may we go to the world of the well-done, ascending to the heavenly light, toward the highest firmament. ||37|| {4} (11.2.1’) O Bhava and Śarva, be gracious; do not come against me! O lords of beings, lords of cattle, homage to you both!
(11.2.1.c) Do not let go of our messenger who has come from afar; do not harm us—neither our bipeds nor our quadrupeds.
(11.2.2’) Do not deliver our bodies to the dog or the jackal, nor to the *aliklavas*, the vultures, or those black scavengers that seek carrion.
(11.2.2.c) O Lord of Beasts, let not the flies or the birds find us as their prey.
To your roaring breath, and to those remedies of yours,
O Bhava, we offer homage, O immortal Rudra with a thousand eyes.
We pay homage to you from the east, from above, and from below.
(11.2.4.c) From the height of heaven down to the mid-air, homage to you!
(11.2.5’) To your mouth, O Paśupati; to those eyes of yours, O Bhava; To your skin, to your form, to your appearance, and to you who face us—homage to you! (11.2.5.c)
Homage to your limbs, to your belly, to your tongue, and to your mouth; homage to your teeth and to your sense of smell.
With the weapon-bearing one, with the blue-crested one, with the thousand-eyed one, and with the vigorous steed.
May we not come into conflict with that Rudra, the slayer of half the body.
May Bhava spare us on every side; may Bhava spare us as fire spares the waters.
Let him not strike us; let there be homage to him.
Four times homage to Bhava, eight times to Paśupati—ten times homage to you! These five classes of creatures are distributed by you: cattle, horses, men, goats, and sheep.
The four quarters are yours; the sky is yours, the earth is yours, and this vast intermediate space, O Mighty One, is yours.
(11.2.10.c) All this that breathes upon the earth is possessed of your self. {5} (11.2.11’) Wide is this treasure-chest of yours, the container of wealth, within which are all these worlds.
(11.2.11.c) As such, be gracious to us, O Lord of Cattle; homage be to you! Let the jackals, the overpowering dogs, and the howling, disheveled women stay far away. {11}

(11.2.12’) You carry a golden, green bow, O crested one, that slays a thousand and kills a hundred. The arrow of Rudra, the weapon of the gods, flies forth; homage be to it from whichever direction it comes here. (11.2.13’) Whoever, having attacked, hides himself, O Rudra, desiring to harm you—
(11.2.13.c) You follow after him like the track of one who has been pierced.
(11.2.14’) Bhava and Rudra, joined together and in harmony, both fierce, move about for the sake of heroic power;
homage to them, wherever they may be in this direction. (11.2.14.c) Homage to them, wherever they may be in this direction.
Homage be to you as you come; homage be to you as you go away.
Homage to you, O Rudra, as you stand, and homage to you as you sit. (11.2.15) Homage in the evening, homage in the morning; homage by night, homage by day. (11.2.16)
(11.2.16.c) To Bhava and to Śarva—to both of them I have paid homage.

(11.2.17’) May we not encounter Rudra, the thousand-eyed one, who looks beyond, who shoots forth from the front, the wise one who appears in many forms; may we not meet him as he flickers with his tongue.
(11.2.17.c) May we not encounter him as he flickers with his tongue.
The dark, black, and tawny one, crushing [all], the terrible chariot that strikes down the long-haired ones—may we first encounter him with homage.
(11.2.18) Do not hurl the mortal divine bolt at us; do not be angry with us, O Lord of Cattle; homage to you! (11.2.19)
(11.2.19.c) Shake down your divine branch elsewhere than upon us!
(11.2.20’) Do not harm us; speak for us; choose us; do not be angry. (11.2.20.c) May we not come into conflict with you. {6}
Do not covet our cattle, nor our men, nor our goats and sheep. O fierce one, turn away elsewhere; destroy the offspring of those who offer no oblations.
He whose fever and coughing attack him like the neighing of a stallion, O bull—[let it pass].

(11.2.22.c) It is determined from of old; let there be homage to him! (11.2.23’) He who stands in the intermediate space, firmly established, crushing those who do not sacrifice and those who revile the gods— (11.2.23.c) To him, homage with ten *śakvarī* verses!
To you belong the wild animals, the beasts dwelling in the forest, the swans, the eagles, the birds, and the winged fowl.
O Lord of Beasts, your power resides within the waters; for your growth, the celestial waters flow.
The porpoises, pythons, purīkaya fish, jaṣa fish, and the fish of the deep—over whomsoever you cast [your net] with the *rajas* [fishing line].

(11.2.25.c) For you there is no distance, nor is there any obstruction; O Bhava, you behold everything instantly. From the eastern ocean, you strike down [the foe] in the western ocean. ‖25‖ (11.2.26’) O Rudra, do not afflict us with fever, nor with the *viṣa* disease, nor let us be struck by divine fire.
‖26‖ Cast your lightning bolt elsewhere than upon us! ‖26‖
Bhava rules over heaven; Bhava rules over the earth; Bhava has filled the vast mid-air.
To him be homage from whichever direction he may be here!
O Bhava, be gracious to the sacrificer; for you have become the Lord of Cattle among all beasts.
(11.2.28.c) To him who has faith that "the gods exist," be gracious toward his four-footed and two-footed creatures.

(11.2.29’) Do not harm our great ones, nor our small ones; do not harm those who carry us, nor those who shall carry us. (11.2.29.c) Do not harm our father and mother; O Rudra, do not destroy our own bodies.
(11.2.30’) To Rudra’s dogs from Elabakāra, those who swallow what is not properly consecrated;
(11.2.30.c) to these large-mouthed dogs, I have paid this homage.
(11.2.31’) Homage to you, the noisy ones; homage to you, the long-maned ones.
(11.2.31.c) Homage to those who have been saluted; homage to those who are enjoying together. (11.2.31.e) Homage to you, O divine armies! May there be well-being for us and fearlessness for us. 31.
{7} (11.3.1’) Of that rice-mess, Bṛhaspati is the head and the Brahman is the mouth. 1.

Heaven and Earth are the ears; the Sun and Moon are the two eyes; the Seven Seers are the out-breath and the in-breath. (11.3.2) The pestle is sight; desire is the mortar. (11.3.3) Diti is the winnowing basket;
Aditi is the one who holds the basket. Vāta has winnowed it clean. (11.3.4)
The horses are the grains; the cows are the rice-grains; the gadflies are the husks.
(5) The liver is the chaff; the reed is the cloud.
(6) Dark iron is his flesh; his blood is red. (7)
(11.3.8) Tin is its ash, green its color, and the lotus its fragrance.
(11.3.9) The threshing floor is its vessel; the two wooden plow-shares are its shoulders, and the two poles are its spine.
(11.3.10) The entrails are its collar-bones, and the intestines are its leather straps.

This very earth becomes the cooking-pot for the rice being prepared; the sky is the lid. (11) The furrows are the ribs; the sand is the undigested food in the belly. (12) Truth is the water for washing the hands; the irrigation channels are the sprinkling water. (13)
(11.3.14’) The *kumbhī* pot is placed upon [the fire] with a *ṛc* verse; it is dispatched by the office of the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*).
(11.3.15’) It is encompassed by the *brahman* and carried around with a *sāman*.
(11.3.16’) The *bṛhat* and *rathantara* [sāmans] are the ladle (*darvī*).
The seasons are the cooks; the seasonal deities kindle [the fire].
(18) He kindles the cauldron, the five-holed vessel, as the heated offering.
(19) Through the cooked rice, the words of sacrifice and all the worlds are to be fully satisfied.
(11.3.20) In whom the ocean, the sky, and the earth—the three, both higher and lower—are contained;
(11.3.21) from whose leavings the gods were fashioned, eighty-six in number;
(11.3.22) him, the rice-offering, I ask concerning his great majesty.
One should know that to be the greatness of the rice porridge.
(23) One should not say, "It is not small," nor "It lacks a condiment," nor "This is this and that is that.
(24) One should not speak beyond what the giver intends to bestow. (25)
(11.3.26) The exponents of the Veda say: "Did you eat the rice facing away, or facing toward?
(26) "You ate the rice as 'you' (tvam), and the rice was 'you' (tvām)"—thus [they ask].
(27) If he has eaten it facing away, he says to him: "Your vital breaths will depart from you. (28)
"If you have eaten him facing backward, your out-breaths will desert you"—thus he said to him.
"Neither am I the rice, nor is the rice me," he replied.
"The rice itself has eaten the rice."
Then he said to him, "You have eaten this with another head than that with which the ancient seers ate it;
therefore, your offspring shall die starting from the eldest.
"I have indeed eaten it neither facing downward, nor facing away, nor facing toward me," he replied.
"Then you have eaten him with other two ears than those with which the ancient seers ate him;
therefore, you shall become deaf," he said to him.
"Indeed, I [have eaten him] neither facing downward, nor facing away, nor facing toward me."
"Then you ate it with those other two eyes with which the ancient seers ate it;
you shall become blind," he said to him.
"Indeed, I did not eat it facing downward, nor facing away, nor facing toward me."

Then he said to him, "You have eaten this with another mouth than that with which the ancient seers ate it; your offspring shall die from the mouth. "Indeed, I have not eaten it facing downward, nor facing away, nor facing toward me," he replied.
"Then you ate this with another tongue than that with which the ancient seers ate it;
your tongue shall perish," he said to him. "Indeed, I did not eat it facing downward, nor facing away, nor facing toward me."
"And then you ate him with other teeth, those very teeth with which the ancient seers ate him.
'Your teeth will fall out,' he said to him.
Indeed, I [ate] him neither facing downward, nor facing away, nor facing toward me."
"And then you ate him with other out-breaths and in-breaths, those with which the ancient seers ate him.
[The teacher] says to him: 'Out-breaths and in-breaths will desert you.
But I [ate] him neither facing downward, nor facing away, nor facing toward me."
(11.3.39’) Then he made him eat it with another measure, with that same measure by which the ancient seers had eaten it.
(11.3.39.c) He said to him, "Royal consumption will slay you.
(11.3.39.e) But I [did not eat it] facing downward, nor facing away, nor facing toward me.
Then he said to him, "Eat it from the other side— the same way the ancient seers ate it—
and [he said], 'Lightning will strike you!
But I did not eat it facing downward, nor facing away, nor facing toward me."
Then he ate it with another breast, the one with which the ancient seers had eaten it.
He said to him, "You shall not succeed through agriculture.
Indeed, I [ate] it neither facing downward, nor facing away, nor facing toward me.
(11.3.42’) Then he said to him: “You have eaten this with another belly than that with which the seers of old ate it.
A ‘belly-breaker’ shall kill you. (11.3.42.c) “I do not [see] him as facing toward me, nor away from me, nor toward me,” he said.
Then he said to him, "Eat this with another vessel, the one with which the seers of old ate it;
you shall die in the waters.
He indeed [ate it] neither facing downward, nor facing away, nor facing toward himself.
"Then you ate him with two other thighs—those very thighs with which the seers of old ate him.
'Your thighs shall perish,' he said to him.
Indeed, I [ate him] neither facing this way, nor facing away, nor facing toward me."
Then he said to him, "You shall become lame," regarding those other two kneecaps with which the ancient seers ate this [food]. Indeed,
I have not eaten it facing downward, nor facing away, nor facing toward me.
"Then he said to him, 'Eat from these other two feet with which the ancient seers ate this;
you shall become one who travels much. But I did not eat it facing downward, nor facing away, nor facing toward me."
"Then you ate it with two other toes—those same ones with which the ancient seers ate it.
'A serpent will kill you,' he said to him.
But I did not eat it facing downward, nor facing away, nor facing toward me."
Then he fed him with two other hands— those very hands with which the ancient seers had previously fed him—
and said to him, "You shall kill a Brahmin.
But I [fed him] neither facing me, nor turning away, nor facing backward.
"And then he said to him: 'You have consumed this with another foundation than that upon which the ancient seers consumed it;
lacking a foundation and lacking a support, you shall die.
Indeed, I [have consumed it] neither facing downward, nor facing away, nor facing toward me."
(11.3.49’) This rice-offering is indeed the summit of the sun.
(11.3.51’) He who knows this becomes the world of the sun; he rests upon the summit of the sun.
(11.3.52’) From this very rice-offering, Prajāpati measured out the thirty-three worlds.
He created the sacrifice for the sake of their discernment.
He who becomes a witness to one who knows thus obstructs his own vital breath;
he does not obstruct the vital breath, yet he suffers a total loss.
(11.3.56’) And he is not deprived of everything; before old age, life does not desert him. {10} (11.3.1’) Homage to Prāṇa, under whose control all this is;
who has come into being as the Lord of all, in whom everything is established. {1}
Homage to you, O Prāṇa, for your roar; homage to you for your thunder.
Homage to you, O Prāṇa, for your lightning; homage to you, O Prāṇa, for your rain.
When, O Prāṇa, you roar with your thunder over the plants...
(11.3.3.c) They are impregnated; they conceive embryos, and then many are born.
(11.3.4’) When the breath [of life] cries out to the plants as the season arrives, then everything that exists upon the earth rejoices. (11.3.4.c) 4.

When Prāṇa rained down upon the great earth with rain, the cattle rejoiced at that, saying, "Great indeed shall our prosperity be! (11.3.5) The plants, drenched by Prāṇa, spoke together in unison. (11.3.6)
(11.3.6.c) You have indeed prolonged our life; you have made us all fragrant.
(11.3.7’) Homage be to you as you approach; homage be to you as you depart.
(11.3.7.c) Homage to you, O Prāṇa, as you stand; and homage to you as you sit.

Homage to you, O Prāṇa, as you breathe out; homage be to you as you breathe in. Homage to you as you move away; homage to you as you move toward us. This homage is for you in your entirety. (11.3.9) That which is your dear body, O Prāṇa, that which is your most beloved, O Prāṇa—
(11.3.9.c) Moreover, whatever healing medicine is yours, grant that to us so that we may live.
(11.3.10’) Breath clothes living beings as a father clothes his beloved son;
breath indeed is the lord of all, both of that which breathes and that which does not. (11)
Breath is death; breath is fever; the gods worship breath.
Breath indeed places the speaker of truth in the highest world.
Breath is the Virāj; breath is the Deṣṭrī; all worship breath.
(11.3.12.c) The sun is indeed the out-breath, and the moon is the out-breath; they call the out-breath Prajāpati.
(11.3.13’) Rice and barley are the out-breath and the in-breath; the ox is said to be the out-breath.
(11.3.13.c) For the out-breath is placed in the barley, while rice is said to be the in-breath.
(11.3.14) Within the womb, the person breathes out and breathes in. When you, O Prāṇa, quicken him, then he is born again.
(11.3.15) They call Prāṇa Mātariśvan; indeed, Vāta is called Prāṇa.
(11.3.15.c) In breath, indeed, are the past and the future; in breath, everything is established.
(11.3.16’) The plants born of Atharvan, of Aṅgiras, of the gods, and those born of men—(11.3.16.c) they all spring forth when you, O Breath, quicken them.
When Prāṇa has rained down rain upon the great earth,
the herbs are born, as well as whatever plants there may be. He who knows this Prāṇa of yours, and that in which you are established— ‖17‖‖18‖
(11.3.18.c) May all bring tribute to him in that highest world.
(11.3.19’) Just as all these creatures bring tribute to you, O Prāṇa, so may they bring tribute to him who hears you, O Śuśravas. (11.3.19.c) 19.
The embryo moves within the deities; having come into being, he is born again.
Having become the past, he enters as the father into the son who is yet to be, through his powers.
As the swan rises from the water, he does not lift one foot from it.
(11.3.21.c) For if someone were to uproot that very [wheel], it would exist neither today nor tomorrow;
(11.3.21.e) there would be no night, no day, and it would never dawn.
(11.3.22’) The eight-wheeled [wheel] with its single rim rolls on; the thousand-syllabled one is in front and behind.
(11.3.22.c) With one half he brought forth the entire world; what is that banner which constitutes his other half?
‖22‖ (11.3.23’) To him who rules over this birth of all beings and over all that moves, (11.3.23.c) O Prāṇa, homage be to you, the swift-bowed archer among others! ‖23‖
(11.3.24) May the tireless, wise Prāṇa, who rules over all this birth and over everything that moves, abide within me through the sacred word (brahman).
(11.3.25) Standing upright, he remains awake while others sleep; indeed, he does not fall prone.

(11.3.25.c) No one at all heard him sleeping while others were asleep. (11.3.26’) O Prāṇa, do not turn away from me; there shall be no other than you for me. Like the embryo of the waters, for the sake of life, O Prāṇa, I bind you fast within me. {13}
The student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) moves through both worlds, warm; in him the gods become of one mind.
He supports the earth and the sky; he satisfies his teacher with ascetic fervor (*tapas*). All the fathers and the divine folk, the various gods, follow after the student of sacred knowledge.

(11.3.2.c) Thirty-three hundred and six thousand Gandharvas followed after him; he satisfies all those gods with his ascetic heat. (11.3.3’) The teacher, initiating him, makes the religious student an embryo within himself. He carries him in his belly for three nights; when he is born, the gods assemble to behold him.
(11.3.4’) This earth is the fuel-stick, and the sky is the second; he fills the intermediate space with the fuel-stick.
(11.3.4.c) The student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*), by means of the fuel-stick, the girdle, toil, and austerity, fulfills the worlds. 4.
(11.3.5’) Born first from the *brahman*, the student of sacred knowledge stood firm through austerity, wearing the *gharma* [vessel]. 5.

(11.3.5.c) From that was born the Brāhmaṇa, the Brahman as the eldest, along with all the gods and immortality. ||5|| (11.3.6’) The student of sacred knowledge goes forth, kindled by the sacrificial fuel, wearing a black garment, consecrated, with long hair and beard.
(11.3.6.c) Having grasped the worlds, he immediately goes from the eastern ocean to the northern one, repeatedly traversing them. ||6||
The Vedic student, generating the sacred word (*brahman*), [produced] the waters, the world, Prajāpati, Parameṣṭhin, and Virāj.
Having become an embryo in the womb of immortality, and having indeed become Indra, he struck down the Asuras.
The Teacher fashioned both these expanses of space—the broad and deep earth and the sky.
(11.3.8.c) The student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) protects them through his ascetic fervor (*tapas*); in him the gods become of one mind.
(11.3.9’) The student of sacred knowledge first brought forth this earth, the broad world (*pṛthivī*), and the sky as alms.
Having made these two into fuel-sticks (*samidh*), he worships them; in them all beings are established.
One is near, the other is beyond the back of heaven; two treasures are deposited in secret within the Brahmin.
The student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) guards them through austerity; the knower of the Veda makes that his own entirely.
One is near, the other is from here on earth; these two fires meet together within the two intermediate spaces of the atmosphere.
(11.3.11.c) Their rays rest upon those two firm ones; the student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) stands upon them through his ascetic fervor (*tapas*).
(11.3.12’) Roaring, thundering, ruddy, white-horned, with a great tail, he has spread along the earth.
(11.3.12.c) The student of sacred knowledge pours his seed upon the height of the earth; by it the four quarters of space live.
In fire, in the sun, in the moon, in Mātariśvan, and in the waters, the student places the fuel-stick.
Their flames move separately through the clouds; their clarified butter is man, their rain is water.
The teacher is Death, Varuṇa, Soma, the plants, and milk.
(11.3.14.c) Having become living beings, they brought this light back;
||14|| (11.3.15’) Having become the teacher, Varuṇa made the ghee his own exclusive possession, whatever he desired from Prajāpati.
(11.3.15.c) That the religious student gave back to himself as Mitra from his own being. ||15||
The teacher is a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*); the student of sacred knowledge is Prajāpati.
Prajāpati shines forth as the sovereign (*virāj*); the sovereign became the self-controlled Indra.
By means of the practice of sacred knowledge and austerity, the king protects his kingdom.
(11.3.17.c) Through the practice of celibacy, the teacher seeks a student. (11.3.18’) Through the practice of celibacy, a maiden finds a young man as her husband.
(11.3.18.c) Through the practice of celibacy, the ox desires fodder; so does the horse.
(11.3.19’) By means of the student’s vow and austerity, the gods struck down death;
(11.3.19.c) indeed, Indra by means of the student’s vow brought back the light from the gods.
‖19‖ (11.3.20’) The plants, the past and the future, day and night, and the lord of the forest—
The year together with the seasons was born as those who practice sacred study.
(11.3.20.c) Terrestrial and celestial animals, both wild and domestic—those that are wingless and those that are winged—they were all born as those who practice sacred study. (11.3.21.c)
Each of all these subjects of Prajāpati bears vital breaths within himself;
Brahman protects them all, which have been brought together in the student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*).
This, the consecrated essence of the gods, moves resplendent, never mounted upon by others.
(11.3.23.c) From that was born the Brāhmaṇa, the Brahman as the eldest, and all the gods together with immortality.
(11.3.24’) The religious student bears the shining Brahman; in him all the gods are gathered together.
(11.3.24.c) Producing out-breath, in-breath, and diffused breath, he produced speech, mind, heart, the Brahman, and wisdom.
(11.3.25’) Bestow upon us sight, hearing, and glory; food, seed, blood, and the belly.
||25|| (11.3.26’) Forming these [limbs], the religious student stood performing austerities upon the surface of the waters, practicing heat in the ocean.
(11.3.26.c) Having bathed there, he shone greatly upon the earth—tawny and reddish-brown. ||26|| {16}
(11.6.1) We invoke Agni, the lords of the forest, the herbs, and the plants;
Indra, Bṛhaspati, and Sūrya—may they deliver us from distress.
(11.6.2) We invoke King Varuṇa, Mitra, Viṣṇu, and Bhaga.
We invoke Aṃśa and Vivasvant; may they deliver us from distress.
We invoke the god Savitṛ, Dhātṛ, and Pūṣan;
we invoke Tvaṣṭṛ, the foremost; may they deliver us from distress.
We invoke the Gandharvas and Apsarases, the two Aśvins, and Brahmaṇaspati;
may the god named Aryaman release us from distress.
We invoke both Day and Night, and both Sūrya and Candramas.
(11.6.5.c) We invoke all the Ādityas; may they deliver us from distress.
(11.6.6’) We invoke Vāta, Parjanya, the intermediate space, and likewise the quarters; we invoke all the regions as well; may they deliver us from distress.
(11.6.7) May Day and Night, and likewise Dawn, release me from the curse;
may the god Soma release me, whom they call the Moon.
(11.6.8) May the domestic and celestial animals, as well as the wild beasts of the forest, [release me].
(11.6.8.c) We speak to the birds, the winged ones; may they release us from distress.
(11.6.9’) We speak this to Bhava and Śarva, and to Rudra who is Paśupati; whatever arrows belong to them, may those be ever auspicious for us.
(11.6.9.c) May those arrows which we know to be theirs be ever propitious for us.
We invoke the sky, the stars, the earth, the yakṣas, and the mountains;
the oceans, the rivers, and the ponds—may they release us from distress.
We invoke the seven seers, the waters, the divine goddesses, and Prajāpati.
(11.6.11.c) We address the ancestors, of whom Yama is the chief: may they release us from distress. 11.
(11.6.12’) Those gods who dwell in heaven and those who dwell in the intermediate space, and those powerful ones who have taken refuge upon the earth—may they release us from distress. 12.
The Ādityas, the Rudras, the Vasus, the gods in heaven, the Atharvans, the wise Aṅgirases— may they deliver us from distress.
We invoke the sacrifice, the sacrificer, the Ṛg-verses, the Sāman-chants, and the healing remedies.
(11.6.14.c) We proclaim the *yajus* formulas and the *hotṛ*-priests’ offices; may they deliver us from distress.
(11.6.15’) We proclaim the five kingdoms of plants, of which *soma* is the best: *darbha*, *bhaṅga*, barley, and *sahas*;
may they deliver us from distress. (11.6.15.c) May *darbha*, *bhaṅga*, barley, and *sahas* deliver us from distress.
We invoke the *arāyas*, the *rakṣases*, the serpents, the *puṇyajanas*, and the *pitṛs*;
we invoke the one hundred and one deaths—may they release us from distress.
We invoke the seasons, the lords of the seasons, the seasonal periods, and the years.
May the years and the months release us from distress.
(11.6.17.c) O gods, rise up from the south, from behind, and toward the east;
O Śakra and all you Viśvedevas, coming together from the front and from the north, may you release us from distress. (11.6.18)
(11.6.19’) We address all the gods, who are true to their promises and who increase the cosmic order (*ṛta*):
together with all their consorts, may they release us from distress.
(11.6.20’) We address all the gods, who are true to their promises and who increase the cosmic order.
(11.6.20.c) May they, together with all their wives, release us from distress.
(11.6.21’) We speak to the Being, the Lord of Beings, and to him who is the ruler of creatures;
(11.6.21.c) may all beings, having come together, release us from distress.
(11.6.22’) The five divine quarters, the twelve gods who are the seasons—
those which are the fangs of the year, may they ever be auspicious to us.
(11.6.23’) That immortal medicine which Mātali knows, acquired by means of his chariot—
Indra caused that to enter into the waters; O waters, grant that healing remedy!
In the *ucchiṣṭa* are name and form; in the *ucchiṣṭa* the world is placed.
In the *ucchiṣṭa* are Indra and Agni; within it all is contained.
In the remnant are heaven and earth; in it all beings are contained.
In the remnant are the waters and the ocean; therein the moon and the wind are placed.
Both the existent and the non-existent are in the remnant—both death, strength, and Prajāpati.
(11.6.3.c) The Ucchiṣṭa is to be honored; in it are contained the Vraś and the Draś, and in it is Śrī.
(11.6.4’) Dṛḍha, Dṛṃha, Sthira, Nya, Brahma, and the ten creators of the universe—(11.6.4.c) like a wheel centered upon its nave, all the deities are supported within the Ucchiṣṭa.

The *Ṛc*, the *Sāman*, the *Yajus*, the *Ucchiṣṭa*, the *Udgītha*, the *Prastuta*, and the *Stuta*—the *Hiṅkāra*, the *Ucchiṣṭa*, the tone (*svara*) of the *Sāman*, and its *Medi*: may all that be in me.
(5) The *Aindrāgna*, the *Pāvamāna*, the *Mahānāmnīs*, and the *Mahāvrata*. (6)
(11.6.6.c) Within the remnant of the sacrifice are its limbs, like a fetus within a mother.
(11.6.7’) The Rājasūya, the Vājapeya, the Agniṣṭoma, and that Adhvara;
(11.6.7.c) the Arka and Aśvamedha are in the remnant—the most exhilarating Jīvabarhis.
The establishment of the sacred fires, as well as initiation, the granting of desires, and the meters;
the sacrifices and the sacrificial sessions—all these are contained within the remnant.
The fire-oblation, faith, the *vaṣaṭ*-call, the vow, and asceticism.
(11.6.9.c) The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), the sacrifice (*iṣṭa*), and the charitable work (*pūrta*) are all contained within the remnant (*ucchiṣṭa*).

(11.6.10.a) The one-night rite, the two-night rite, the *sadyaḥkrī*, the *prakrī*, and the *ukthya*—(11.6.10.c) these, along with what is woven and what is deposited, are known through knowledge as the subtle parts of the sacrifice within the remnant. {19}
The four-night rite, the five-night rite, and the six-night rite—both together;
the sixteen-fold rite and the seven-night rite—all these sacrifices established in immortality were born from the Residue.
The *pratīhāra*, the *nidhana*, and that which is the *viśvajit* and the *abhijit*.
The *sāhna* and *atirātra* sacrifices are in the remnant; the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) is also contained therein.
(12) Truthfulness, conciliation, security, self-satisfaction, vigor, immortality, and force—(13) all desires are directed toward the remnant; through desire, they have been satisfied. (13)

The nine earths and the oceans rest upon the *ucchiṣṭa* of heaven; the sun shines within that *ucchiṣṭa*, and day and night are likewise contained therein. The *upahavya* sacrifice, the *viṣūvant*, and those sacrifices hidden in the secret cave—[all these are in me].
The supporter, the remnant of all, the father of the progenitor, sustains [the world].
(11.6.15.c) The father, the remnant of the progenitor, the grandson of *asu*, the grandfather—he dwells as the ruler of all, the bull upon the earth, transcending all obstacles. (11.6.16)
Order, truth, ascetic heat, dominion, toil, righteousness, and action;
the past and the future, vigor in the remnant, fortune, and strength in power;
prosperity, vital force, impulse, the ruling class, the kingdom, and the six expanses.
The year, the *ucchiṣṭa*, the *iḍā*, the *praiṣas*, the cups, and the oblation;
(18) the *caturhotṛ* formulas, the *āprīs*, the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices, and the *nīvits*;
in the *ucchiṣṭa* are the sacrifices, the *hotrā* offices, the animal sacrifices, and the *iṣṭis*. (19)
The half-months and the months, the seasonal periods together with the seasons;
the noisy waters upon the remnant, the thunder, and the great hearing. Pebbles, sand, stones, herbs, creepers, and grasses.
The clouds, lightning, and rain are contained within the *ucchiṣṭa*.
Success, attainment, completion, pervasion, greatness, and growth;
exceeding attainment and prosperity—these are placed, deposited, and established within the *ucchiṣṭa*.
Whatever breathes with breath and whatever sees with the eye—all these were born from the Residue; the gods in heaven are supported in heaven.
The *ṛc*s, the *sāman*s, the meters, the *purāṇa* along with the *yajus*—all were born from the Residue.

(11.6.24.c) From the *ucchiṣṭa* were born all the gods who dwell in heaven. (11.6.25’) In-breath and out-breath, sight and hearing, as well as non-decay and decay— (11.6.25.c) from the *ucchiṣṭa* were born all these; the gods in heaven who dwell in heaven.
Ānandas, modas, pramudas, and those who are abhimodas and mudas—
all these gods dwelling in heaven were born from Ucchiṣṭa.
So too were the gods, the ancestors, human beings, and the gandharvas and apsarases.

(11.6.27.c) From the remains were born all the gods who dwell in heaven. {21} (11.6.1’) When Manyu brought home his wife from the house of Saṃkalpa— Who were the kinsmen? Who were the suitors? And who was the eldest suitor? ||1||
Austerity and action both existed within the great ocean; they were the suitors for her hand, and Brahmā became the suitor of highest rank. Ten gods were born together from the gods in ancient times.
(11.6.3.c) Whoever indeed should know them directly, he may today speak with great authority.
(11.6.4’) In-breath and out-breath, sight and hearing, that which is imperishable and that which is perishable, (11.6.4.c) Vyāna and udāna, speech and mind— these, O winds, bring about our intention.
The seasons were yet unborn, as were Dhātṛ and Bṛhaspati;
at that time, Indra, Agni, and the Aśvins—whom did they worship as their eldest?
Both austerity and ritual action existed within the great ocean.
(11.6.6.c) From ritual action, austerity was born; therefore, they venerate that as the eldest.
(11.6.7’) That which was the primordial earth, which those who possess direct knowledge know—verily, he who would know it by its name might consider himself a knower of antiquity.
(11.6.7.c) Verily, he who would know that by its name might consider himself a knower of antiquity.

From where was Indra born? From where Soma? From where was Agni born? From where did Tvaṣṭṛ come into being? From where was Dhātṛ born? (11.6.8–9) From Indra came Indra; from Soma came Soma; from Agni came Agni.
Tvaṣṭṛ was born from Tvaṣṭṛ; from Dhātṛ he was born.
Those ten gods who were born from you before the [other] gods—having given a world to their sons, in what world do they dwell? {22}
(11.6.11’) When he brought together hair, bone, sinew, flesh, and marrow, and having fashioned a body with feet, into which world did he enter?
(11.6.11.c) From where did he bring the hair, from where the sinew, and from where the bones? ||11||
(11.6.12.c) Whence did the limbs, the joints, the marrow, and the flesh come to me?
12 (11.6.13’) Those gods who gathered the constituent parts are named the *saṃsic* (the pourers together).
Having poured everything together, the gods entered into the mortal Puruṣa. 13
The thighs, the feet, the kneecaps, the head, the hands, and then the face;
the spine, the breasts, and the sides—what seer assembled all that together?
(11.6.14) The head, the hands, and then the face, the tongue, the neck, and the vertebrae. (11.6.15)
(11.6.15.c) Covering all that with skin, the Great One joined it together.
(11.6.16’) When that great body lay there, joined together by the seam,
who brought the color to it so that it shines today?
All the gods learned [this], and the virtuous bride understood it;
she who is the wife of the Lord of Power brought her own form into this [new] state.
When Tvaṣṭṛ pierced [her], he who is higher than Tvaṣṭṛ [did so].
Having made the mortal man their dwelling, the gods entered him. (11.6.18.c) Sleep, lethargy, ruin, and the deities named Sins—old age, baldness, and graying hair—entered his body. (11.6.19.c)

Theft, evil-doing, and sin, as well as truth, sacrifice, and great glory— strength, dominion, and vital force entered into the body. Prosperity and adversity, those things that are gifts and those that are not, [all entered into it].
All forms of hunger and thirst entered the body;
(21) both blame and praise, as well as "yes" and "no," and faith, sacrificial gifts, and lack of faith entered the body. (22)
Knowledge and ignorance, and whatever else is to be taught—
the *brahman* entered the body as the *ṛc*, the *sāman*, and the *yajus*.
Joy, delight, gladness, and all forms of rapture and exultation;

(11.6.24.c) Laughter, the *nariṣṭa* cries, and dances entered into the body. (11.6.25’) And whatever utterances, lamentations, and whispered conversations there were—all these entered the entire body, whether they were unyoked, joined in motion, or yoked. (11.6.25)
In-breath and out-breath, sight and hearing, that which is indestructible and that which is destructible, diffused breath and upward breath, speech and mind— these move through the body.
Blessings and commands, instructions and distinctions— whatever they may be.

(11.6.27.c) All thoughts and intentions entered into the body. (11.6.28’) Those waters which are of the earth and those of the dwelling, the swift and the miserable—those bright, gross waters settled into the loathsome [womb]. (11.6.28.c) Those bright, gross waters settled into the loathsome [womb]. (11.6.28.c) Those bright, gross waters settled into the loathsome [womb]. Having made the bones the fuel, the gods established the waters upon those eight; having made the semen the clarified butter, they entered into Puruṣa.
Those waters and those deities, together with Virāj and Brahman—‖29‖
(11.6.30.c) Brahman entered the body; Prajāpati [resided] within the body.
(11.6.31’) The Sun [took] the eye, and Vāta the breath; they distributed these among the Person. (11.6.31.c) Then the gods bestowed his other self upon Agni.
Therefore, the wise man indeed regards this person as Brahman;
for all the deities abide within him, like cows in a cow-pen.
Through the first stroke of death, he goes forth in three directions in every way.
(11.6.33.c) Here he goes with one, there he goes with one; here he rests with one.
(11.6.34’) Within the swelling waters, the body has been placed. (11.6.34.c) Within that, there is vigor; therefore it is called "vigor-filled" (*śavas*). {24}
(11.6.1’) Those arms, those arrows, and the powers of the bows;
(11.6.1.c) the swords, the axes, the weapons, and whatever intention is in the heart— (11.6.1.e) all that, O Arbudi, you must make visible to our enemies, and show them our noble wives! ‖1‖
(11.6.2’) Arise and gird yourselves, O you divine folk, you who are our friends!
May those who are our friends, O Arbudi, be watched over and protected by you.
(11.6.3’) Arise! Seize them with the seizing-noose and the binding-noose!
(11.6.3.c) O Arbudi, strike down the armies of our enemies!
(11.6.4’) The god named Arbudi and Nyarbudi, who are lords— (11.6.4.c) By whom the intermediate space and this great earth are encompassed.
(11.6.4.e) Following that victory won by those two, Indramedi, I advance with my army.
(11.6.5’) Arise, O Arbudi, you who belong to the divine host, together with your army! Shattering the army of our enemies, surround them with your coils.
Beholding the seven noble *nyarbudas* that have been born,
arise with all of them and with your army when the clarified butter has been offered.
Let her who strikes back, whose face is tearful, and whose ears are small, cry out.
(11.6.7.c) With disheveled hair, when a man is slain—O Arbudi, it is at your bidding!
(11.6.8’) Dragging away the *karūkara* while longing in her heart for her son, she seeks her husband, her brother, and even her own kin—O Arbudi, it is at your bidding! (11.6.8.c) 8.
Let the *aliklava*, the *jāṣkamada*, the vultures, the hawks, the winged birds, the crows,
and the fowls find satisfaction among the enemies as they look upon them, O Arbudi, when they have been torn apart by you.
Furthermore, let every beast of prey, the fly, and the worm find satisfaction.
(11.6.10.c) Upon the human corpse, O Arbudi, you have struck!
10 (11.6.11’) Seize them, crush them—O Nyarbudi, seize their out-breath and in-breath!
(11.6.11.c) Let the whistling sounds of their sighs gather upon the enemies, making them visible as they are struck by you, O Arbudi! 11
Make them tremble; let them be struck with fear; strike down the enemies! With wide-reaching arms and hooks, pierce the enemies, O Arbudi!
Let their arms be confounded, and whatever intention or thought is in their hearts.

(11.6.13.c) Let nothing whatsoever remain of them when you have struck them down, O Arbudi! (11.6.14’) Striking one another, they run together, beating their breasts and their faces; with disheveled hair and weeping, they do so when a man has been slain, when you have struck him down, O Arbudi!

The Apsarases who possess dogs, the Rūpakās, and Arbudi—[all those] who lick at the inside of the vessel, the devouring one who seeks what is ill-placed: O Arbudi, make all of them visible to our
