(11.6.16’) Upon the *khadūra*, the *adhicaṅkrama*, the *kharvikā*, and the *kharvavāsinī*;
those who are noble and hidden, the *gandharvas* and *apsarases*, the serpents, the *itarajanas*, and the *rakṣases*.
(11.6.17’) Those with four tusks, with yellowish-white teeth, with testicles like jars, and with blood upon their faces.
(11.6.17.c) Those who are well-practiced and those who are overbearing.
(11.6.18’) O Arbudi, cause those enemies' streams to tremble!
(11.6.18.c) May Jaya and Jiṣṇu, who delight in Indra, conquer the enemies.
Completely overwhelmed, crushed, and slain—let the enemy lie at Nyarbuda.
Let the victorious ones, whose tongues are fire and whose crests are smoke, go forth with their army.
With that [army], let Indra slay the very best of those who have been driven away by Arbuda.
(11.6.20.c) Let the Lord of Might [overcome] my enemies; let not one among them escape.
(11.6.21’) Let their hearts burst open; let their life-breath rise upward.
Let dryness of mouth seize the enemies, and not those who are my friends. (11.6.21)

Those who are wise and those who are unwise, those who are turned away and those who are deaf, those who are hornless through darkness and those who are clothed in skins— O Arbudi, make all of them visible to your enemies, and show forth the noble ones.
May Arbudi and Triṣandhi pierce through our enemies,
so that we, O Indra, slayer of Vṛtra, Lord of Might, may destroy these foes by the thousands.
[23] The lords of the forest, the products of the forest, the herbs, and the climbing plants—
(11.6.24.c) Gandharvas, Apsarases, serpents, gods, holy folk, and ancestors—
(11.6.24.e) all of them, O Arbudi, make visible to the enemies, and show forth the noble ones!
(11.6.25’) Over you, O Maruts, is the god Āditya, the Lord of Prayer (Brahmaṇaspati).
(11.6.25.c) Indra and Agni, Dhātṛ, Mitra, and Prajāpati—may they be your lords;
(11.6.25.e) may the seers make you their lords, O Arbudi, as you gaze upon our enemies when they have been struck down by you.
(11.6.26’) O you who are the lords of them all, arise and gird yourselves! You, O divine folk, are the allies.
(11.6.26.c) Having won this battle, take your stand according to the light.
{27} (11.10.1’) Arise! Bind yourselves together! O noble ones, with your banners raised, pursue the serpents, the common folk, the *rakṣas* demons, and the enemies. {1}
I know your sovereignty, O Triṣandhi, together with your ruddy banners.
Those who are in the intermediate space, those in heaven, and those who are on earth—
let those ill-named ones wait upon the mind of Triṣandhi.
With iron mouths, needle-mouths, and likewise with mouths like the *vikaṅkata* wood,
let the flesh-eaters, swift as the wind, seize the enemies with the three-jointed thunderbolt.
O Jātavedas, Aditya, place within [the fire] many corpses.
(11.10.4.c) May this army of Trisandhi remain well-satisfied and under my control! (11.10.5’) Arise, O Arbudi, you who belong to the divine host, together with your army!
This offering is presented for you; it is the beloved oblation of Trisandhi. (11.10.5.c) 5.
Let this four-footed arrow, with white feet, strike together;
O Kṛtyā, become three-jointed along with your army against our enemies.
Let the smoke-eyed one fall down, and let the short-eared one shriek.
When Triṣandhi was conquered by his army, let the banners be crimson.
(7) Let the winged birds that move in the atmosphere and those that roam in heaven depart.
Let the beasts of prey, the flies, the raw-flesh eaters, the vultures, and the scavengers seize [the corpse] and tear at the carcass. (8)

(11.10.9) The alliance which you have established with Indra and with Bṛhaspati, O Bṛhaspati—by that alliance with Indra, I summon all the gods here; let them conquer from here, and let me conquer from there.
(11.10.10) Bṛhaspati Āṅgirasa and the seers sharpened by sacred knowledge.
Resorting to the three-jointed weapon, the destroyer of the Asuras, which is celestial;
by means of which that Sun is protected and both Indra and [the other] remain secure—
the gods distributed the three-jointed [weapon] for the sake of vigor and strength.

By means of this oblation, the gods conquered all the worlds— Bṛhaspati Āṅgirasa, who poured forth that thunderbolt, the weapon that destroys the Asuras. Bṛhaspati Āṅgirasa poured forth that thunderbolt, the weapon that destroys the Asuras.
(11.10.13.c) With that, O Bṛhaspati, I smear that army; I slay the enemies with my might.
(11.10.14’) All the gods come forth who partake of the *vaṣaṭ*-offered oblation; enjoy this offering, conquer here and conquer there!
(11.10.14.c) Enjoy this offering, conquer here and conquer there!
(11.10.15’) May all the gods come hither; the oblation of Triṣandhi is dear.
(11.10.15.c) Guard the great covenant by which the Asuras were conquered in the beginning.
(11.10.16’) May Vāyu bend the arrow-tips of our enemies.
(11.10.16.c) May Indra shatter many of these; let them not be able to fix their arrow.
(11.10.16.e) May Āditya destroy their weapon; may the Moon close the path of him who has not yet arrived. 16.
(11.10.17’) If they have fled to the strongholds of the gods, they have made the *brahman* their armor.
Whatever they have whispered as a protection for the body and a safeguard around it—make all that sapless.
17 Driving away the flesh-eaters and Death as your domestic priest, O Triṣandhi, go forth with your army; conquer your enemies and advance! 18
O Triṣandhi, with your darkness, surround the enemies on all sides;
let not one among them escape, who have been driven away by the speckled butter.
Let the white-footed [bird] fly together against those enemies, striking down their ranks.
(11.10.20.c) Let these great armies today crush the enemies in their thousands.
{29} (11.10.21’) O Arbudi, strike down the bewildered enemies; slay the best of them one by one. (11.10.21.c) Slay them with this army!
Whether the enemy be armored or unarmored, whether he be upon the battlefield or not,
let him lie struck down by the snares of the bowstring and the snares of armor, and by the path of the chariot.
Whether they be those who wear mail or those who do not, and whatever enemies there be who are armored— let them all fall.
(11.10.23.c) Let dogs devour all those slain by Arbuda upon the earth.

(11.10.24’) Those who were chariot-warriors and those who were without chariots, those who were foot-soldiers and those who were horsemen—let vultures, hawks, and winged birds devour them all when they are slain. (11.10.24.c) Let them all devour those slain ones. 24.
Let the enemy army lie in battle with a thousand corpses,
slaughtered and torn apart by the birds of prey.
Let the evil-minded one, pierced in his vital organs, wailing as he lies crushed, be devoured by the Suparṇas.
(11.10.26.c) May Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, strike with his three-jointed thunderbolt that enemy who seeks to fight against this oblation of ours directed westward.

(11.10.27’) May Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, strike with his three-jointed thunderbolt that [oblation] which the gods attend to and which is never subject to failure. (11.10.27.c) With that, may Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, strike with his three-jointed thunderbolt. (30)
Truth, the vast, the mighty Law, consecration, austerity, sacred formulation, and sacrifice sustain the earth.
May she, the mistress of what has been and what is to be, the earth, grant us a wide world.
Unconfined in the midst of human beings, she whose heights, slopes, and plains are many and level.
(12.1.2.c) May the earth, which bears for us herbs of manifold potency, spread out for us and grant us prosperity.

(12.1.3’) Upon whom the ocean and the Sindhu river, and upon whom the waters and the cultivated fields have come into being; (12.1.3.c) Upon whom all this that breathes, moves, and stirs finds its life—may that Earth grant us the first draught.
(12.1.4’) She whose four quarters are the earth, in whom the food of the ploughmen came into being;
she who bears the many things that breathe and move—may that Earth bestow upon us cattle and also food.
(12.1.5’) In whom the men of old strode forth, in whom the gods overcame the Asuras.
(12.1.5.c) May the Earth bestow upon us fortune and splendor—the source of cattle, horses, and birds.
(12.1.6’) The all-sustaining, treasure-bearing foundation, golden-breasted, the resting place of the world;
(12.1.6.c) may that Earth, bearing Vaiśvānara Agni, with Indra as her bull, grant us wealth.
(12.1.7) That earth, the broad ground, which the gods guard vigilantly at all times without sleep— may she yield for us what is dear and sweet, and may she sprinkle us with splendor.
(12.1.8) She who was the water upon the ocean in the beginning, whom the wise pursued by means of their creative powers (*māyā*).
(12.1.8.c) She whose heart, in the highest heaven, is the immortal covered by truth upon the earth—
(12.1.8.e) may that Earth bestow upon us brilliance and strength in the supreme kingdom.
8 (12.1.9’) In whom the waters flow together in a common course, day and night pouring forth without fail—
(12.1.9.c) May that Earth, yielding many streams, milk forth for us nourishment; may she likewise sprinkle us with splendor.
(12.1.10’) She whom the Aśvins measured out, upon whom Viṣṇu strode, and whom Indra, the Lord of Might, made for himself free from enemies.
(12.1.10.e) May that Earth, our mother, release her milk for me, as for her son. ‖10‖ {1} (12.1.11’) May your mountains and snowy peaks, and your forest, O Earth, be pleasant to us.
(12.1.11.c) [I take refuge in] the brown, the black, the ruddy, the multiform, the firm Earth, the Pṛthivī protected by Indra.
(12.1.11.e) Unconquered, unslain, unhurt, I have stood firm upon the earth.
(12.1.12’) That which is your middle, O Earth, and that which is your center, and those strengths that have arisen from your body—bestow those upon us;
flow over us. The Earth is the mother, I am the son of the Earth; Parjanya is the father; may he indeed protect us. (12)
On her they enclose the altar-ground; on her the Viśvakarman-sages perform the sacrifice.
On her, the earth, the sacrificial posts are erected—bright and upright—before the oblations.
May that Earth, ever increasing, cause us to prosper. 13.1.13e–f.
(12.1.14’) Whoever hates us, O Earth, whoever attacks us, whoever seeks to harm us with his mind or with a weapon—(12.1.14.c) deliver him over to us, O Earth, you who have been made so from of old!
(12.1.15’) Born from you, mortals move upon you; you support the two-footed and the four-footed.

(12.1.15.c) O Earth, these five human races belong to you—to those mortals the immortal light, as the rising sun spreads it with his rays. ‖15‖ (12.1.16’) May they milk for us all our offspring together; O Earth, bestow upon me the honey of speech. ‖16‖ The mother of all herbs, the steadfast Earth, the broad ground, supported by the cosmic order. ‖17‖
May we evermore follow after that which is auspicious and pleasant.
(17) Great is your dwelling place; you have become great. Great is your surge, your movement, and your trembling. Great Indra protects you with vigilance. (18)
(12.1.18.e) O Earth, cause us to shine forth, like the appearance of gold; let no one whatsoever hate us.
‖18‖ (12.1.19’) Agni is in the earth, in the plants; the waters bear Agni; Agni is in the stones.
(12.1.19.c) Agni is within men, and there are Agnis in the cows and in the horses. ‖19‖
Agni shines from heaven; the vast mid-air belongs to Agni, the god.
Mortals kindle Agni, the bearer of oblations, who loves clarified butter.
Clad in fire, with dark knees, may the Earth make me radiant and sharpened.
Upon the earth they offer to the gods the sacrifice, the oblation well-prepared;
upon the earth mortals live by means of *svadhā*, their food.
May that Earth grant us breath and long life; may the broad Earth make me reach old age.‖22‖
(12.1.23) That fragrance which has arisen from you, O Earth, which the plants bear and which the waters hold;
that fragrance which the Gandharvas and Apsarases have shared—by means of that, make me fragrant; let no one whatsoever hate us.
(12.1.24) That fragrance of yours which entered the lotus, which they gathered together at the wedding of Sūryā.

(12.1.24.c) O immortal Earth, [take] the fragrance first; by that, make me fragrant. Let no one at all hate us. ‖24‖ (12.1.25’) That fragrance of yours which is among men, among women and men, which is fortune and splendor;
(12.1.25.c) that which is in horses, in heroes, and that which is in wild beasts as well as in elephants—
(12.1.25.e) Whatever splendor there is in the maiden and in the earth, with that unite us; let no one whatsoever hate us.
‖25‖ (12.1.26’) Stone, earth, rock, dust—that earth is firmly established and supported. (12.1.26.c) To her, the golden-breasted Earth, I have paid homage. ‖26‖
Upon whom the trees of the forest stand firm forever;
we call upon that Earth, the all-sustaining, the firmly established.
||27|| Whether rising up, or sitting, standing, or moving forward—
(12.1.28.c) May we not stumble upon the earth with our right and left feet.
‖28‖ (12.1.29’) I address the wide-spreading earth, the patient ground that has grown great through sacred knowledge (*brahman*).
O Earth, may we sit down upon you, who bear strength, nourishment, and a portion of food, and who are rich in clarified butter (*ghṛta*). ‖29‖
(12.1.30’) May pure waters flow over our bodies; him who has settled upon what is displeasing to us, him we cast down. With the purifier, O Earth, I cleanse myself.
(30) (12.1.31’) Those quarters of yours that face the east, those that face the north, those of yours, O Earth, that are below and those behind—
(12.1.31.c) May they be pleasant for me as I move about; may I not fall down while resting upon this world.
(12.1.32’) Do not push us from behind, nor from the front, nor from above, nor from below. (12.1.32.c) O Earth, be auspicious to us! Let not highwaymen find us; drive far away the weapon of death.

(12.1.33) As long as I gaze upon you, O Earth, with the sun as my companion, so long may my sight not fail me through each succeeding year. (12.1.34) When lying down, I turn toward my right side, O Earth; when supine, I lie upon you facing upward; and when on our backs, we rest against you with our ribs.
Do not harm us there, O Earth, you who receive all things.
(34) Whatever of yours I dig up, O Earth, may that grow back quickly;
do not let me strike your vital parts, O seeker of forms, nor let me pierce your heart. (35)
(12.1.36) Summer, O Earth, is yours; the rains, autumn, winter, the cool season, and spring—these seasons are ordained for you as your years. May day and night milk for us, O Pṛthivī.
(12.1.37) You who glide along, leaving behind the serpent, you who are free from wild beasts—in you were placed the fires that dwell within the waters.

(12.1.37.c) Driving away the Dasyus, the revilers of the gods, and choosing Indra as her lord, the Earth, like a woman, has yielded Vṛtra for the sake of Śakra, the bull, the strong one. (12.1.38’) Upon whom the Sadas and the Havirdhāna sheds are established, upon whom the sacrificial post is erected;
upon whom the Brahmins, knowers of the Yajus, sing praises with Ṛks and Sāmans; upon whom the officiating priests are joined together to press Soma for Indra to drink—(38)

(12.1.39’) May that earth point out to us the wealth for which we long— she upon whom the ancient seers, the creators of beings, the wise ones, sang forth the cows with the sacrificial session, the sacrifice, and ascetic fervor. (12.1.40’) May she point it out to us.
(12.1.40.c) May Bhaga bestow [his favor]; may Indra come as the leader before us.
{4} (12.1.41’) On that earth where mortals sing and dance, unrestrained;
where they fight, where the war-cry resounds and the drum speaks—

(12.1.41.e) May that Earth drive away our rivals; may the Earth make me free from enemies. ‖41‖ (12.1.42’) On whom food, rice, and barley depend, and upon whom these five human tribes rely— (12.1.42.c) Homage be to the Earth, the consort of Parjanya, whose essence is rain. ‖42‖

May Prajāpati make that earth—which has cities fashioned by the gods and whose field they transform—our source of delight in every direction and in every hope. ‖43‖ May the Earth, who bears treasures in many ways within her secret depths, grant me wealth, jewels, and gold. ‖44‖
May the Goddess, the bestower of wealth, being well-disposed and bestowing riches upon us, grant us prosperity.

‖44‖ Bearing people of many voices and diverse customs according to their respective dwellings, may the Earth yield for me a thousand streams of wealth, like a steady cow that does not kick away. ‖45‖

(12.1.46) That serpent of yours, the scorpion with the sharp sting, hidden in its lair during winter, restless and dwelling in the cave—the worm that stirs, O Earth, whatever moves at the onset of the rains—let it not crawl upon us nor glide over us; with that which is auspicious, be gracious to us. (12.1.47) Those many paths of yours, frequented by people, the tracks for the chariot and for the traveler to pass—
(12.1.47.c) May we conquer that path by which both the auspicious and the evil travel—a path free from enemies and thieves. Be gracious to us with that which is auspicious.
(12.1.48’) Bearing the wicked, supporting the heavy, enduring the destruction of both the auspicious and the evil, the Earth, in harmony with the boar, opens herself wide for the wild swine.

Those wild animals and beasts that dwell in the forest, the lions, tigers, and man-eaters that roam there— drive away from us the hyena, the wolf, misfortune, the *ṛkṣīkā*, and the *rakṣas*. The Gandharvas and Apsarases, and those who are *ārāyas* and *kimīdins*— [drive them away].
Drive away from us, O Earth, all the Piśācas and the Rākṣasas.
(50) Upon whom the two-footed winged creatures fly together—the swans, the eagles, the birds, and the fowls;
upon whom Mātariśvan the wind blows, raising the dust and shaking the trees. (51)
(12.1.51.e) The flame blows along the wind’s forward breath and its backward breath.
‖51‖ (12.1.52’) Upon which earth day and night, the black and the ruddy, are joined and ordained;
(12.1.52.c) may that earth, the broad world, covered and encompassed by rain, bestow upon us what is auspicious in every beloved dwelling-place. ‖52‖
May Heaven and Earth, and the mid-air, grant me wide space.
May Agni, Sūrya, the Waters, and all the gods bestow wisdom upon me. (53) I am the Conqueror, named the Overcomer, upon the earth. (54)
(12.1.54.c) I am all-conquering, all-subduing, the overcomer of every quarter.

||54|| (12.1.55’) O Goddess, when you first expanded in the east and were addressed by the gods, you spread abroad your majesty. (12.1.55.c) Prosperity entered into you at that time; you fashioned the four quarters. ||55||

(12.1.56’) Whatever villages, whatever wildernesses, and whatever assemblies exist upon the earth; (12.1.56.c) whatever battles and gatherings there may be—in all of these, may we speak what is pleasing to you.
(12.1.57’) Like a horse shaking off dust, he has shaken off those people who have encompassed the earth since it was born.
(12.1.57.c) Melodious, foremost, guardian of the world, you are the seizer of the lords of the forest and of the plants.
‖57‖ (12.1.58’) What I speak, that I speak as honeyed; what I look upon, that they desire for me.
(12.1.58.c) I am radiant and impetuous; I strike down the others who are defiant. ‖58‖
Peaceful, fragrant, pleasant, with curdled milk for her udder and rich in milk—
may the Earth, the broad ground, speak in my favor along with her milk.
(12.1.59) Her whom Viśvakarman sought with an oblation as she had entered into the ocean within the intermediate space— (12.1.60)

(12.1.60.c) That which was placed as a hidden treasure, a vessel for enjoyment, became manifest for those who possess mothers. 60 (12.1.61’) You are the receptacle of men, Aditi, the cow of plenty, spreading far and wide. (12.1.61.c) Whatever is deficient in you, may Prajāpati, the first-born of Cosmic Order (*ṛta*), fill that up for you. 61

May your laps, O Earth, be free from disease and free from consumption when we are born from you; may they be for us a long life as we awaken. May we be those who bring tribute to you. O Mother Earth, place me in a blessed state, well-established.
(12.1.63.c) Being in harmony with the day, O Sage, bestow upon me glory and prosperity.

{6} (12.2.1’) Climb the reed; there is no place for you here. This lead is your allotted portion; come! (12.2.1.c) Whatever wasting disease is in cattle, whatever wasting disease is in men—with that, depart downward together! ||1||
From the one who speaks evil and the one who speaks ill, from the hand and the foreleg— by means of this,
we drive away every consumption and death from here.
We drive death away from here, we drive away destruction and we drive away hostility from here.
(12.2.3.c) O Agni, devour him who hates us; we drive away him whom we hate, so that you shall not eat his raw flesh.

(12.2.4’) Whether it be Agni the raw-flesh eater, or a tiger, that has entered this cow-pen as a stranger—having made him [the intruder] into a bean-cake with clarified butter, I send him far away; let him go to the fires that dwell within the waters.
Whatever they have done to you in anger when a man has died, O Agni, that [injury] we repair for you; we kindle you once again with perfect skill.
Again, O Agni, may the Ādityas, the Rudras, the Vasus, and Brahmā Vasunīti restore you.
(12.2.6.c) May Brahmaṇaspati place you again for long life, for a hundred autumns.

(12.2.7’) That flesh-eating Agni who has entered our house, seeing this other Jātavedas— (12.2.7.c) him I carry far away for the sacrifice to the ancestors; may he kindle the heat in the highest dwelling-place.
(12.2.8) I send the flesh-eating Agni far away; let him go to the realm of Yama, carrying off the impurities.
Here, let this other Jātavedas, the god who knows all beings, carry the oblation to the gods, for he is wise.
(12.2.9) Impelled, I drive away the flesh-eating Agni, who makes men firm, [and I ward off] Death with the thunderbolt.
(12.2.9.c) As one who knows, I shall restrain him with the *gārhapatya* fire; let there be a portion for him even in the world of the ancestors.
(12.2.10’) I send forth the flesh-eating Agni, who is being praised with hymns, along the paths traveled by the ancestors.
Let him not return again by the paths of the gods; remain right here among the ancestors and be watchful.
They kindle Saṃkasuka for well-being—becoming pure, bright, and purifying. He leaves behind impurity; he passes beyond it. Kindled, Agni purifies with perfect purification.
(12.2.12) The divine Agni Saṃkasuka has ascended to the ridges of heaven.
(12.2.12.c) Being released from sin, may we be freed from ill repute.
||12|| (12.2.13’) In this Agni, the support of all, we wipe away our impurities; (12.2.13.c) We have become pure and worthy of sacrifice; may he prolong our lives. ||13||
Saṃkasuka, Vikasuka, Nirṛtha, and he who is voiceless— may they, sharing your knowledge,
drive the consumption far away from us. Whatever [consumption] is among our horses, our heroes, our cattle, or our goats and sheep— may it be destroyed.

(12.2.15.c) We drive away the flesh-eater, that Agni who is a bringer of destruction to people. ||15|| (12.2.16’) From other men, from cattle, and from horses, we drive away the flesh-eater, that Agni who is a bringer of destruction to life. ||16||
In that [place] where the gods cleansed themselves, and where men likewise, having cleansed yourself there, O Agni whose praise is ghee, ascend to heaven.
17 O Agni, kindled and invoked with offerings, do not depart from us. 18
(12.2.18.c) Shine right here in the sky, so that we may long behold the sun!
(12.2.19’) Be gracious in the head, be gracious in the river, and whatever [injury] is in the fire or in the crumbling ground;
furthermore, [be gracious for] the headache in the woolly fleece, in the dark night, and in the pillow. (12.2.19.c) 19.
Having laid down the filth upon the head, [and] the headache upon the pillow;
having wiped them away in the dark sheep’s wool, become pure and worthy of sacrifice.
Go forth, O Death, along the other path which is yours, distinct from that of the gods.
(12.2.21.c) To you who have eyes and hear, I speak: let there be many heroes here.
(12.2.22’) These living ones have turned away from the dead; today our invocation of the gods has become auspicious.
We have gone forward for dancing and laughter; as men of noble heroes, may we proclaim the assembly. (12.2.22.c) 22.
(12.2.23’) “I set up this boundary for the living, so that no other among them may now go to this goal.
Living a hundred abundant autumns, let them pass over death by means of this mountain.
(12.2.24’) “Ascend [to life], choosing old age, striving one after another, as many as you are.”
(12.2.24.c) May Tvaṣṭṛ, the well-born, in harmony with you, lead them all through their full span of life for the sake of living.

(12.2.25’) Just as the days follow one after another, and just as the seasons proceed together with the seasons, so, O Ordainer, arrange their lifespans such that the later does not abandon the earlier.
(12.2.25.c) Just as the later does not abandon the earlier, even so, O Dhātṛ, ordain their lifespans. (12.2.25)
(12.2.26) The stony river flows; hold fast, show your heroism, cross over, O friends!
Here leave behind those who are evil-minded; free from disease, may we cross over to strengths.
(12.2.27) Arise, cross over, O friends! This stony river flows onward.
(12.2.27.c) Here, let us leave behind those who are inauspicious; may we cross over toward auspicious and pleasant strengths.
||27|| (12.2.28’) Take hold of the splendor belonging to the All-Gods, becoming pure, bright, and purifying yourselves.
(12.2.28.c) Passing beyond the steps of misfortune, may we rejoice for a hundred winters with all our heroes intact. ||28||
Traversing the upward paths that lead to Vāyu, passing beyond the lower by means of the higher,
the seers have gone forth thrice seven times, warding off death by treading upon its track.
Treading upon the track of death, come hither, prolonging our life-span further.
(12.2.30.c) Seated together in the assembly hall, let us drive away death; then, as living ones, may we proclaim our wisdom.

(12.2.31’) Let these women, not widows and having good husbands, touch themselves with collyrium and clarified butter. Let the wives, tearless, free from disease, and adorned with fine jewels, ascend first to the place of birth.
With the oblation I distinguish these two; with the sacred word (*brahman*) I arrange them.
I prepare an undecaying *svadhā* for the fathers and unite them with long life.
O fathers, that immortal Agni who has entered into our hearts among mortals—‖32‖
(12.2.33.c) In me I encompass that god; let him not hate us, nor may we hate him.
(33) (12.2.34’) Having turned away from the *gārhapatya* fire, O flesh-eater, go forth toward the south.
(12.2.34.c) Do what is pleasing to the ancestors, to yourself, and to the *brahmans*; do what is pleasing. (34)
Taking two shares of the wealth, he squanders it through misfortune— Agni, the flesh-eater, who was not installed as the eldest son.
Whatever he acquires by plowing, whatever he gains by begging, and whatever he obtains by purchase;
(12.2.36.c) All that belongs to a mortal man is lost if a flesh-eating [dog] is not driven away.

(12.2.37’) He becomes unfit for sacrifice and his luster is destroyed; he is no longer fit to consume the oblation. (12.2.37.c) The flesh-eater follows him who cuts off the cow from the field or from his wealth.
(12.2.38’) Again and again, through greed, the mortal man, led astray by his own conduct, utters cries of distress;
the flesh-eating fire, knowing them well, pursues them closely from nearby. (12.2.39’) When a husband dies because of a woman, the houses are seized and consumed by the flames.
(12.2.39.c) Only the wise one is to be sought after, he who drives away the flesh-eater.
(12.2.40’) Whatever impurity, stain, or evil deed we have committed, (12.2.40.c) may the waters cleanse me from that, and from whatever [sin] comes from the fire-pit. {10}
(12.2.41) They have turned back from the south toward the north, knowing the way, along the paths traveled by the gods; upon the back of the mountain, the bull, the ancient rivers flow anew.
41 (12.2.42) O Agni, drive away the flesh-eaters, the raw-flesh devourers; bring hither the place of sacrifice for the gods. 42
The flesh-eater has entered this one; this one has followed after the flesh-eater.
Having made two tigers of different kinds, I carry him away, leaving behind what is auspicious.
(43) The secret place belongs to the gods, the enclosure to human beings; Agni Gārhapatya rests between both. (44)
O Agni, prolong the life of the living; let those who have died go to the world of the ancestors. As a good *gārhapatya* fire, burning away hostility, grant him ever more excellent dawns.
(45) O Agni, overcoming all rivals, bestow upon us their vigor and wealth. (46)
(12.2.47) Seize upon this Indra, the bearer, the protector; may he carry you out from misfortune and from reproach.
With him, drive away the arrow flying toward us; with him, may the two protectors ward off Rudra.
(12.2.48) Seize upon the ox, the boat; may it carry you out from misfortune and from reproach.
(12.2.48.c) Ascend this ship of Savitṛ; by means of the six wide expanses, may we cross over want.
(12.2.49’) Following day and night, you move along, bearing [us], dwelling in security, furthering us, and rich in heroes.
O bed, bearing us, be ever free from disease and well-disposed toward us; be for a long time possessed of the fragrance of manhood for us.

They cut themselves off from the gods; they live perpetually in sin—those who, like flesh-eaters, sit together out of a desire for wealth, while the fire, like a horse, devours them from nearby as it consumes reeds. 50.51.11–12.2.51’c.
(12.2.51.c) Or they always carry a cooking-pot for others. (12.2.52’) He wishes to fly away with his mind, yet he turns back again and again;
the flesh-eating fire, though knowing well, spreads out from nearby. (12.2.52.c) 52.
The black sheep is the portion of the beasts; they say that lead is your share, O flesh-eater, and also silver.
Ground beans are your sacrificial portion; enter the thicket of the forest-dweller as your oblation.
Having sacrificed an old reed, a tilpiñja, a staff, and a reed.
(12.2.54.c) Indra, having made him into fuel, cast him into the fire of Yama.
||54|| (12.2.55’) Having sent back the sun, the wise one has indeed entered the path;
he has directed their lives away, and I unite these [others] with long life. ||55|| {12}
(12.3.1’) O man, mount the man; step upon the hide! Summon there those who are dear to you.
As many as you two first met together in the beginning, so much is your common vitality in the realm of Yama.
(12.3.2’) So great is your sight, so many your heroic powers, so great your splendor, and so many your strengths.
Agni attends the body when it is fuel; then, once cooked, you two shall become a union.
(2) May you be united in this world and in the path of the gods; may you come together in the realms of King Yama.
Purified by the means of purification, call upon that [offering] for whatever seed has been produced within you two. (3)

(12.3.4’) O Waters, sons, come together and enter this living man, you who bring life to the living! Partake of that immortality which they call yours—the porridge which your mother cooks for you both. (12.3.5’) That which your father cooks and that which your mother cooks, for the sake of release from blemish and from the impurity of speech.

(12.3.5.c) That rice-porridge, flowing in a hundred streams, has pervaded both worlds with its greatness, reaching up to heaven. (12.3.6’) Both worlds and both those heavenly realms won by the sacrificers—of these, that which is foremost, luminous and honey-sweet—in that, O sons, may you both take refuge in your old age. (12.3.6.c) In that, O sons, may you both take refuge in your old age. (12.3.6.c) In that, O sons, may you both take refuge in your old age. (12.3.7) Seizing upon the eastern direction, one after another, those who have faith resort to this world.
Whatever cooked food has been served for you in the fire, O husband and wife, take refuge together for its protection. (12.3.8) Reaching toward the southern direction, turn around toward this vessel.

(12.3.8.c) Therein Yama, in harmony with the ancestors, shall grant you both abundant protection for the sake of the cooked offering. 8 (12.3.9’) This western direction is indeed excellent, in which Soma is the sovereign lord and the one who bestows mercy. (12.3.9.c) In that [direction] may you two take refuge; may you two associate with the doers of good deeds, and then, as a pair, partake of the cooked offerings. 9
May the northern realm, preeminent through progeny, make the northern direction our foremost among the quarters.
May we be united with all our limbs, together with the fivefold *chandas* and the person (*puruṣa*).
May this Virāj be firm; let there be homage to her. May she be auspicious to my sons and likewise to me.
(12.3.11.c) O Goddess Aditi, possessor of all boons, protect our ripened [grain] like a vigilant guardian.
(12.3.12’) Embrace us closely as a father embraces his sons; may auspicious winds blow for us here upon the earth.
May that rice-porridge which you two deities cook here know us, and may it recognize both our fervor and our truth. (12.3.12)
Whatever the black bird, having come here and flying about, has reached while clinging to the hole;
or whatever the female slave with moist hands has smeared—cleanse the mortar and the pestle with heat!
This stone, broad-based and bestowing vigor, purified by strainers, shall drive away the demon.
(12.3.14.c) Ascend the hide; grant me great protection! May husband and wife not fall into the sin of their offspring.
||14|| (12.3.15.a) The Lord of the Forest has come to us together with the gods, driving away the *rakṣases* and the *piśācas*.
||12.3.15.c) May he rise up and let forth his voice; through him may we conquer all the worlds. ||15||
The animals have encompassed seven sacrificial portions: that which among them is luminous and that which has grown lean.
Thirty-three deities attend upon them; may they lead us toward the heavenly world.
Lead us toward the heavenly world; may we be united with our wife and our sons.

(12.3.17.c) I take your hand; follow me here. May Destruction not overcome us, nor ill-will. 17 (12.3.18’) Let us pass beyond the Seizer and evil; may we drive away the darkness. You shall speak what is lovely.
(12.3.18.c) O you who are raised from the tree, do not harm him, nor shatter the grain of this man who seeks the gods. 18
O all-pervading one, whose back is anointed with ghee, becoming co-natured, go to this world.
Reach out to the winnowing basket increased by rain; let it separate the chaff and the husks.
The three worlds are measured out by the Brāhmaṇa: yonder sky, the earth, and the intermediate space.
(12.3.20.c) Having grasped the stalks, take hold of them; let them swell again, and let them return to the winnowing basket.
{14} (12.3.21’) Though the forms of cattle are manifold, you become of one form through prosperity.
(12.3.21.c) Push away this red skin; the pressing-stone shall cleanse it as a washerman cleanses garments.
I cause you, who are the earth, to enter into the earth; this body of yours is uniform yet transformed.
Whatever has been rubbed away or scratched by the instrument, may that not be lost; I restore it with a sacred prayer (*brahman*).
Like a mother toward her son, receive me with favor; I unite you, the earth, with the earth.
(12.3.23.c) O cauldron, jar, do not tremble upon the altar, being closely joined with the sacrificial implements and the clarified butter.

(12.3.24’) May Agni, cooking [the food], protect thee from the east; may Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, protect thee from the south. (12.3.24.c) May Varuṇa make thee firm in the western support; from the north, may Soma unite thee.
Purified by the filters, they flow clear; from the cloud they go to heaven and to earth, to the worlds.
Those life-sustaining, wealth-bestowing supports, poured into the vessel, may Agni kindle around them.
They come from heaven to earth; they attend upon the ground and they attend upon the mid-air.
(12.3.26.c) Being pure, let them indeed adorn themselves; may they lead us toward the heavenly world.
||26|| (12.3.27’) Both powerful and well-proportioned, bright and pure, and immortal;
(12.3.27.c) may those waters, instructed by the husband and wife, being helpful, cook the rice-mess for you, O well-protected ones. ||27||
Counted drops attend the earth, equalized by the out-breath and in-breath along with the plants;
incalculable, being poured forth, the brilliant and pure ones have pervaded all purity.
(28) Boiling up, they leap about; heated, they cast forth foam and many droplets. (29)
(12.3.29.c) Like a woman in her season seeing her husband, O waters, come together with these rice grains.
(12.3.30’) Raise them up from the bottom where they sit; let them touch their own selves with the waters.
I have measured out this water with vessels—these measured rice grains and these very quarters of space. (12.3.30) {15}
(12.3.31) Hand over the axe with haste; let it cut the plant without harming it at the joint.
Soma has attained sovereignty over these plants; may they be free from wrath toward us.
(12.3.32) Spread out fresh sacrificial grass for the rice-offering; may it be dear to the heart and pleasing to the eye.

(12.3.32.c) Into this may the gods together with the divine hosts enter; having sat down, let them consume it according to the seasons. (12.3.33’) O Lord of the Forest, sit upon the strewn sacrificial grass, measured out by the Agniṣṭoma chants and the deities. Like Tvaṣṭṛ, with a well-fashioned form, we have beheld these [sacrificial vessels] here around the ladle. (12.3.33.c) With the sharp axe, we have looked upon these [vessels] in their place. In the sixtieth autumn, may the guardians of the treasure desire him; may they attain heaven through that which is ripened.
May the living fathers and sons come to him; O Agni, lead him to this heavenly world.
34 O Sustainer, be supported upon the foundation of the earth; may the deities cause you, the immovable one, to move forth. 35

(12.3.35.c) May the husband and wife, living and with living sons, lift you up from the fire-chamber. ||35|| (12.3.36’) Having conquered all the worlds and attained as many desires as there were, may you two plunge into them; may the stirring-ladle and the vessel together draw this [offering] up into a single bowl. ||36||
Spread it out; extend it before you; sprinkle this vessel with clarified butter.
O gods, like lowing cows, make this youngling, who longs for the breast, utter its cry.
You have spread it out; you have made this world. Let the vast, peerless heaven expand.

(12.3.38.c) Upon it shall rest the buffalo, the fair-winged one; may the gods deliver it over to the deities. (12.3.39’) O wife, whatever you cook further than what the husband eats, or O husband, whatever you eat beyond what the wife cooks—let the two of you join that together; let it be yours in common, as you bring about a single world together.
(12.3.40) As many as there are who attend upon this earth—our sons who have been born around it—invite them all to the vessel; knowing their kinship, let the young ones come together.
(12.3.41) Those streams of wealth which are swollen with honey, mixed with ghee, the centers of immortality.
(12.3.41.c) He wins all of them; in the sixtieth autumn, the guardian of the treasure shall seek him out.
(12.3.42’) May the guardian of the treasure seek him for his treasure; may those others who are not masters be on all sides.
(12.3.42.c) Bestowed and deposited by us, heaven has ascended to the three heavens by means of the three sections.
(12.3.43’) May Agni burn away the Rakṣas; may the flesh-eating Piśāca who seeks the godless be driven away from here.
We thrust him away, we ward him off from us; may the Ādityas and the Aṅgirases attend to him.
(12.3.44’) To the Ādityas and the Aṅgirases, I offer this honey mixed with ghee.
(12.3.44.c) With pure hands, having not slain this [sacrifice], we two, the doers of good deeds, have drunk the heavenly [soma] of the Brāhmaṇa.
(12.3.45’) I have attained this supreme section of it, which Parameṣṭhin reached from that world.
(12.3.45.c) Pour out the clarified butter; anoint it thoroughly; this is our portion here, O Aṅgiras.
For truth and for austerity, for the deities, we entrust this treasure, this storehouse.
Let it not fall away from us in gambling, nor in the assembly; let them not surrender it to another before my time.
I cook; I give; my wife is born for my sake, devoted to my work.

(12.3.47.c) The world of youth has been born; as sons, may you both take hold of a future life. (12.3.48’) There is no sin here, nor is there any deficiency, for he comes together with his friends. (12.3.49) May we do what is pleasing to those who are dear; may darkness go to those who hate you.
May the cow, the ox, and the various birds drive away death that comes from men. (12.3.50) The fires know one another, he who dwells with the plants and he who dwells with the rivers.
(12.3.50.c) As many gods as shine in heaven, gold has become their ripening light.
{17} (12.3.51’) This skin has come together upon the man; all other animals are without it.
Clothe yourselves with dominion as your own garment; the face of the rice-porridge is an unsewn cloth. {51}

Whatever falsehood I may have spoken at dice, or whatever I may have spoken as untruth in the assembly out of a desire for wealth—O you two who dwell together enveloping the same thread, upon that [thread] deposit all impurity!
Rain down, go even unto the gods; from the skin, cause the smoke to fly upward.
(12.3.53.c) All-pervading, with ghee upon your back, becoming one who possesses a common womb, come to this world!
||53|| (12.3.54’) The heavenly one has fashioned his body in many ways according to his knowledge, [appearing] in a different color within himself.
Purifying himself, he has cast off the black and the white; that which is red, I offer that to you in the fire. ||54||

To the eastern quarter, to Agni as overlord, to the black protector, to the Ādityas who possess arrows—him we entrust to you; guard him for us until he returns. May it lead us here to old age; may old age deliver us unto death, and then may we be united with the cooked [world]. 55.
(12.3.56’) To the southern quarter, to Indra as overlord, to Tiraścīrāji as guardian, and to Yama who possesses the arrow—(12.3.56.c) we entrust this [child] to you;
protect him for us until he returns.
(12.3.56.e) May you lead him here to old age according to our destiny; may old age deliver him unto death, and then may we be united with him once more in the cooked [state]. ||56||
To the western quarter, to Varuṇa the overlord, to the viper as guardian, who possesses food and arrows—to him we entrust this man. Guard him for us until he returns.
May he lead us here to old age; may old age deliver us unto death. Then may we be united with the cooked [world]. 57.
To the northern quarter, with Soma as its overlord, with Svaja as its guardian and Aśanī as its arrow-wielding protector—to you we entrust this man.
Guard him for us until his return.
May he be led here to old age according to our destiny; may old age deliver him unto death, and then may we be united with him once more in the world of the cooked (the realm of immortality). 58.
(12.3.59’) For the fixed quarter, for Viṣṇu the overlord, for Kalmāṣagrīva the protector, for the herb-bearing plants:
(12.3.59.c) We entrust him to you; guard him for us until he returns.
(12.3.59.e) May he lead us here to old age as ordained; may old age deliver us unto death, and then may we be united with the cooked [world]. ||59||
(12.3.60’) For the upward quarter, for Bṛhaspati the overlord, for Śvitra the protector, for Varṣā the archer—(12.3.60.c) we entrust this man to you;
protect him for us until he returns.
(12.3.60.e) May you lead him here to old age as ordained; may old age deliver him unto death, and then may we be united with him once more in the world of the cooked. 60. {18}
"I give," he should simply say, and they have consented to her;
[he gives] a cow to the Brahmins who ask for it—this is [the gift] accompanied by offspring and descendants. Through offspring he ransoms himself, and he prospers with cattle.

(12.4.2.c) He who does not wish to give a cow to the ancestral seers when they come as supplicants to the gods— (12.4.3.a) With a crippled cow his [limbs] fall apart; with a lame one he crushes a bone;
(12.4.3.c) With a tailless cow his houses are burned; with a one-eyed cow his own property is lost. ||3||
From the foundation of the deep-red one, he finds the lord of cattle;
likewise, having found it in the barren cow, you are indeed called Duradabha.
From the foundation of her feet, he finds that which is named Viklindu.

(12.4.5.c) Through not being named, those [parts] wither away which she sniffs at with her mouth. (12.4.6’) He who pierces her ears is cut down among the gods; thinking "I am making a mark," he makes himself smaller.
(12.4.6.c) Thinking "I am making a mark," he makes himself smaller.
If someone plucks out the hair of this [cow] for some pleasure of his own,
then the colts will die and the murderous wolf will slay the calves.
If a crow has pecked at the hair of this truthful cow while her master was present—
(12.4.8.c) Then the young children die; consumption finds him through lack of mindfulness.
(12.4.9’) When a female servant gathers her washing-water and dung, (12.4.9.c) from that an ugly form is born; therefore, one should avoid this sin.
The cow, when born, gives birth to the gods together with the Brahmins;
therefore, she must be given to the Brahmins, for they say this is the protection of one's own property. Those who come seeking her as their prize—the cow is created by the gods for them.
(12.4.11.c) They have declared that to be the destruction of the Veda for him who hates this [Veda].
(12.4.12’) He who does not wish to give the cow of the gods to the descendants of sages when they beg for it— (12.4.12.c) he is struck down among the gods and by the wrath of the Brahmins.
If he should have the enjoyment of her at his disposal, yet he should desire another, she harms the man by being ungiven; she who is requested does not wish to give herself.
Just as a treasure-trove deposited belongs to the Brāhmaṇas, so is the cow in heat.
(12.4.14.c) They revile her thus: "In whomever she is born. (12.4.15’) The Brahmins revile her as their own when they [claim] the barren cow;
just as one might overcome them in another matter, so too is the suppression of her. (12.4.15.c) Thus is her confinement. 15.
"Even though she has not yet been recognized as having calved for three years, one should indeed treat her as such;
and one should know her as a *vaśā* (a barren cow), O Nārada—for then the Brāhmaṇas will come.
"He who says of this [cow], 'She is not a *vaśā*, but a treasure deposited by the gods'—"

Desires do not succeed for him when he seeks to accomplish something without having given it.
(12.4.20) The gods, making the Brahmin their mouth, asked for the cow.

(12.4.20.c) Of all those [who fail to give], the mortal incurs the wrath of the gods. ||20|| (12.4.21’) He who does not give a cow to the Brahmins incurs the wrath of the cattle; if a mortal shows hostility toward the portion set aside for the gods, ||21||

(12.4.23.c) Therefore, the Earth, together with its presiding deity, became difficult to traverse for him.
||23|| (12.4.24’) The gods begged for the cow at the very beginning when she was born;
Nārada, along with the gods, recognized her and brought her forth. ||24||
A barren cow makes a man childless and possess few cattle;
moreover, when she is solicited by Brahmins, she causes him to lose his beloved.
[This applies] to Agni and Soma, to Kāma, and to Mitra and Varuṇa.
