Whoever, having overheard this verse, then wanders among the cows—the gods, being provoked to anger, cut off both his life-span and his prosperity. (28) The cow wanders in many ways; she is the treasure deposited for the gods. (29)
(12.4.29.c) Manifest your forms when he seeks to strike us down. (12.4.30.a) He makes himself manifest when he seeks to strike us down;
(12.4.30.c) then indeed the cow sets her mind upon the Brahmins for the sake of begging. {21}
(12.4.31’) What one intends with the mind, even that reaches the gods;
(12.4.31.c) from there the Brahmins approach the cow to request it.
(12.4.32’) With the cry of "svadhā" for the ancestors, and with sacrifice for the deities.
(12.4.32.c) Through giving, a kṣatriya does not incur the wrath of his mother, the cow.
(12.4.33’) The cow is the mother of the kṣatriya; thus was she produced in the beginning.
(12.4.33.c) They say that the non-giving of her consists in what is bestowed upon the Brahmins.
(12.4.34) Just as one might snatch the clarified butter held in the ladle from Agni,
even so he who does not give snatches away the cow from the Brahmins for himself.
(12.4.35) A well-milking cow, like a sacrificial cake, stands by his side in this world.
To him who bestows [the cow], the wish-fulfilling cow (*vaśā*) yields all desires. To him who bestows all desires in the realm of Yama, the wish-fulfilling cow yields them.
But they say that for one who refuses what has been asked for, there is the world of hell.
Being impregnated, the barren cow wanders in anger toward the bull.
Thinking her to be barren, O Death, let him be bound in your snares.
He who, thinking her to be barren, cooks this cow here—
(12.4.38.c) Bṛhaspati even begs from his sons and grandsons.
(12.4.39’) Even a cow, while wandering among the cattle, emits great heat; moreover, she yields poison for the one who, though a lord of cows, is ungrateful. (12.4.39.c) 39.

That which is given to the Brahmins is dear to the cattle; likewise, that which is an oblation for the gods is dear to the barren cow. (40) The barren cows which the gods fashioned, having emerged from the sacrifice— (41)
Nārada brought forth from among them the terrifying Viliptyā.
(41) The gods deliberated over her: "Is she submissive or unsubmissive? Nārada said of her: "She is the most submissive of all submissive things. (42)
(12.4.43) "How many barren cows, O Nārada, do you know that are born of man? I ask you, the wise one: of which may a non-Brahmin not eat?
(12.4.44) "The *viliptī*, O Bṛhaspati, and the cow that has miscarried after giving birth—the barren cow."
(12.4.44.c) No non-Brāhmaṇa who desires prosperity should eat of it.
(12.4.45’) Homage be to you, O Nārada; well have you spoken concerning the cow.
Which among them is the most terrible, by not giving which one would suffer defeat? (12.4.45.c) [Which is that?]
The *viliptī*, O Bṛhaspati, and likewise the *sūtavaśā* and the *vaśā*—no non-Brāhmaṇa should eat of her who would desire prosperity.
(12.4.47) Indeed, there are three types of *vaśā*-born: the *viliptī*, the *sūtavaśā*, and the *vaśā*.
(12.4.47.c) He should bestow them upon the Brahmins; thus he incurs no breach before Prajāpati.
(12.4.48’) If he is asked, he should think: "This is the sacrificial oblation for you, O Brahmins.
(12.4.48.c) But if they should ask him for a barren cow, he should give one that is in the house of a person who has never committed an offense.
The gods spoke to Vaśā, saying, "She has not given us," and they were filled with resentment.
By means of these verses, Bheda was indeed defeated by her.
Furthermore, even when entreated by Indra, Bheda did not give up that cow.
(12.4.50.c) Therefore, the gods cut that offense away from me, leaving me superior.

(12.4.51’) Those wretched men who, as revilers, speak against the giving of the barren cow—by their thoughtlessness, they cut themselves off through the wrath of Indra. (12.4.51.c) Through their lack of understanding, those scoundrels destroy themselves.
(12.4.52’) Those who, having led the lord of cattle away, say, "Do not give him [back],"—
may you avoid the missile of Rudra through lack of awareness.
(12.4.53’) Whether it be offered or unoffered, if one cooks a cow at home...
(12.4.53.c) Having offended the gods together with the Brahmins, the crooked man falls away from the worlds.
{23} (12.5.53’) Created by Brahmā through toil and austerity, she is found and resorted to by those who possess knowledge.
(12.5.2’) She is covered by truth, enveloped by prosperity, and surrounded by glory.
Enveloped by *svadhā*, clothed in *śraddhā*, protected by *dīkṣā*, established in sacrifice—*loka* is the finale.
The *brahman* is the goal; the Brāhmaṇa is the overlord.
For a Kṣatriya who seizes that Brahman-cow and defeats the Brāhmaṇa who possesses her...
(12.5.6) Truthfulness departs, as do heroic power and auspicious fortune.
(6) (12.5.7) Vital force, brilliance, endurance, strength, speech, sensory faculty, prosperity, and righteousness.
(7) (12.5.8) The priesthood and the nobility, the kingdom and the commoners, luster, fame, splendor, and wealth. (8)

(12.5.9) Life-span and form, name and fame, out-breath and in-breath, sight and hearing; (12.5.10) Milk and sap, food and nourishment, cosmic order and truth, sacrifice and charity, progeny and cattle— (12.5.11) all these depart from the Kṣatriya who seizes the Brahmin’s cow and defeats the Brahmin. {25}
This very one is the terrible cow of Brahman, the poison of evil, a manifest *kṛtyā* enveloped in the *kūlbaja* [plant].
(12) In her are all horrors and all deaths;
(13) in her are all cruelties and all murders of men. (14)
(12.5.15) That cow, being seized as the property of a Brahmin, drags the oppressor of Brahmins and the reviler of the gods into the path of death.
(12.5.16) For she is a weapon with a hundredfold slaying; for she is the destruction of the oppressor of Brahmins.
(12.5.17) Therefore, indeed, the cow of the Brahmins is inviolable by one who possesses true knowledge.
The thunderbolt, Vaiśvānara, runs as it is driven forth;
the weapon, the great god, uproots the hooves as it looks on.
With razor-sharp edges, looking about and lowing, it thunders aloud.

Death utters the *hiṅ* sound; the fierce god tosses about the tail. (21) Universal loss makes the ears ring; consumption makes one urinate. (22) The curse is being milked; the headache has been milked out. (23)
Sitting, she stands near; mutually striking, she is seized.
(24) An arrow-point fastened upon the mouth; a calamity being struck down.
(25) Falling with evil poison; fallen into darkness. (26)

Following after his vital breaths, the Brahman-cow brings low the one who injures the Brahman. (27) When she is being torn apart, it is enmity; when she is being divided, it is the destruction of one's descendants. (28) When she is being carried off, she is the weapon of the gods; when she has been taken away, she is failure. (29)
Evil being laid upon her, harshness being laid upon her;
poison being cast forth, fever being cast forth;
sin being driven away, the evil dream being cooked away.

(12.5.33) Being ploughed, the earth was being ploughed; having been ploughed, it was the root-destroyer. (12.5.34) Being dug up, the unconscious pain was dug up; [it was] a venomous serpent that had been dug up. (12.5.35) Being carried away, non-existence was carried away; having been carried away, it was utter defeat.
(12.5.36) Śarva is enraged; Śimidā is being crushed; Piśitā is crushed. (12.5.37) Avarti is being eaten; Nirṛti is eaten.
(12.5.38) Eaten, the Brahman-cow cuts off from this world and from yonder world the one who treats the Veda with contempt. {27}

(12.5.39) Its slaughter is a magical spell (*kṛtyā*), its thought is a curse (*meni*); its entrails are a secret charm (*valaga*). (40) It is unapproachable and driven away. (41) Having become a flesh-eating fire, the Brahmin’s cow enters and devours the oppressor of Brahmins.
(12.5.42) It cuts away all her limbs, joints, and roots.

(12.5.43) It severs his paternal kin and drives his maternal kin away. (12.5.44) The Brahman-cow, when not returned by a Kṣatriya, consumes all the relatives of the one who has violated the Veda through marriage.

He makes him homeless, without cattle, and without offspring; he becomes one who lacks support, and he perishes—(45) the Kṣatriya who seizes the cow of a Brāhmaṇa who knows thus. (46) Indeed, soon after his slaughter, vultures will make a feast of him. (47)
(12.5.48) Indeed, quickly they dance around his funeral pyre—long-haired women, beating their breasts with their hands and committing the Ailaba sin.
(12.5.49) Indeed, quickly wolves commit the Ailaba sin upon his dwellings.
(12.5.50) Indeed, quickly they ask concerning him: "What was that? Is this now that?"
Cut it! Cut it down! Cut it away! Burn it up! Burn it up! (51) O daughter of Aṅgiras, make the oppressor of the Brahmin who seizes [the property] fall into subjection.
(52) For you are called Vaiśvadevī; you are a magical spell (kṛtyā), encompassing the root-born [evil]. (53)
Burning, fiercely burning, you are the thunderbolt of the sacred word (*brahman*).
(54) Become the razor-edged death and run forth! (55) You seize the splendor of those who conquer, as well as their sacrifices, charitable works, and blessings. (56)
(12.5.57) Having taken the victory, you bestow it upon the victor in that other world.
(57) (12.5.58) O inviolable one, become the path-finder for the Brahmin against his curse. (58) (12.5.59) Become an arrow, a shaft; become a poison of sin against the sinner. (59)
O Invincible One, strike off the head of the oppressor of Brahmins, the evildoer, the scorner of the gods, and the one who offers no gifts!
{29} Let Agni burn the evil-minded one crushed and trampled by you! {31} Tear him apart, tear him asunder, tear him to pieces! Burn him up, burn him away, consume him utterly! {32}
O divine, inviolable one, burn the oppressor of Brahmins down to his very roots.
So that he may go from the abode of Yama to the worlds of the wicked, far away.
Even so, O divine, inviolable one, [burn] the oppressor of Brahmins, the wrongdoer, the scorner of the gods, the one who bestows no gifts.
With the hundred-jointed thunderbolt, sharp and with a razor-edged tip, strike down his shoulders, strike down his head! Cut off his hair; rend his skin apart!
Cut away his flesh; tear out his sinews.
Crush his bones; strike out his marrow.
Loosen all his limbs and joints.
(12.5.72) May Agni, the consumer of raw flesh, drive him out from the earth; may Vāyu burn him up from the great expanse of the intermediate space.
(12.5.73) May Sūrya drive him away from heaven and consume him.
(13.1.1) Rise up, O vigorous one, who art within the waters; enter this kingdom, which is full of prosperity.

(13.1.1.c) He who, as the Red One, generated this entire universe—may he sustain you well for the sake of sovereignty. (13.1.2’) May strength come forth; he who is within the waters, ascend to the clans that have their origin in you!
Holding Soma, establish here the waters, the plants, the cattle, and all bipeds and quadrupeds.
(13.1.3’) You, O fierce Maruts, sons of Pṛśni, with Indra as your ally, crush the enemies!
(13.1.3.c) May Rohita hear you, O bounteous Maruts, you who are thrice-sevenfold and delight in sweet joy.
3 (13.1.4’) Rohita has ascended; Rohita has mounted the lap of the wombs, the source of all births.
(13.1.4.c) With those [powers], they found him in his agitation; seeing a way through the six expanses, he has brought the kingdom here.
(13.1.5’) Rohita has brought the kingdom here for you; the adversaries have been dispersed, and safety has come to you.
May Heaven and Earth, with their rich and powerful songs, milk forth your desire here for you.
Rohita generated heaven and earth; there Parameṣṭhin stretched out the thread. There the one-footed goat took his stand; by his strength he made heaven and earth firm.
Rohita made heaven and earth firm; by him the sky was propped up, by him the vault of heaven.
(13.1.7.c) By him the intermediate space was measured out, the regions; by him the gods found immortality.
(13.1.8’) The ruddy one has touched the multiform [world], fashioning both the ascending and the descending growths.
Having ascended to heaven with great majesty, may your kingdom be anointed with milk and ghee. (13.1.8.c)
(13.1.9) Those shoots of thine, those sprouts, those upward-growing ones, with which thou fillest the sky and the mid-air—

increasing by their sacred word (*brahman*) and their milk, be watchful for the clan and the kingdom, O Rohita! (13.1.10) Those clans of thine that have arisen from fervor (*tapas*), they have come here following the calf and the *gāyatrī* verse.
(13.1.10.c) May they enter you with a gracious mind; may the mother come together with her red calf. (13.1.11’) The youthful sage Rohita, generating all forms, has stood erect upon the firmament.
With his sharp light, Agni shines forth, cherishing his beloved things in the third realm. (13.1.11.c) 11.

The thousand-horned bull, Jātavedas, invoked with clarified butter, whose back is laden with Soma, the possessor of great heroism—may he not desert me, for I have sought his protection; may I not abandon you. Bestow upon me the nourishment of cattle and the nourishment of heroes!
Rohita is the progenitor and the mouth of the sacrifice; for Rohita I offer with speech, with hearing, and with mind.

(13.1.13.c) The gods go toward the red one with well-disposed minds; may he cause me to ascend by means of the ascents for the sake of companionship. 13 (13.1.14’) The red one distributed the sacrifice to Viśvakarman; from him these splendors have come to me.
(13.1.14.c) I would proclaim your navel upon the height of the world. 14
The Bṛhatī has mounted upon thee, O Jātavedas, and the Paṅkti, and the Kakubh with splendor;
the Uṣṇih meter with its syllables has mounted upon thee, and the Vaṣaṭ-call has mounted upon thee; Rohita has mounted upon thee together with seed.
This one clothes himself in the womb of the earth; this one clothes himself in heaven and this one in the intermediate space.
(13.1.16.c) This [sun] has pervaded the worlds in the height of the firmament.
||16|| (13.1.17’) O Lord of Speech, may the earth be pleasant for us; may our womb and our bed be pleasant and very gracious.
(13.1.17.c) May breath remain right here in our friendship. O Parameṣṭhin, may Agni endow you with long life and splendor. ||17||

O Lord of Speech, the five seasons which have come together for us, belonging to Viśvakarman—let our vital breath remain right here in this friendship. May Parameṣṭhin, the Red One, endow you with long life and splendor.
O Lord of Speech, grant us a benevolent mind; produce cattle for us in the cow-pen and offspring in our wombs.

(13.1.19.c) Right here let our vital breath be in friendship with you. O Supreme Lord, may he establish you with life and splendor. ||19|| (13.1.20’) May the divine Savitṛ, Agni, Mitra, and Varuṇa establish you with splendor.
Treading upon all enemies, come hither; you have made this kingdom full of truth and joy. ||20|| {2}
(13.1.21) You, whom the spotted deer-drawn side-horse carries on your chariot, O ruddy one— you go forth in splendor, releasing the waters.
(13.1.22) The ruddy cow, devoted to his will, the patroness of the ruddy one— golden-hued, vast, and full of luster.
(13.1.22.c) Through her may we win spoils of every form; through her may we overcome all hostile armies.
22 (13.1.23’) This is the seat of Rohiṇī, the red one; that is the path of the speckled one by which she goes.
(13.1.23.c) The Gandharvas and the Kaśyapas lead her up; the seers guard her with vigilance. 23
The immortal, golden horses of the Sun, possessing banners, always carry his easy-moving chariot.
Rohita, the radiant god who drinks the clarified butter, has entered the speckled heaven.
That Rohita, the bull with sharp horns, has encompassed both Agni and Sūrya.

(13.1.25.c) He who supports the earth and the sky—from him the gods create their emanations. (13.1.26’) Rohita ascended to heaven from the great ocean; Rohita, the grower, caused everything to grow. (13.1.26.c) Rohita, the grower, caused all things to grow.
Measure out the milch-cow, rich in milk, dripping with ghee; she is the cow of the gods, never-failing.
Let Indra drink the Soma; let there be peace; let Agni offer praise; drive away the adversaries!
27 Agni is kindled, being enkindled, increased by ghee, and offered ghee.
(13.1.28.c) May Agni, the overcomer, the all-conquering, slay those rivals who are mine. ||28|| (13.1.29’) Let him slay them; let him burn up the enemy who assails us.
(13.1.29.c) With the flesh-eating fire, we utterly consume our rivals. ||29||
(13.1.30) O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt, strike down those who are below with your arm!
Then, by the splendors of Agni, I consume my rivals.
(13.1.31) O Agni, cast our rivals beneath us; O Bṛhaspati, cause the one who seeks to surpass his kinsman to tremble.
(13.1.31.c) May Indra and Agni, Mitra and Varuṇa, cast them down, they who are beyond all measure of wrath. ||31|| (13.1.32’) O divine Sūrya, as you rise, strike down my rivals!
(13.1.32.c) Strike them down with a stone; let them go to the lowest darkness. ||32||
The calf of Virāj, the bull of hymns, has ascended the atmosphere with his radiant back.
With clarified butter they worship the Sun; being the Vatsa, who is Brahman, they cause him to grow by means of Brahman.
33 Ascend to heaven and ascend to earth; ascend to the kingdom and ascend to wealth.
(13.1.34.c) O Rohiṇī, ascend with offspring and immortality; touch thy body with Rohita.
(13.1.35’) Those gods who, as upholders of the kingdom, move around the sun—with them may Rohita, being in harmony and well-disposed, establish sovereignty for thee.
(13.1.35.c) With them may Rohita, being in harmony and well-disposed, establish sovereignty for thee.
(13.1.36) The sacrifices, purified by prayer, carry you upward; the bay steeds carry you as you travel the path.
You shine across the ocean, over the billowing sea. (13.1.37) O Rohita, heaven and earth rest upon you—the conqueror of wealth, the winner of cattle, the victor in the gathering of spoils.

(13.1.37.c) I shall proclaim for you his thousand and seven births, and his navel within the expanse of the world. (13.1.38’) Glorious, you traverse the intermediate quarters and the cardinal directions; glorious among cattle and among men; glorious in the lap of Aditi, the earth—may I become as beautiful as Savitṛ. (13.1.38.c) May I be as lovely as Savitṛ.
Whether you exist there or here, you perceive those things from this place;
from here they behold the radiant sun in heaven, the wise one.
As a god, you strengthen the gods; you move within the ocean.
(13.1.40.c) They kindle the same fire; the wise know him as the highest.

{4} (13.1.41’) Beneath the higher realm and beyond this lower one, the cow has risen up, bearing her calf with her foot. (13.1.41.c) Whitherward has she gone? To which region has she departed? Where indeed will she give birth? For she is not in this herd. {41}
She has become one-footed, two-footed, four-footed, eight-footed, and nine-footed;
she is the thousand-syllabled sequence of the world, from which the oceans flow forth.
Ascending to heaven, the immortal one has favored my speech.
(13.1.43.c) The sacrifices, purified by prayer, carry you upward; the bay steeds carry you along the path.
(13.1.44’) O Immortal One, I know that ascent of yours which is in heaven;
I know that dwelling place of yours in the highest firmament. (13.1.44.c) 44.
The Sun gazes beyond the sky, the Sun beyond the earth, the Sun beyond the waters;
the Sun, the sole eye of all that exists, has ascended to the great heaven. (45) The wide expanses were the enclosing sticks; the earth was fashioned as the altar. (46)
There Rohita established these two fires: cold and heat.
Having established cold and heat and having fashioned the sacrificial posts as mountains, the two fires of rain and clarified butter performed sacrifice for Rohita, the finder of heaven.
By means of the sacred word (*brahman*), Agni is kindled with the prayer of the one who knows the tones, of the ruddy one.
From him [Agni] came heat; from him, cold; from him, sacrifice was born.
(13.1.49) The two fires, increasing through the sacred word, strengthened by the sacred word, offered with the sacred word—

(13.1.49.c) Kindled by the *brahman*, the two fires of the ruddy, light-finding [sun] perform the sacrifice. (13.1.50’) One is established in truth; the other is kindled in the waters. (13.1.50.c) Kindled by the *brahman*, the two fires of the ruddy, light-finding [sun] perform the sacrifice. {5}
Whom the wind caresses, whom Indra and Brahmaṇaspati [caress]—
the two fires, kindled by the sacred word (*brahman*), have sacrificed for the ruddy one who finds the light of heaven.
Having fashioned the earth as the altar and having made the sky the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
(13.1.52.c) Having made that *ghraṃs* his fire, Rohita performed the sacrifice for all things endowed with self by means of rain as the clarified butter.
||52|| (13.1.53’) Rain became the sacrificial butter, *ghraṃs* the fire, and the earth was fashioned as the altar.
(13.1.53.c) There, Agni, by means of sacred hymns, fashioned these mountains upward. ||53||
Having fashioned the upward-tending [beings] with his words, Rohita spoke to the Earth:
"In you let all this be born—whatever has been and whatever is yet to be.
He became that first sacrifice, both what had been and what was to be.
(13.1.55.c) From that indeed was born all this, whatever shines here; it was brought forth by the seer Rohita.
(13.1.56’) And whoever kicks a cow with his foot or urinates facing the sun—for him I cut off your root; I shall not grant you further shade. (13.1.56.c) 56.

(13.1.57) Whoever passes between me and my shadow, and between me and the fire—of him I shall cut off the root; he shall cast no further shadow. (13.1.58) O divine Sūrya, whoever today comes between you and me...
(13.1.58.c) Upon him we wipe away bad dreams, impurities, and misfortunes.
||58|| (13.1.59’) May we, O Indra, not stray from the path, nor from the sacrifice, we who possess the Soma;
(13.1.59.c) may no enemies stand against us. ||59||
May we partake of that oblation which is the thread that accomplishes the sacrifice, stretched out among the gods.
His pure rays rise up, shining brightly in the sky.

(13.2.1.c) Of the Sun, who beholds men, whose laws are great, the bounteous one; ||1|| (13.2.2’) Him who makes the quarters known, who shines with his radiance, the swift-winged one flying swiftly upon the ocean— (13.2.2.c) Let us praise Sūrya, the guardian of the world, who illuminates all the quarters with his rays. ||2||
(13.2.3) When you go swiftly toward the east and the west by your own power, you fashion the two days of different forms through your creative might.
O Āditya, that is yours, that is your great glory, that as the one you are born encompassing the entire world.
(13.2.4) The many golden bay horses carry him, the wise, the crossing one, the radiant.
(13.2.4.c) You whom Atri drew up from the flowing [waters] to heaven—you, as you go around the racecourse, they behold you.
(13.2.5’) Let them not deceive you as you go around the racecourse; swiftly pass safely across the difficult passes.
(13.2.5.c) O Sūrya, as you travel, measuring out heaven and the goddess earth, day and night.
(13.2.6’) Blessing be upon your chariot, O Sūrya, as you move, wherewith you traverse both ends in a single day;
(13.2.6.c) that which your bay steeds, most swift to carry, draw—whether they be a hundred horses or many seven.
(13.2.7’) Ascend, O Sūrya, your comfortable, radiant, pleasant, well-drawing, and powerful chariot.

(13.2.7.c) Those bay steeds, most excellent at drawing, which carry you—whether they be a hundred horses or many seven; ||7|| (13.2.8’) Seven bay mares, vast and gold-skinned, has Sūrya yoked to his chariot to travel. (13.2.8.c) The bright one has been released from beyond the region; shaking off the darkness, the god has ascended to heaven. ||8||
(13.2.9) With his lofty banner the god has come; he has rolled back the darkness and turned toward the light. That celestial, well-winged hero, the son of Aditi, has looked out upon all beings.
(13.2.10) Rising, you extend your rays; you nourish all forms.

(13.2.10.c) You shine forth by your power over both oceans, encompassing all the worlds as you blaze. ||10|| (13.2.11’) These two move one after the other by means of their creative power; like two children at play, they traverse the ocean. (13.2.11.c) One beholds all beings, while the other is borne by bay steeds with golden ornaments. ||11||
Tvaṣṭṛ has established you in heaven so that Sūryā may be made into a month.
Thus you go, well-sustained, heating and looking down upon all beings. You flow toward both ends like a calf toward its two mothers.
(13.2.13.c) Surely even before this, these gods knew this Brahman.
(13.2.14.a) That which rests along the ocean, the Sun desires to win. (13.2.14.c) His path is stretched out vast, both that which is eastern and that which is western.
He attains him with his impulses; from that point on, he does not depart.
Through him, they do not fail to obtain a share of the nectar of the gods.
15 His rays bear aloft that god Jātavedas.
(13.2.16.c) So that all may behold the Sun.
(13.2.17’) Away go those stars with the nights, like thieves, before the Sun who beholds all things.
(13.2.17.c) Before the Sun who beholds all things.
His banners have been seen, his rays extending across the people,
shining like fires. O Sūrya, you are the one who crosses over, visible to all, the maker of light.
(13.2.19.c) You illuminate the entire radiant realm.
||19|| (13.2.20’) Facing the clans of the gods, facing the human tribes, you rise up; facing all, so that the sun may be seen. ||20|| {8}
O Purifier, with that eye wherewith thou beholdest the people as they stir about,
O Varuṇa, thou seest them.
Thou traversest the broad expanse of heaven, measuring out the day by means of the nights.
Beholding all births, O Sūrya.
||22|| Seven bay horses carry you in your chariot, O divine Sūrya, you whose hair is flame, the far-seeing one. ||23||
Seven pure ones, the granddaughters of the Sun’s chariot, have been yoked;
with them, self-yoked, he goes forth.
Rohita, the ascetic, has ascended to heaven through his fervor.
(13.2.25.c) He enters the womb; he is born again; he has become the sovereign lord of the gods.

(25) (13.2.26’) He who belongs to all people, who has faces on every side, whose hands are on every side, and who extends everywhere—(13.2.26.c) he, the one God, bringing forth heaven and earth, holds them together with his arms and wings. (26)
The one-footed has stepped out further than the two-footed; the two-footed follows after the three-footed.

Indeed, the two-footed has stepped out further than the six-footed; they rest together within the body of the one-footed. When the tireless one, moving forward, has mounted his bay steeds, he assumes two forms as he shines forth.
(13.2.28.c) Rich in banners, rising up, overcoming the regions, O Āditya, you shine forth across all the slopes.
(13.2.29’) Truly, you are great, O Sūrya; truly, O Āditya, you are great.
Great is your majesty, being so great; you, O Āditya, are great.
(13.2.30) You shine in heaven, you shine in the intermediate space; O Bird, you shine upon the earth, you shine within the waters.
(13.2.30c) You have pervaded both oceans with your radiance; you are the god among gods, the mighty one, the winner of the light.
(13.2.31) Directed hitherward from afar, moving along the path, the swift and wise Bird flies on.

(13.2.31.c) Viṣṇu, discerning through his power, stands firm; with his banner, he overcomes all that moves. (13.2.32’) Wondrous, observant, a buffalo, a fair-winged bird, he illumines the two worlds and the mid-air.
Enveloping sun and moon in day and night, he surpasses all heroic deeds. (13.2.32.c) Enveloping sun and moon in day and night, he surpasses all heroic deeds.
Sharp, shining forth and whetting his body, hastening forward and bestowing gifts upon the slopes,
the radiant, winged, mighty bull, bestowing vital strength, has occupied all the quarters as he ordains them.
The wondrous banner of the gods, the face, the radiant Sun, rising toward the quarters.
The Maker of Day, with his splendors, has driven away the darkness; the radiant one has dispelled all difficulties.
(34) The wondrous face of the gods has risen: the eye of Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni.
It has filled the heaven, the earth, and the mid-air. Sūrya is the soul of all that moves and stands. (35)
We behold you, the ruddy, fair-winged bird flying aloft, the crossing one shining in the midst of heaven— Savitṛ, whom they call the eternal light which Atri discovered.
Desiring protection, I, afraid, approach the fair-winged son of Aditi as he hastens upon the back of heaven.
(13.2.37.c) O Sūrya, extend for us a long life; may we not suffer harm, but remain within your benevolent favor.
37 (13.2.38’) The two wings of this golden swan, as he flies toward heaven, extend across a thousand days.
38.c) Having placed all the gods upon his breast, he travels while beholding all the worlds. 38
Rohita became Time; Rohita was Prajāpati in the beginning.
Rohita is the mouth of sacrifices; Rohita brought down the light from heaven.
Rohita became the world; Rohita heated the sky intensely.
(13.2.40.c) Rohita, with his rays, traverses the earth and the ocean. ||40|| {10} (13.2.41’) Rohita, the sovereign lord of heaven, has traversed all the quarters;
from heaven, the ocean, and the earth, he guards every living being. ||41||
Ascending the lofty heights, the tireless Śukra, shining brightly, assumes two forms;
wondrous, wise, and mighty, possessing the power of the wind, he blazes forth over as many worlds as there are.
One form he approaches, while the other is cast away, as the mighty one adapts himself to day and night.
(13.2.43.c) In our distress, we invoke Sūrya, who dwells in the mid-air, the finder of the path.

(13.2.44’) The Earth-pervading Great Bull, whose eye is undeceived, has encompassed all that exists as a path for him who invokes. (13.2.44.c) Seeing all, the benevolent one worthy of sacrifice, let him hear this which I speak.
His greatness extends beyond the earth and the ocean, shining with light around the sky and the mid-air;
seeing all, the benevolent one worthy of sacrifice, may he hear this which I speak.
(13.2.45) Agni has been awakened by the fuel of men, facing the approaching Dawn like a cow. (13.2.46)
(13.2.46.c) Like young birds springing up to the branch, his rays of light shoot forth toward the vault of heaven.
{11} (13.3.1’) He who brought these two, heaven and earth, into being; he who, having made them a mantle, clothes himself in all the worlds;
in whom the six wide quarters abide—over whom the winged bird gazes.
(13.3.1.e) This is the offense against that god when one oppresses a Brahmin who possesses such knowledge.
(13.3.2’) From whom the winds blow in their seasons, from whom the oceans flow forth;
(13.3.2.c) this is the offense against that god when one oppresses a Brahmin who possesses such knowledge.

(13.3.2.e) Make him tremble, O Rohita; destroy him! Cast thy snares upon the oppressor of the Brahmin! (13.3.3’) He who causes death and gives life, from whom all beings breathe—the offense belongs to that god when he is enraged against one who oppresses a Brahmin who knows thus.

(13.3.3.e) Shake him up, O Rohita; destroy him! Cast your snares upon the oppressor of the Brahmin! (13.3.4’) He who satisfies heaven and earth with his out-breath (*prāṇa*), and who fills the belly of the ocean with his in-breath (*apāna*)—against that god, when he is enraged, belongs this offense: whoever oppresses a Brahmin who knows thus.
(13.3.4.e) Make him tremble, O Rohita; destroy him; cast your snares upon the oppressor of the sacred word!
(13.3.5’) He in whom Virāj, Parameṣṭhin, Prajāpati, and Agni Vaiśvānara abide together with the Paṅkti— (13.3.5.c) He who has seized the breath of the highest and the splendor of the supreme.
(13.3.5.e) This is the offense against that god when one oppresses a Brahmin who possesses such knowledge.
(13.3.6’) He upon whom the six expanses, the five directions, the four waters, and the three syllables of the sacrifice are founded;
(13.3.6.c) he who, enraged, looked between the two worlds with his eye.
(13.3.6.e) This is the offense against that god when one oppresses a Brāhmaṇa who possesses such knowledge.
(13.3.7’) He who has become the eater of food, the lord of food, and he who is Brahmaṇaspati;
(13.3.7.c) he who is the past, the future, and the lord of the world.

(13.3.7.e) This is the offense against that god when he is enraged: whoever oppresses a Brahmin who knows thus. (13.3.8’) He who constructs the thirteenth month, measured by days and nights and consisting of thirty parts—this is the offense against that god when he is enraged: whoever oppresses a Brahmin who knows thus.
(13.3.8.e) Make him tremble, O Rohita; destroy him! Cast thy snares upon the oppressor of the Brahmin!
(13.3.9’) The dark path, the tawny-winged birds, clothed in the waters, fly up to heaven.
They have returned from the seat of Cosmic Order.
(13.3.9.e) This is the offense against that god when one oppresses a Brahmin who possesses such knowledge.
(13.3.10’) O Kaśyapa, that which is yours— the radiant, the well-joined, the abundant, the many-beamed, in which the seven suns are placed together—
(13.3.10.c) this is the offense against that god when one oppresses a Brahmin who possesses such knowledge.
(13.3.10.e) Make him tremble, O Rohita; destroy him! Cast your snares upon the oppressor of the Brahmin!
10 (13.3.11’) The Bṛhat hymn clothes him from the front; the Rathantara hymn grasps him from behind.
(13.3.11.c) He is ever vigilant, clothed in light.
(13.3.11.e) This is the offense against that god when one oppresses a Brahmin who possesses such knowledge.
(13.3.12’) On one side was the *Bṛhat*, on the other side the *Rathantara*; together they were powerful and united. (13.3.12.c) When the gods generated the Red One.
(13.3.12.e) This is the offense against that god when one oppresses a Brahmin who knows thus.
(13.3.13’) He becomes Varuṇa in the evening, he becomes Agni; he becomes Mitra as he rises in the morning.
(13.3.13.c) Having become Savitṛ, he moves through the intermediate space; having become Indra, he burns from the middle of the sky.
(13.3.13.e) This is the offense against that god when one oppresses a Brahmin who possesses such knowledge.
(13.3.14’) His two wings extend for a thousand days’ journey, like those of a flying golden swan bound for heaven.
(13.3.14.c) Having laid all the gods upon his breast, he goes beholding all the worlds.
(13.3.14.e) This is the offense against that god when one oppresses a Brahmin who possesses such knowledge.
(13.3.15’) This is that god within the waters, thousand-rooted, leafy, the devourer; he who has generated this entire world.
(13.3.15.c) He who has brought forth this whole universe.
(13.3.15.e) This is the offense against that enraged god, who oppresses a Brahmin possessing such knowledge.
(13.3.16’) The bay steeds, swift-moving, carry the bright god who blazes with splendor in heaven.
(13.3.16.c) Whose upward bodies heat the sky, and who shines hitherward with golden wings.
(13.3.16.e) This is the offense against that enraged deity who oppresses a Brāhmaṇa knowing this.
(13.3.17’) By which [light] the green horses carry the Ādityas, by which sacrifice many go, being fully aware;
(13.3.17.c) That single light which shines forth in many ways.
(13.3.17.e) This is the offense against that god when one oppresses a Brahmin who possesses such knowledge.
(13.3.18’) Seven yoke the single-wheeled chariot; a single horse, seven-named, draws it.
(13.3.18.c) The wheel has three naves, is undecaying and unassailable, upon which all these worlds stand.
(13.3.18.e) This is the offense against that god when one, knowing this, harms a Brāhmaṇa who possesses such knowledge.
(13.3.19’) The fierce carrier, yoked in eight ways, bears [the oblation]; he is the father of the gods, the progenitor of inspired thoughts.
Measuring out the thread of cosmic order with his mind, Mātariśvan purifies all the quarters.
(13.3.19.e) This is the offense against that god when one oppresses a Brahmin who knows thus.
(13.3.20’) He weaves the thread throughout all directions within the womb of the immortal Gāyatrī.
(13.3.20.c) This is the offense against that god when one oppresses a Brahmin who knows thus.
(13.3.20.e) Quake up, O Rohita; destroy him! Cast thy snares upon the oppressor of the Brahmin!

20 {13} (13.3.21’) Three are the sunsets, three indeed the dawns; three are the realms of space, and three the limbs of heaven. (13.3.21.c) We know thy triple birth, O Agni; we know the triple generations of the gods.
(13.3.21.e) This is the offense against that god when one, knowing this, oppresses a Brāhmaṇa.
(13.3.22’) He who, being born, spread out the earth and placed the ocean in the intermediate space;
(13.3.22.c) this is the offense against that god when one, knowing this, oppresses a Brāhmaṇa.
(13.3.22.e) Make him tremble, O Rohita; destroy him! Cast your snares upon the oppressor of the Brahmin!
(13.3.23’) O Agni, established by rites and signs, you, the radiant one, kindled, have shone forth in heaven.
(13.3.23.c) What did the Maruts, sons of Pṛśni, sing in praise when the gods brought forth the ruddy one?
(13.3.23.e) This is the offense against that god when one oppresses a Brahmin who possesses such knowledge.
(13.3.24’) He who gives life and gives strength, whose command all wait upon, even the gods;
he who rules over his two-footed creatures and his four-footed creatures.
(13.3.24.e) This is the offense against that enraged god, who oppresses a Brahmin possessing such knowledge.
(13.3.25’) The one-footed has stepped out further than the two-footed; the two-footed follows after the three-footed.
(13.3.25.c) The four-footed, beholding the fivefold row as it stands, has placed itself under the command of the two-footed.
(13.3.25.e) This is the offense against that enraged god: he who oppresses a Brahmin who possesses such knowledge.
(13.3.26’) Arjuna, the son of Kṛṣṇāyas, was born as the calf of the night. (13.3.26.c) He indeed ascends to heaven; the red one, the grower, has grown upon the heights. ||26|| {14}
(13.4.26’) He goes forth, Savitṛ, to the light, looking down from the back of heaven.
(13.4.2’) With his rays, he approaches the sky brought near; Mahendra goes, encompassing it.
(13.4.3’) He is the Ordainer, he is the Disposer, he is Vāyu—the sky uplifted.
He is Aryaman, he is Varuṇa, he is Rudra, he is Mahādeva;
he is Agni, he is Sūrya, and he is indeed Mahāyama.
To him the calves, ten in number, having a single head, approach together.
From behind, they stretch it forward as it rises and shines forth.
(7) This host of Maruts follows it; he goes along, fashioned like a sling. (8) Borne by rays, the cloud is brought near; Mahendra approaches, encompassed by it. (9)
For him there are these nine sheaths, established as ninefold supports.
He looks out upon all creatures—both that which breathes and that which does not.
This power has come together unto him; he is this one, the sole increaser, truly one alone.
In him these deities become the Ekavṛt.
Fame and glory, water and the sky, the luster of Brahman and food, and the eating of food—
[these belong to] him who knows this god as the Ekavṛt.
It is not called the second, nor the third, nor even the fourth;
it is not the fifth, nor the sixth, nor even the seventh;
it is not the eighth, nor the ninth, nor even the tenth.
He looks out upon everything—both that which breathes and that which does not. This conquering power has entered him; he is this one, the sole increaser, truly alone.
In him all the gods become contained within that single one. {16}

(13.4.21’) Brahman and austerity, renown and fame, water and sky, the splendor of the Brāhmaṇas, food and the eating of food. (2) (13.4.23’) The past and the future, faith and desire, heaven and the ancestral offering. (23) (13.4.24’) He who knows this god as the one-in-many. (24)
He alone is death; he is immortality; he is the vast; he is the Rakṣas.
He is Rudra, the winner of wealth, joined with the invocation of "namas" and the exclamation of "vaṣaṭ" at the gift of wealth.
All these spirits wait upon his command.
In her, all those constellations together with the moon abide under his control.
He was indeed born from the day; therefore, the day was born.
He was indeed born from the night; therefore, the night was born.
(13.4.31) He indeed was born from the intermediate space; from him the intermediate space was born.
(13.4.32) He indeed was born from the wind; from him the wind was born.
(13.4.33) He indeed was born from heaven; from him heaven was born above.
(13.4.34) He was indeed born from the quarters; therefore, the quarters were born from him. (13.4.35) He was indeed born from the earth; therefore, the earth was born from him.
(13.4.36) He was indeed born from fire; therefore, fire was born from him.
(13.4.37) He was indeed born from the waters; therefore, the waters were born from him. (13.4.38) He was indeed born from the Ṛg-verses; therefore, the Ṛg-verses were born from him.
(13.4.39) He was indeed born from the sacrifice; therefore, the sacrifice was born from him.
He is that sacrifice; he is the sacrifice; he has been made the head of the sacrifice.
He thunders, he flashes with lightning, and he hurls the thunderbolt at a man—whether for evil or for good, whether he be a human or an *asura*.
Whether you create the plants, or rain down with auspiciousness, or have strengthened the people;
such is your greatness, O Maghavan, and a hundred are your bodies.
A hundred are your bound fetters, whether you are indeed Nyarbuda.
Greater than Namuci art thou, O Indra; greater than deaths art thou, O Indra.
(46) Greater than ill-will art thou; thou art the Lord of power, O Indra, all-pervading and sovereign—thus do we worship thee.
(47) Homage be unto thee! Look, look at me; look! (48)
With food, with fame, with splendor, and with the luster of Brahman— (49) We worship you as Ambhas, Amas, Mahas, and Sahas— (50) We worship you as Ambhas, Aruṇa, Rajata, Rajas, and Sahas— (51) {19}
"We worship you as the wide, the broad, the well-being, and the world. (13.4.52) "We worship you as the expanse, the choice, the space, and the world.
(13.4.53) "We worship you as the one whose wealth is existence, the one whose wealth is food, the one whose wealth is union, and the one whose wealth is arrival. (13.4.54)
Homage be to you! Look, look at me; look!
[Endowed] with food, with glory, with splendor, and with the luster of a Brahmin.
{20} The earth is supported by truth; the sky is supported by the sun.
(14.1.1.c) By means of *ṛta* the Ādityas stand; Soma is established in heaven. (14.1.2’) By means of Soma the Ādityas are strong; by means of Soma the earth is great.
(14.1.2.c) Furthermore, Soma is placed within the lap of these constellations.
(14.1.3’) When they crush the plant, one thinks, "I have drunk Soma.
(14.1.3.c) But that which the Brahmins know as Soma, no earthly being consumes it.
(14.1.4’) O Soma, when they drink you, you swell up again from that very source.
(14.1.4.c) Vāyu is the guardian of Soma; the month is the form of the year.
(14.1.5’) Guarded by various coverings and protected by the Bṛhatī meters, O Soma, you stand listening to the pressing-stones; no earthly being eats of you.
Thought was her cushion, sight her ointment;
heaven and earth were the bridal chest when Sūryā went to her husband.
Raibhī was her attendant, Nārāśaṃsī her guide.
(14.1.7.c) A beautiful garment was for Sūryā; she was adorned as she sang her song.
||7|| (14.1.8’) The hymns were the side-pieces, the *kurīra* was the head-band, and the meter was the crest-ornament.
(14.1.8.c) For Sūryā, the two Aśvins were the suitors; Agni was the leader of the procession. ||8||
Soma became the suitor for the bride; both Aśvins were the two wooers, when Savitṛ gave Sūryā to her husband with his mind as she was praising him.
Her mind was the cart-pole, and the sky was the canopy.

(14.1.10.c) Two bright oxen were there when Sūryā went to her husband. (14.1.11’) Your two oxen, harnessed with the *Ṛc* and the *Sāman*, came together as the *Sāman*. Your two ears were your wheels; your path was the moving and unmoving world in heaven.
(14.1.11.c) Your two ears were your wheels; your path was the moving and unmoving world in heaven.
Pure were your two wheels as you went; the *vyāna* breath was the axle fixed within.
Sūryā, ascending her mind-made chariot, set forth toward her husband.
The bridal procession of Sūryā has gone forth, which Savitṛ sent away.
Under the Maghās the cattle are slaughtered; under the Phalgunīs the bride is led away.
When you two Aśvins came as suitors for Sūryā on your three-wheeled vehicle, where was the one wheel of yours? Where did you stand for the sake of the bridegroom?
When you two, O Lords of Splendor, came to Sūryā to choose her as your bride, all the gods recognized that deed of yours; Pūṣan, the son, chose his father.
O Sūryā, the Brahmins know your two wheels according to the seasons.
(14.1.16.c) Now, that one wheel which is hidden, those who seek the truth know it.
(14.1.17’) We worship Aryaman, the good kinsman, the finder of a husband.
Like a gourd from its stem, I release him from here, but not from there. (14.1.17.c) Like a gourd from its stem, I release him from here, but not from there.

(14.1.18’) From here I release you, not from there; I loosen that bond with which Savitṛ, the most gracious, bound you. (14.1.18.c) So that, O bounteous Indra, she may be rich in sons and fortunate. (14.1.19’) From the noose of Varuṇa I release you, with which Savitṛ, the most gracious, bound you.
(14.1.19.c) In the womb of Cosmic Order, in the world of good deeds, may there be a pleasant place for you, O lady with a skilled husband.
(14.1.20’) May Bhaga lead you from here by the hand; may the Aśvins carry you away on their chariot.
Go to the house so that you may be the mistress of the household; as one who has power, may you speak at the assembly.

(14.1.21’) Here, may what is dear to your offspring prosper; be watchful in this house for the sake of the household fire. (14.1.21.c) With this husband, touch your body together; then, full of vigor, you shall proclaim the assembly.
(14.1.22’) Remain right here; do not be parted; enjoy the full span of life.
(14.1.22.c) Playing with their sons and grandsons, rejoicing, well-established;
(14.1.23’) These two move one after the other by means of their creative power (*māyā*); like two children at play, they traverse the ocean.
(14.1.23.c) One beholds all beings; the other, ordaining the seasons, is born anew.
Being born, you become ever new; as the banner of the days, you go at the forefront of the dawns.
Coming, you distribute a portion to the gods; O Moon, you extend a long life. (14.1.25) Give away the woolen garment; distribute wealth among the Brahmins.
(14.1.25.c) This *kṛtyā*, having become footed, enters her husband as a wife.
(14.1.26’) She becomes blue-and-red; the attachment of the *kṛtyā* is manifested.
(14.1.26.c) Her kinsmen prosper, while the husband is bound in fetters. (14.1.26)
(14.1.27) Her body becomes unseemly and repulsive through that evil deed,
when the husband covers his own limb with the garment of the bride.
(14.1.28) [The acts of] tearing, cutting apart, and then carving out.
(14.1.28.c) Behold the forms of Sūryā; the Brahman adorns them.
(14.1.29’) This is harsh, pungent, like a splinter, like poison—it is not for eating.
(14.1.29.c) Only that Brahman who knows Sūryā is worthy of the bridegroom’s fee.
He, the Brahman priest, takes that auspicious garment, the pleasant seat,
he who knows the expiation by which the wife is not harmed.
O you two, speakers of Truth at the rites of Truth, bring together abundant fortune!
(14.1.31.c) O Brahmaṇaspati, make him pleasing to her as a husband; let the matchmaker speak these words.
(31) (14.1.32’) Stay right here, do not go further away; O cows, increase this man with progeny.
(14.1.32.c) Moving toward beauty, possessing the luster of Soma—O All-Gods, turn your minds here toward you. (32)
O cows, enter into this man with his offspring; he does not diminish the portion of the gods.
For him, O Pūṣan and all you Maruts, for him may Dhātṛ and Savitṛ impel you.
May the paths be thornless and straight by which our friends go to choose a bridegroom.

(14.1.34.c) May Bhaga unite her, may Aryaman, may Dhātṛ endow her with splendor. (14.1.35’) Whatever splendor is in dice and whatever is placed in surā, whatever splendor is in cattle, O Aśvins, with that splendor protect this woman. With that by which the great inviolable [cow] was impregnated, O Aśvins, or with that by which the Surā was produced,
and with that by which the dice were consecrated— with that splendor, endow this woman.
He who shines within the waters without being kindled, whom the sages praise at the sacrifices—
(14.1.37.c) O Son of the Waters, grant us waters rich in sweetness, those by which Indra, the heroic one, grew strong.
(14.1.38’) Here I cast away this glowing grasp that corrupts the body; I draw up that auspicious light. (14.1.38.c) I draw it up.
(14.1.39’) Let the Brāhmaṇas bring waters for her lustration; let the waters rise up, not slaying heroes.
Let Pūṣan escort Agni around from Aryaman; the father-in-law and the brother-in-law await them.
(14.1.40’) May gold be auspicious to you, and may the waters be auspicious; may the wedge be auspicious, and may the chink of the yoke be auspicious.
(14.1.40.c) May the waters, with their hundred purifiers, be auspicious for you; and may you, with your husband, touch your body in peace.
40 (14.1.41’) O Śatakratu, having cleansed Apālā three times through the hole of the chariot, the hole of the cart, and the hole of the yoke, you made her one whose skin is like the sun. 41
Desiring goodwill, offspring, good fortune, and wealth—
being devoted to your husband, gird yourself for the sake of immortality.
Just as the bull Sindhu brought forth sovereignty over the rivers...
(14.1.43.c) Thus, O sovereign lady, become the queen after having gone to your husband’s home.
(14.1.44’) Be a sovereign lady among your father-in-laws, and a sovereign lady among your brothers-in-law; be a sovereign lady among your sister-in-law, and a sovereign lady among your mother-in-law.
(14.1.44.c) Be a sovereign lady among your sister-in-law, and a sovereign lady among your mother-in-law.
(14.1.45) Those goddesses who cut, who wove, and who stretched [the cloth], and those who fixed the borders all around—may they clothe you for old age; put on this garment, O long-lived one!
(14.1.46) They weep for the living and lead him away to the sacrifice; the men have looked toward the long-lasting course of life.

(14.1.46.c) What is pleasant for the fathers, whom they have sent here—may that be a joy for my husbands, as I embrace my wife. (14.1.47’) I place this pleasant and firm stone for you in the lap of the goddess Earth, for the sake of offspring.
Ascend it, O lady of noble splendor, being approved by all; may Savitṛ grant you a long life.
With that [power] by which Agni grasped the right hand of this earth, with that I grasp your hand; do not falter, together with me, with offspring, and with wealth.
(14.1.48) May the god Savitṛ grasp your hand; may King Soma make you possessed of good offspring. (14.1.49)
(14.1.49.c) May Agni Jātavedas make the fortunate woman reach old age as a wife for her husband.
49 (14.1.50’) I take your hand for the sake of good fortune, so that you may reach old age with me as your husband.
(14.1.50.c) Bhaga, Aryaman, Savitṛ, and Purandhi—the gods have given you to me for the household life. 50 {5}
Bhaga has taken your hand; Savitṛ has taken your hand.
You are the wife by sacred law (*dharman*); I am your householder.
May she be my nourishment; Bṛhaspati has given you to me.
(14.1.52.c) With me as your husband, O mother of offspring, live for a hundred autumns!
(14.1.53’) Tvaṣṭṛ has bestowed this garment for the sake of beauty, by the instruction of Bṛhaspati and the wisdom of the seers.
(14.1.53.c) With that, may Savitṛ and Bhaga clothe this woman with offspring, even as they clothed Sūryā.
May Indra and Agni, Heaven and Earth, Mātariśvan, Mitra and Varuṇa, Bhaga, both Aśvins, Bṛhaspati, the Maruts, Brahma, and Soma cause this woman to increase with progeny.
(54) Bṛhaspati was the first to fashion the hair upon the head of Sūryā. (55)
(14.1.55.c) Therefore, O Aśvins, we adorn this woman for her husband. ||55|| (14.1.56’) This is that form which you have assumed; I seek with my mind the maiden who moves about as a wife.
(14.1.56.c) I shall follow her with my friends, the Navagvas; who, knowing this, has untied these bonds? ||56||
I shall release her form from myself; seeing it, I shall know the dwelling-place of the mind.
I do not eat the theft of the mind; I am released, untying by myself the bonds of Varuṇa.
57 I release you from the bond of Varuṇa, with which Savitṛ, the most gracious, bound you.
(14.1.58.c) "I make wide space here for you, O bride, and an easy path for you together with your husband.
(14.1.59’) "Lift her up; drive away the demon! Place this woman in a state of well-being.
The wise Dhātṛ has found a husband for her; may King Bhaga go before her, knowing the way."
Bhaga fashioned the four feet; Bhaga fashioned the four poles.
Tvaṣṭṛ shaped the side-pieces along the middle. May she be auspicious for us.
The bridal procession, beautiful with *kiṃśuka* flowers, multiform, golden-hued, well-rolling, and with good wheels—may it bear her away.
(14.1.61.c) Ascend to the world of immortality, O Sūryā; make for your husbands a pleasant bridal procession.
(14.1.62’) One who slays neither brother nor cattle, O Bṛhaspati;
one who slays neither husband nor child, O Savitṛ—bring her to us. 62.
"Do not harm the young bride, O two pillars, on this path prepared by the gods.
We make the door of the divine hall auspicious as a path for the bride.
"May the sacred word (*brahman*) be joined at the rear; may the sacred word be joined at the front; may the sacred word be at the end, in the middle, and everywhere."
(14.1.64.c) Having entered the invulnerable city of the gods, may you be auspicious and gracious; shine forth in the world of your husband!
{6} (14.2.1’) For you they first led Sūryā around with her bridal procession. O Agni, grant this wife to our husbands, together with offspring! {1}
Agni has given back the wife together with life and splendor;
may he who is her husband live a long life for a hundred autumns.
Soma was your first husband, the Gandharva was your next.
(14.2.3.c) Agni is your third husband; the fourth is born of man.

(14.2.4’) Soma gave her to the Gandharva; the Gandharva gave her to Agni. Agni has given me wealth and sons, and likewise this woman. (14.2.4.c) Agni has given me wealth and sons, and likewise this woman.

(14.2.5’) May your benevolence come to us, O lords of ample wealth; O Aśvins, desires have settled within our hearts. (14.2.5.c) You have become our protectors, a pair, lords of splendor; may we reach the dear dwellings of Aryaman. 5 (14.2.6’) Rejoicing with a gracious mind, bestow upon us wealth consisting of all-heroic sons and eloquence.
(14.2.6.c) May there be a pleasant ford and a good drinking place; O Lord of Splendor, strike down the stump standing in the path and the evil-minded one!

(14.2.7’) The herbs that exist, the rivers that flow, the fields that are, and the forests that stand—may they, O bride, protect you, who are rich in offspring, from demons for the sake of your husband!
(14.2.8) We have ascended this path, easy to traverse and carrying one to well-being, upon which a hero does not suffer harm and acquires wealth from others.
(14.2.9) O men, listen well to this from me: by means of this blessing, a husband and wife obtain what is desirable.
(14.2.9.c) Those Gandharvas and divine Apsarases who dwell upon these trees—(14.2.9.e) may they be gracious to this bride; may they not harm the bridal procession as it is being led away.
(14.2.10’) Those wasting diseases that follow people after the bride’s radiant bridal procession—

(14.2.10.c) May the gods worthy of sacrifice lead them back again to the place from which they came. ||10|| (14.2.11’) May those waylayers who lie in wait not find the couple; may they pass through the difficult path by an easy way, and may their enemies flee away. ||11||
With a friendly eye, with benevolence, I cause the bridal procession to be revealed through the sacred word and the house;
may Savitṛ make that which is bound around, multiform, and pleasant for her husbands.
This auspicious woman has come home; the Creator has assigned this world to her.
(14.2.13.c) May Aryaman, Bhaga, both Aśvins, and Prajāpati cause her to increase with progeny.
13 (14.2.14’) This woman has come, a fertile field endowed with life-force; sow your seed in her, O men.
14 May she bring forth offspring for you from her wombs, bearing the milk that is the bull’s semen. 14
(14.2.15’) Stand firm; you are the Virāj. Like Viṣṇu, O Sarasvatī, be here.
(14.2.15.c) O Sinīvālī, let her give birth; may she abide in the favor of Bhaga.
(14.2.16’) Let your wave rise up, O waters, striking against the pins; release the thongs.
(14.2.16.c) May the two inviolable bulls, free from malice and sin, not bring us misfortune.
||16|| (14.2.17’) With eyes that are not terrible, not slaying her husband, pleasant, helpful, very kind, and easy to manage for the household;
(14.2.17.c) a mother of heroes, desiring her brothers-in-law—may we dwell with you, being well-disposed toward one another. ||17||
Do not be a hater of your brothers-in-law, do not be a hater of your husband; be auspicious toward the cattle, easy to manage, and full of luster.
Bearing offspring, giving birth to heroes, desiring your brothers-in-law, and being pleasant, worship this Gārhapatya fire.
Arise from here! Seeking what have you come here? I, the conqueror, call you back from your own home.

(14.2.19.c) O Nirṛti, you who seek the empty, you have come; arise, O Arāti, fly away! Do not stay here. (14.2.20’) When this bride has honored the Gārhapatya fire, the former fire, then, O woman, pay homage to Sarasvatī and to the Fathers. {8}
(14.2.21’) Bring this protection and armor to be spread beneath this woman;
O Sinīvālī, let her give birth and abide in the favor of Bhaga.
(14.2.22’) The *balbaja* grass upon which you set it down, and the skin which you spread beneath—
(14.2.22.c) Let her ascend it, she who, blessed with good offspring, finds a husband.
(14.2.23’) Spread out the *balbaja* grass upon the red hide;
having sat down there, let her, blessed with good offspring, worship this fire. (14.2.23.c) 23.
Ascend the hide; sit down near the fire. This god slays all the Rakṣases.
Beget offspring here for this husband; may this son of yours be preeminent in excellence.
Let the cattle of various forms be born from the womb of this mother as they spread forth.
(14.2.25.c) O auspicious one, sit down near this Agni; as his wife, adorn the gods here.

(14.2.26’) Auspicious, a furtherer of the household, most gracious, bringing welfare to her husband and her father-in-law, pleasant to her mother-in-law—may we enter these houses. (14.2.26.c) May we enter these houses.
Be gracious to her parents-in-law, gracious to her husband and his household;
be gracious to this entire community, and be gracious for the prosperity of these people.
(27) This bride is most auspicious; come together and behold her. (28)
(14.2.28.c) Having bestowed good fortune upon her, depart with misfortunes!
(14.2.29’) O young women who are ill-disposed, and you who are here, even those who are old—bestow your splendor upon her now, and then go back to your homes!
(14.2.29.c) Bestow your luster upon her, and then depart and stay away! 29.
(14.2.30) Sūryā Sāvitrī has ascended the litter, which is spread with gold and bears all forms, for the sake of great good fortune.
(14.2.31) Ascend the couch with a well-disposed mind; here, procreate offspring for this husband.

(14.2.31.c) Like Indrāṇī, being well-awakened and awakening, you shall watch over the dawns that have light at their head. (14.2.32’) In the beginning, the gods descended; they united with their wives, body with body. (14.2.32.c) Like Sūryā, O woman of all forms, endowed with greatness, be united here with your husband, bringing forth offspring.
Arise from here, O Viśvāvasu; we pay homage to you with reverence.
Seek a sister who dwells among the fathers and is well-disposed; that is your portion by birth—know this! 33 The Apsarases rejoice in the communal feast between the oblation-holder and the sun.
(14.2.34.c) These are your birthplace; go toward them. I pay homage to you, O Gandharva, according to the season.
||34|| (14.2.35’) Homage to the Gandharva’s homage, and homage we offer to his wrath and his eye.
(14.2.35.c) O Viśvāvasu, with this sacred prayer we pay homage to you; go toward your wives, the Apsarases. ||35||
(14.2.36’) Through wealth may we be well-disposed; let us now bring the Gandharva hither from here.
That god has gone to the supreme dwelling; we have gone to where they prolong their life. (14.2.37’) May you two parents unite in due season; may you both become the mother and father of the seed.
(14.2.37.c) Like a man mounting a woman, mount her; produce offspring here and prosper in wealth.
(14.2.38’) O Pūṣan, send forth that most auspicious woman upon whom men sow their seed—she who, longing for us, shall part her thighs, and upon whom we, longing, may strike our member.
(14.2.38.c) [She] who, longing for us, shall part her thighs, and upon whom we, longing, may strike our member.
(14.2.39) Place your hand upon her thigh; embrace your wife with a well-disposed mind.
May you two create offspring here, rejoicing; may Savitṛ grant you both a long life.
(14.2.40) May Prajāpati generate progeny for you both; may Aryaman unite you with day and night.
(14.2.40.c) Free from ill fortune, may we enter this world of husbands; be auspicious to us, for our bipeds and our quadrupeds!
‖40‖ (14.2.41’) This bridal garment and the cloth for the bride were given by the gods together with Manu. He who gives [it] to the wise Brahmin indeed strikes down the demons and their couches. ‖41‖
That portion of the sacred word which was given to me, the bridal garment for the two brides,

and the cloth for the bride— O Bṛhaspati and Indra, you two, granting your consent to the sacred word, have given this together. Being bound from a pleasant womb, laughing and exulting with great joy.
(14.2.43.c) With good cattle, good sons, and a good home, may you two cross over; may we live through the radiant dawns.
(14.2.44’) Clothed in new raiment, fragrant and well-attired, I have risen alive through the radiant dawns.
Like a bird from its egg, I have emerged free from every sin.
May the beautifying Heaven and Earth, who are near with their favor and possess great ordinances;
may the seven divine waters have flowed forth—they shall release us from distress.
To Sūryā, to the gods, to Mitra, and to Varuṇa.

(14.2.46.c) To those who are mindful of what has come to be, to them I have offered this homage. (14.2.47’) He who, even without a binding, before the piercing of the collarbones, is the knitter of the joint, Maghavan, the possessor of many riches; he repairs again that which was torn asunder. (14.2.47.c) He is the knitter of the joint, Maghavan, the possessor of many riches, the restorer of that which was dislocated. (14.2.47.c) He is the restorer of that which was dislocated.
