O breath, protect my breath; be gracious to this life-force.
O Nirṛti, release us from the nooses of destruction.
You are the offspring of the ocean, the flower of the lightnings.
The wind is the breath, the sun is the eye; [you are] the milk of heaven.
(5) O divine collyrium from Mount Trikakud, protect me on every side!
Neither the plants of the plains nor those of the mountains surpass you. (6)
This [soma], the slayer of demons and the driver away of disease, has descended into the middle [of the world]; driving away all maladies, he has destroyed the threats from here.
O King Varuṇa, a man has spoken much falsehood here.
Therefore, O thou of a thousand powers, release us from distress.
(8) Whatever we have uttered—“O Waters, O inviolable ones,” or “O Varuṇa”—therefore, O thou of a thousand powers, release us from distress. (9)
May Mitra and Varuṇa both follow after you, O Āñjana;
having followed you far, may they bring you back again for our enjoyment.
Like debt from debt, lead the sorcery back to the house of the sorcerer.
O Durhārd, may the mantra of the eye crush even your ribs!
Whatever evil dream is among us, whatever is among our cattle, and whatever is in our house—
let that which is nameless and hateful be cast back upon Durhārd!

Increasing with the strength and vigor of the waters, born from Agni Jātavedas—may this mountain-born collyrium, possessing four heroes, make the quarters and intermediate directions auspicious for you.
This collyrium of yours is bound as one with four heroes; may all the quarters be free from fear for you.
(19.45.4.c) Stand firm like Savitṛ, O noble one; let these subjects bring tribute to you.
(19.45.5.a) Win one jewel for yourself, make one for another, bathe with one, and drink from one of these.
(19.45.5.c) May she protect us from the four bonds of Grāhī belonging to the four Nairṛtas, which hold four heroes captive.
(19.45.6) May Agni protect me with Agni for out-breath and in-breath, for life, for splendor, for vigor, for brilliance, for well-being, and for prosperity— svāhā!
(19.45.7) May Indra protect me with his virility for out-breath and in-breath, for life, for splendor, and for vigor.
(19.45.7.c) To brilliance, for well-being, for prosperity—svāhā!
‖7‖ (19.45.8.a) May Soma protect me with his Soma-nature for out-breath, in-breath, life-span, luster, vigor, (19.45.8.c) brilliance, for well-being, for prosperity—svāhā! ‖8‖
May Bhaga protect me with his fortune for the sake of out-breath, in-breath, long life, splendor, vigor,
brilliance, well-being, and prosperity— svāhā!
(9) May the Maruts protect me with their hosts for the sake of out-breath, in-breath, long life, splendor, vigor, and brilliance.
(19.45.10.c) For well-being and prosperity, Svāhā!

‖10‖ (19.46.1’) Prajāpati bound you first, for the sake of invincible valor. (19.46.1.c) That I bind upon you for long life, for splendor, for vigor, and for strength; may the invincible one protect you. ‖1‖
Let him stand upright, guarding vigilantly; let not the Paṇis or Yātudhānas deceive you.
Like Indra, shake off the Dasyus who attack; overcome all enemies; let the one who lies prostrate guard you.
Even a hundred attackers, though striking and slaying, have not prevailed against us.
(19.46.3.c) Upon him Indra bestowed sight, breath, and strength; may the invincible one protect you.
(19.46.4’) We clothe you with the armor of Indra, who became the sovereign king of the gods; may all the gods lead you forth again; may the invincible one protect you.
(19.46.4.c) May all the gods lead you forth again; may the invincible one protect you.
In this amulet are a hundred powers; in this invincible one are a thousand vital breaths.
As a tiger, trample upon all enemies. Let him who seeks to attack you fall low; may the invincible one protect you.
Drawn from clarified butter, honeyed, full of milk, possessing a thousand breaths and a hundred origins, it bestows vigor.
May Śambhu, Mayobhū, Urjasvān, and Payasvān protect you from behind; may the invincible one guard you.
(6) Just as you have become superior, without rivals, and a slayer of rivals, so may Savitṛ make you the controller of your kinsmen; may the invincible one guard you. (7)
O Night, the earthly dust has been moistened by the domains of your father;
vast one, you spread across the seats of heaven, and the shimmering darkness rolls in upon you.
Whose further shore is not seen, and who does not weary—into her everything that moves goes to rest.
(19.47.2.c) Unharmed, O wide and dark night, may we reach your further shore; O auspicious one, may we reach your further shore.
(19.47.3’) Those watchers of yours, O Night, who look upon men—ninety-nine of them there are; eighty, or eight, or even seventy-seven.
Sixty-six, O wealthy one; fifty-five, O gracious one;
forty-four, thirty-three, O spirited one;
twenty-two, and eleven nights are yours as your lowest portion.
With those very guardians, O Daughter of Heaven, protect us this day!
(5) Protect us! Let no one who speaks evil against us have power over us; let no one who utters curses have power over us.
Let not the thief of our cattle, nor the wolf of our sheep, have power over us this day! (6)
O auspicious lady, let no thief pursue the horses, nor let any sorceress pursue the men.
Let the robber and the thief run away by the highest paths; let the cord with its teeth be far away, and let the malevolent one flee beyond.
Now, O Night, make the serpent smoke-mouthed and headless;
crush the jaws of the wolf; strike the thief upon the wooden post.
(8) In you, O Night, we dwell; we shall sleep; keep watch! (9)
Grant us protection for our cattle, for our horses, and for our men.
(9) Moreover, whatever [parts] there are of you, and whatever is within your belly—those we entrust to you. (1)
O Night, our Mother, entrust us to the Dawn; may the Dawn entrust us to the Day, and the Day to you, O Radiant One. Whatever here flies, and whatever here creeps—[entrust all that to us].
Whatever effort you exert against the mountains, O Night, protect us because of that.
Protect us from behind, protect us from before, and from above as well as from below.
Guard us, O radiant one; we here are your praisers.

Those who attend to the night, those who remain vigilant toward living beings, and those who protect all cattle—they are watchful over our own selves; they are watchful over our cattle. O Night, we truly know your name; you are indeed named Ghṛtācī.
Bharadvāja knows you; may she watch over our wealth for us.

The vigorous maiden, the youthful mistress of the house, Night—the wife of the god Savitṛ and of Bhaga—she who is as swift as a horse, easy to invoke, and endowed with gathered splendor, has filled heaven and earth with her greatness.
The deep one has risen above all things; the most excellent ones have ascended to the highest.
The longing Night follows her auspiciously, as Mitra does with his own powers.
O Night, worthy of choice, praised, fortunate, well-born, you have arrived; may we be here with a gracious mind.
Protect us with the manly powers that have been born, and likewise with those nourishing powers that belong to cattle.
From the lion, from the longing night, from the tiger, and from the leopard, I take luster.
From the horse’s fiery brilliance and the man’s cry, you assume many forms as you shine forth.
May the auspicious Night, the mother of the snow, who is favorable to the sun, be well-disposed toward our invocation. O blessed one, take heed of this hymn with which I praise you in all directions.
O radiant Night, you take pleasure in our hymn like a queen.

(19.49.6.c) May we all be heroes; may we possess all wealth as the dawns break forth. (19.49.7.a) You indeed hold the name "Peace" (śamyā); those who wish to harm my riches— (19.49.7.c)—O Night, drink the breath of life from them! There is no thief to be found, none at all to be found.
(19.49.8) You are auspicious, O Night; like a well-fashioned cup, you bear the form of a cow in every direction, a young woman.
Possessing eyes, longing for my beauty, you have looked upon me as a celestial one looks upon the earth. (19.49.9) Whatever thief comes today, a mortal enemy seeking to do evil—
May the Night, having approached him, strike down his neck and his head.
May she strike down his feet so that he cannot move; may she strike down his hands so that he cannot seize.
He who approaches as a plunderer departs crushed.
He moves away, he retreats, he retreats from the dry stump.
Now, O Night, make the serpent headless and of pungent smoke.
Cast out the two eyes of the wolf; with that, strike him down upon the wooden post.
O Night, those oxen of yours that have sharp horns and swift paces—
by means of them, may you carry us safely across all difficulties today. Night after night, may we cross over with our bodies unharmed.
Like those without a boat, let the enemies not cross over this deep [space].
Just as a grain of millet falling away from its stalk is no longer found,
even so, O Night, cast down him who seeks to harm us.
Drive away the thief who hides among our cattle and goats, as well as the robber;
and him who, having seized the horse's head, seeks to lead it away.
O auspicious Night, whatever wealth they distribute today—‖5‖
(19.50.6.c) Since you provide for others, feed us as well.
(19.50.7’) O Night, deliver us all to the Dawn free from sin;
may the Dawn grant us to the Day, and the Day to you, O Radiant One.
I am unbounded; my self is unbounded; unbounded is my eye, unbounded is my ear.
Unbounded is my out-breath, unbounded is my in-breath, unbounded is my diffused breath; I am all, unbounded.
On the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, being impelled, I take hold of you.
In the beginning, desire arose, which was the first seed of the mind.
O Desire, being of one womb with the Great One through desire, bestow upon the sacrificer an increase of wealth.
O Desire, you are established by power; you are all-pervading, radiant, a friend to him who seeks friendship.
(19.52.2.c) You are fierce, victorious in battles; bestow strength and power upon the sacrificer.

2 (19.52.3’) For him who desired from afar, for the one who offered a counter-stake, for the imperishable one— (19.52.3.c) The quarters of space listened to him; through desire, they brought forth the light of heaven. 3
O Desire, let desire not come to me from heart to heart. May that mind of theirs which is over there come here to me.
O Desire, whatever we do for you as an oblation while longing for you, [may it be effective].
(19.52.5.c) May all that be fulfilled for us; partake now of this oblation, Svāhā!

‖5‖ (19.53.1’) Time, a horse with seven reins, thousand-eyed, undecaying, and rich in seed, draws [the world]. (19.53.1.c) Upon him mount the seers who possess inspired wisdom; his wheels are all the worlds. ‖1‖

This Time carries seven wheels; its nave is sevenfold, and its axle is indeed immortality. Anointing all these worlds, Time moves as the first god. A full jar is placed upon Time; we behold it indeed existing in many forms.
(19.53.3.c) Facing all these worlds, they call him Time in the highest heaven.
(19.53.4.ab) He alone brought together the worlds; he alone went around the worlds.
(19.53.4.cd) Being their father, he became their son; therefore, indeed, there is no other splendor higher than that.
Time generated this heaven; Time [generated] these earths as well.
In Time, indeed, the past and the future are set in motion and abide.
Time created prosperity; in Time the sun burns.
In time all beings exist; in time the eye sees clearly.
In time the mind, in time the breath, and in time name are established.
When time has arrived, all these creatures rejoice.
In time is austerity, in time is the eldest [Brahman], and in time is the concentrated Veda;
for Time is the lord of all, who was the father of Prajāpati.
By him it was impelled, by him it was born, and in him it is established.
Time, having become Brahman, sustains Parameṣṭhin.
Time created progeny; in the beginning, Time created Prajāpati.
From Time was born the self-existent Kaśyapa, and from Time was born ascetic fervor (tapas).
From Time the waters came into being; from Time arose the sacred word, austerity, and the directions.
By Time the sun rises, and by Time it sets again.
By Time the wind blows, and by Time the earth is vast.
The great heaven was placed upon Time.
In ancient times, Time indeed brought forth the past and the future as his sons;
from Time the Ṛg-verses arose, and from Time the Yajus was born.
Time has impelled the sacrifice for the gods, providing an inexhaustible portion.
In Time the Gandharvas and Apsarases abide; in Time the worlds are established.
In Time this divine Aṅgiras and Atharvan stand firm.
Having conquered this world and the highest world, as well as the meritorious worlds and the sacred supports,
he who is Time traverses all worlds by means of Brahman— he is indeed the supreme god. Night after night, they bring him inexhaustible sustenance, like fodder for a standing horse.
Rejoicing in abundance of wealth and in nourishment, may we, as thy neighbors, O Agni, not come to harm.
(1) That arrow of thine which is in Vāta, the wind, that is this very one; with it, be gracious to us.
Rejoicing in abundance of wealth and in nourishment, may we, as thy neighbors, O Agni, not come to harm. (2)
Every evening our householder Agni, every morning the giver of goodwill; be the bestower of wealth upon every wealth! Kindling you, may we nourish our own bodies.
Every morning our householder Agni, every evening the giver of goodwill.
(19.55.4.c) O giver of wealth, prosper for us at every dawn; kindling you, may we flourish for a hundred winters.
(19.55.5’) May I never be one who eats food that has been burnt. Homage to Rudra, the eater of food, the lord of food, and to Agni.
(19.55.5.e) O member of the assembly, protect my assembly, as well as those members who sit in the assembly. (19.55.6’) O Indra, invoked by many, may they attain all life through you;
day after day bringing tribute to you, O Agni, like fodder for a standing horse.
(19.56.1) From the world of Yama you have come hither; O wise one, you join with mortal women.
(19.56.1c) Knowing [the way], you travel in a single chariot alone, measuring out sleep in the womb of the Asura.
(19.56.2) Bandha saw you first, in the all-encompassing [space], before the birth of night, on a certain day.
(19.56.2.c) Then you became this very dream, hiding your form from the physicians.
(19.56.3’) Seeking greatness, he turned away from the great cattle and the Asuras toward the gods;
(19.56.3.c) the thirty-three [gods], having attained the light of heaven, bestowed sovereignty upon that Dream.
Neither the ancestors nor the gods know this [speech] which wanders as idle chatter within these people.
The men, instructed by Varuṇa, the Ādityas, placed the dream in Trita Āptya.
Those who do evil have shared in its cruelty, while those who do good have shared in its auspiciousness through sleeplessness.
(19.56.5.c) You revel in light with your supreme kin; you have been born from the mind that is being heated.
(19.56.6’) We know all your origins from of old; we know you, O Sleep, who are the sovereign lord here. Protect us, who possess glory, for the sake of glory here; go far away from our enemies.
Just as they pay back a sixteenth part, just as an eighth, just as a debt, so do we collect all evil dreams upon our enemy.
The kings have come together; the debts have come together; the *kuṣṭhas* have come together; the sixteenths have come together.

Whatever evil dream has settled upon us, may we drive that evil dream away from our enemy. O auspicious Sleep, you who are the offspring of the wives of the gods and the son of Yama— let that which is mine be good, and let that which is evil we send forth to our enemy.
(19.57.3.e) You are not the mouth of the harsh black bird.

(19.57.4’) O Dream, we know you as such; like a dream-horse, you are like a horse that carries a load. Strip away from us the one who reviles the gods, the hater, whatever evil dream is among us, whatever is among our cattle, and whatever is in our house. (19.57.4.c) Strip it away!
That which is not ours—the hater of the gods, the one who seeks to harm—let him fasten it on himself like a golden necklace.
Let him cast away our nine treasures from there;
we drive all evil dreaming upon the one who hates us.

The impulse of clarified butter, established equally among the gods, increasing through the oblation for a year—may our hearing, sight, and breath remain unimpaired; may we ourselves remain uninjured in life and luster. May breath call upon us; we invoke breath.
(19.58.2.c) May the Earth take up splendor; may Soma and Bṛhaspati bestow splendor upon the mid-region.
2 (19.58.3’) You two, Heaven and Earth, have become the gatherers of splendor. Having taken up splendor, may we move along following the Earth.
3 The cows, approaching, attend upon the glorious lord of cattle. Having taken up glory, may we move along following the Earth. 3
"Build a cow-pen; for he is your protector. Sew together many broad shields.
Make iron fortresses, unassailable. Let not your chalice leak; make it firm.
The eye and the beginning of the sacrifice, and its mouth—I offer with speech, with hearing, and with mind.
(19.58.5.c) May the gods, being well-disposed, come to this sacrifice spread out by Viśvakarman.

(19.58.6’) Those who are the officiating priests of the gods and those who are worthy of sacrifice, to whom the oblation is offered as their portion—may all the powerful gods, having come to this sacrifice together with their wives, rejoice.
(19.58.6.c) 6. May all the powerful gods, having come to this sacrifice together with their wives, rejoice.
(19.59.1) O Agni, you are the guardian of vows, a god among mortals;
you are to be praised at the sacrifices.
(19.59.2) O gods, if we, being more ignorant than the wise, violate your laws, [may you forgive us].
(19.59.2.c) May Agni, the wise one who has entered into the Brāhmaṇas through the Soma, fulfill all that from every side.
(19.59.3’) We have come unto the path of the gods, so that we may carry out what we are able to do.
Agni, the wise one, shall sacrifice; he indeed is the Hotṛ; he shall arrange the rites and the seasons.

May speech be in my mouth, breath in my nostrils, sight in my eyes, and hearing in my ears; may my hair be free from grayness, my teeth free from discoloration, and may there be great strength in my arms,
vigor in my thighs, speed in my calves, and stability in my feet.
May my foundations be unharmed; may I, undecaying, be firm in all my limbs.
(19.60.2.c) May my body be united with my body; may I, through my teeth, attain a full lifespan.
(19.61.1’) Sit comfortably upon me; fill me abundantly, O Pavamāna, in the heavenly realm. (19.61.1.c)
Make me dear among the gods; make me dear among kings;
make me dear to every beholder, whether he be a Śūdra or an Ārya.
Arise, O Brahmaṇaspati! Awaken the gods with the sacrifice.
(19.63.1.c) Increase my life-span, vital breath, progeny, cattle, fame, and the sacrificer.
(19.64.1’) O Agni, I have brought this fuel for the great Jātavedas;
may that Jātavedas bestow upon me faith and wisdom.
O Jātavedas, we strengthen you with this fuel-stick and kindling;
likewise, do you strengthen us with progeny and with wealth.
O Agni, whatever pieces of wood we place before you—
(19.64.3.c) May all that be auspicious for me; O youngest one, take pleasure in that.
(19.64.4’) These are your fuel-sticks, O Agni; once kindled, may you become the fuel itself. Bestow long life upon us and immortality upon our teacher.

Hari, the fair-winged one, has ascended to heaven with his radiance. O Jātavedas, strike down with your heat those who seek to harm you as you fly up to heaven! Ascend to heaven with your flame, O Sūrya, formidable and fearless.
The illusory Asuras, wearing iron nets, wander about marked by their iron fetters.
(19.66.1.c) O Jātavedas, with your heat I subject them to you; as a thousand-pronged thunderbolt, crush the rivals and protect us.
(19.67.1’) May we see a hundred autumns. (19.67.2’) May we live for a hundred autumns.
May we wake for a hundred autumns.
May we grow for a hundred autumns.
May we thrive for a hundred autumns.
May we live for a hundred autumns. (6) May we adorn [the world] for a hundred autumns. (7) May we live for more than a hundred autumns. (8)
I open the aperture of both the narrow and the wide by means of my creative power (*māyā*).
Having extracted the Veda from those two, we shall then perform the ritual acts.
Ye are living beings; may I live; may I live out the full span of life.

(19.69.2) You are those by whom one lives; may I live, may I live out my full span of life. (19.69.3) You are those who cause one to live together; may I live together, may I live out my full span of life.
(19.69.4) You are the givers of life; may I live, may I live out my full span of life.
O Indra, live! O Sūrya, live! O gods, live! May I live!
May I live out the full span of life!
Praised by me, may the boon-granting Mother of the Vedas, the Purifier (*pāvamānī*), who impels the twice-born, inspire them.
Having bestowed upon me life, breath, progeny, cattle, fame, wealth, and Vedic splendor,
depart for the world of Brahmā.
From whatever treasury we have drawn forth this Veda, into that very place we now deposit it.

(19.72.1.c) What has been performed and sacrificed was done through the power of Brahmā; therefore, O gods, protect me here with your ascetic heat. (20.1.1’) O Indra, we invoke you, the bull, when the Soma is pressed; as such, drink of the sweet food.
O Maruts, of great splendor from heaven, that person in whose dwelling you drink [the soma] is indeed the most well-guarded of men.
To him who provides bulls as food, who provides cows as food, whose back is laden with soma, and who is the wise ordainer— [to him, O Maruts, grant protection].
(20.1.3.c) Let us worship Agni with hymns of praise.

||3|| (20.2.1’) May the Maruts drink the Soma from the Potṛ’s cup, with the *suṣṭubh* chant and the *svarka* song, according to the season. ||1|| (20.2.2’) May Agni drink the Soma from the Āgnīdhra’s cup, with the *suṣṭubh* chant and the *svarka* song, according to the season. ||2||
(20.2.3) May Indra, the Brahman, drink the Soma with the *ṛtu* [seasonal cup] from the well-praised, well-sung Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin.
(20.2.4) May the god Draviṇodas drink the Soma with the *ṛtu* [seasonal cup] from the well-praised, well-sung Potṛ.
(20.3.1) Come hither, for we have pressed it for you; O Indra, drink this Soma!
(20.3.1.c) This sacred grass is my seat.
||1|| (20.3.2’) O Indra, let the two long-maned bay horses, yoked by prayer, bring you hither;
listen to our prayers. ||2||
O Indra, we Brahmins, possessing Soma and having pressed it, invoke you as our companion, the drinker of Soma.
(3) Come to us who have pressed the juice; come to our well-spoken hymns. (1)
(20.4.1.c) O fair-cheeked one, drink well of the soma-juice!
(20.4.2’) I pour it into your two flanks; let it flow through your limbs.
Seize the sweetness with your tongue! (20.4.2.c) Seize the sweetness with your tongue!
(20.4.3’) May it be sweet for your enjoyment, honeyed for your body;
(20.4.3.c) may the Soma be a blessing to your heart.
3 (20.5.1’) And this one, O you who observe all people, has encompassed you like women [embracing a man].
(20.5.1.c) O Soma, flow forth to Indra! ‖1‖ (20.5.2’) Broad-necked, pot-bellied, strong-armed, seated at the soma-juice, Indra strikes down the Vṛtras. ‖2‖
O Indra, go forth at the head; you are the lord of all by your might.
O slayer of Vṛtra, strike down the Vṛtras.
Let your hook be long, with which you bestow wealth.
(20.5.4.c) For the sacrificer who presses the soma.
(20.5.5’) This soma of yours, O Indra, is purified upon the sacred grass; come hither, hasten to it, and drink!
(20.5.5.c) Come hither, hasten to it, and drink! (5)
O Śācigu, for you who are honored as powerful, this [soma] is pressed for your delight;
O Ākhaṇḍala, you are invoked.
That Kuṇḍapāyya which is yours, O grandson, great-grandson, like a bull with horns—
(20.5.7.c) Let them fix their minds upon him.
7 (20.6.1’) O Indra, we invoke you, the bull, when the soma is pressed;
(20.6.1.c) so drink of the sweet food. 1
O Indra, much-praised one, take pleasure in this pressed Soma that finds the power of the mind;
drink and fill yourself with full satisfaction!
O Indra, together with all the gods, further our sacrifice which is accompanied by our prayers.
O Lord of the People, being praised, come hither!
(20.6.3.c) O Indra, these pressed Soma-drops are moving forth for you, O Lord of the Good; the bright drops seek your dwelling. (20.6.4)
(20.6.5) Place within your belly the pressed Soma, O Indra, the most excellent;
yours are the celestial drops.
(20.6.6) O lover of songs, drink our pressed juice; you are anointed by the streams of honey.
(20.6.6.c) O Indra, glory is indeed bestowed by you alone.
||6|| (20.6.7.a) Unfailing splendors attend upon Indra, like those who possess the woods;
(20.6.7.c) having drunk of the Soma, he has grown strong. ||7||
Come to us from nearby and from afar, O slayer of Vṛtra;
take pleasure in these our songs.
When you are invoked from the space between the distant and the near, [come to us].
(20.6.9.c) O Indra, come here from there!
9 (20.7.1’) O Sūrya, you rise up toward the bull of renowned bounty, the performer of manly deeds, the archer. 1
He who by the strength of his arms shattered ninety-nine fortresses,
he, the slayer of Vṛtra, struck down the serpent.
May that Indra be our auspicious friend, [bestowing] horses, cattle, and barley.
(20.7.3.c) She yields like a cow with a broad udder.
‖3‖ (20.7.4’) O Indra, much-praised one, take pleasure in the pressed Soma that awakens the mind;
drink and pour it down until you are fully satisfied. ‖4‖
(20.8.1) Thus protect us as of old; let [the Soma] exhilarate you. Hear our prayer and be strengthened by our songs.
Make the sun manifest, cause the nourishments to swell, slay the enemies, and pierce through for the cattle, O Indra!
(20.8.2) Come hither; they say to you, "We desire Soma. This has been pressed; drink of it for intoxication.
O wide-extending one, fill your belly; being invoked, hear us like a father.

(20.8.2.c) His beaker is full—svāhā! Like a pourer, he has filled the vessel for drinking. Together the dear Soma juices have turned toward Indra for exhilaration, moving clockwise around him. (20.8.3)

We praise with songs that Indra for you—the wondrous one, the subduer of enemies, who rejoices in the exhilarating soma-juice—just as cows low toward their calf in the stalls. (1) We praise him, the celestial one, the bounteous giver, encompassed by powers, who possesses manifold nourishment like a mountain. (2)

We implore you for food accompanied by cattle, hundredfold and thousandfold— swiftly, we seek it rich in herds of kine. I beg of you that heroic power, that sacred prayer (*brahman*) for the sake of first thought,
by which you helped the *yatis* and Bhr̥gu when the prize was staked, and by which you protected Praskaṇva.
When you released the great waters toward the ocean, O Indra, that was your manly might;
instantly, his greatness cannot be fully grasped, he whom the worlds have cried out after.
4 Upward indeed rise your most honey-sweet songs and hymns of praise.
Like chariots seeking booty, the Satrājits—winners of wealth and possessors of unfailing aid—have sped forth.
Like the Kaṇvas, like the Bhr̥gus, like suns, they have attained every desire.
Magnifying Indra with hymns, the Āyus and the Priyamedhas have raised their voices.
Indra, the breaker of forts, has overcome the Dāsa with his hymns; the finder of wealth, bestowing gifts, he has scattered his enemies.
Urged by prayer and increasing in body, the giver of much has filled both heaven and earth.
I send forth my voice to stimulate you, the powerful Makha, adorning it for the sake of the immortal.
(20.11.2.c) O Indra, you are the one who goes before the human settlements and the divine tribes alike.
(20.11.3’) Indra, whose aim is to destroy, encompassed Vṛtra; he, whose aim is to transform, frustrated the wiles of the guileful.
He struck down Vyansa, burning fiercely among the woods, and made manifest the lowing of the cows during the nights.

Indra, winner of the light, generating the days, has conquered the hostile armies with his helpers, being victorious. He made the banner of the days shine for Manu; he found the light for great joy. Indra entered into the strength and power, performing many heroic deeds like a man.
(20.11.5.c) For he has willed these thoughts for the singer; he has extended this bright hue of theirs.

(20.11.6’) They celebrate his great and mighty deeds—Indra’s many well-performed exploits. With his strength, he crushed the crooked ones with his might; with his magical powers, he overcame the Dasyus through superior force. (20.11.6.c) He who possesses overwhelming power. 6.
Yudhendra, by his greatness, has created wide space for the gods; the Lord of the True, the filler of the peoples.
At the seat of Vivasvat, the inspired singers and sages praise those deeds of his with hymns.
[He is] the ever-conquering one, the most excellent, the giver of victory, who has won the light and the divine waters.
(20.11.8.c) They have won over this earth and even this heaven; the wise ones rejoice after Indra.
8 (20.11.9’) Indra has won the steeds and he has won the sun; Indra has won the cow that provides much nourishment.
9.c He has won golden wealth as well; having slain the Dasyus, he protected the Aryan race. 9.d-ef
Indra has won the plants and the days; he has won the trees and the mid-air.
He shattered the strength [of the enemy] and drove away the disputants; thus he became the subduer of those who act with hostile intent.
We invoke for our welfare Indra the Bounteous, the most heroic in this battle, the winner of booty.
(20.11.11.c) Hear him, the fierce one, for aid in battles; he who slays the Vṛtras and wins riches.
(20.12.1’) The sacred hymns have risen up toward Indra for glory; magnify him, O Vasiṣṭha, in the assembly.
He who has extended all things with his power—he shall listen to the words of one such as me.
The cry has gone forth, O Indra, born of the gods, as you exercise sovereignty over the spoils in the contest.
For one’s own lifespan is not known among men; therefore, carry us across these distresses.
I yoke the booty-seeking chariot with the two bay horses; my prayers have reached you who take pleasure in them.
(20.12.3.c) By his greatness, Indra forced asunder the two worlds, he who struck down the Vṛtras without opposition.

(20.12.4.a) Even the waters swelled like barren cows; your singers, O Indra, have reached the eternal Law (*ṛta*). (20.12.4.c) Come toward us with your teams as Vāyu does, for through our prayers you distribute the spoils of victory.
(20.12.5) May those exhilarating draughts intoxicate you, O Indra, the impetuous one who bestows abundant wealth upon the singer.
For you alone among the gods have compassion for mortals; O hero, rejoice at this libation!
(20.12.6) Thus do the Vasiṣṭhas honor with their hymns Indra, the bull whose arm wields the thunderbolt.
(20.12.6.c) May he, when praised, bestow wealth consisting of heroes and cattle; do you [gods] protect us always with your blessings!

6 (20.12.7’) The consumer of the dregs, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the bull, the overcomer of the swift, the impetuous king, the slayer of Vṛtra, the drinker of Soma—having yoked his two bay horses, may Indra come hither and exhilarate himself at the midday libation. 7

O Indra and Bṛhaspati, drink the Soma, rejoicing at this sacrifice, O you who possess bull-like wealth! May the self-sustaining drops enter into you both; bestow upon us wealth consisting of all heroic sons.
May your swift-gliding, fleet-flying coursers carry you hither; come forth with your arms.
Sit upon the sacred grass; a wide seat has been prepared for you. Rejoice, O Maruts, in the sweet juice of the soma-plant.
Let us fashion this hymn with our intellect for Jātavedas, who is worthy of it, just as one constructs a chariot.
For his providence toward us is auspicious in the assembly; O Agni, may we never suffer harm in your friendship.
Come hither with these, O Agni, on one chariot or on many chariots, for thy horses are powerful;
bring hither according to thy wont the thirty-three gods accompanied by their wives, and rejoice!
We, seeking thy aid, O peerless one, bringing [offerings] to thee as if supporting a massive pillar, [pray to thee].
(20.14.1.c) We invoke the wondrous one for the prize.
(20.14.2’) To you, for aid in the rite, let our fierce and bold one come, he who is the youth.
For we have chosen you alone, O Indra, as our victorious friend and protector.
Him who brought this and that wealth here in the past—him indeed do I praise for you, O friends, Indra, for our protection.
Him, the lord of the bay horses, the lord of the good, the subduer of peoples; for he is indeed the one who has gladdened us.
(20.14.4.c) May that Maghavan bestow upon us, his worshippers, hundreds of cattle and horses.
(20.15.1’) To the most generous, the lofty one of vast wealth, whose strength is true and who is powerful—to him I bring my hymn of praise.
Like waters down a slope, his irresistible bounty, which sustains all life, has been opened wide for our power.

Then let everything laugh at your sacrifice, as the waters flow downward to the libations of the one who offers oblations; when, like a mountain, the beloved golden thunderbolt of Indra has settled, it shall strike down the foe.
To this formidable one, bring worship with reverence at the sacrifice, as you would bring the bright light of the dawn to the most praiseworthy one.
(20.15.3.c) For whom his abode, his name, his power, and his light have been made for glory—he who is like a bay steed to be led.
(20.15.4’) O Indra, praised by many, we here are yours, we who move about having taken hold of you, O Lord of abundant wealth.
For there is none other than you, O lover of songs, who can sustain our hymns; accept this speech of ours as you would the two worlds.
Great is your heroic power, O Indra; we belong to you. O Maghavan, fulfill the desire of this singer.
The vast heaven yields to your heroism, and this earth, too, bows before your might.
O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt, you have shattered that great and wide mountain into pieces with your bolt.
(20.15.6.c) You let loose the waters that were held back to flow; you have truly possessed all conquering power as your own alone.

(20.16.1’) Like birds plunging into water while guarding their young, like the thunderous roars of a rain-cloud, like waves breaking from the mountains in their exhilaration, the hymns of praise have resounded toward Bṛhaspati.
Approaching with the cows, like Bhaga he has led Aryaman, O Aṅgiras. Like Mitra among the people, he anoints the husband and wife; O Bṛhaspati, urge on the swift steeds for the prize as in the race.
The sacrificial offerings are successful, hospitable, vigorous, desirable, golden-hued, and of irreproachable form.
(20.16.3.c) Bṛhaspati, having pierced through the mountains, drove out the cows like barley from winnowing baskets.
(20.16.4.a–c) Sprinkling the seat of Order with honey, casting down the firebrand of the sun as if from heaven,
Bṛhaspati, lifting the cows from the rock, split the skin of the earth as if with water.
With light he drove away the darkness from the mid-air; as the wind drives the foam from the water, so Bṛhaspati, having seized the cattle of Vala, brought them hither like the wind driving a cloud.
When Bṛhaspati shattered the strength of the reviling Vala with his fire-heated hymns—
(20.16.6.c) With his teeth he took up that which had been surrounded by the tongue; he made manifest the hidden treasures of the ruddy cows.
(20.16.7’) For Bṛhaspati knew that name of these lowing ones, which was hidden in the secret place of their dwelling.
As one breaks open the egg of a bird, he himself brought forth the ruddy cows from the mountain.
He beheld the honey fastened with a stone, like a fish dwelling in shallow water;
Bṛhaspati, having split it open with his roar, drew it forth as one draws a cup from a tree.
He found the dawn, he found the sun, he found the fire; with his song of praise, he drove away the darkness.
Bṛhaspati extracted the marrow from Vala, who had the form of a cow, as one extracts [the pith] from a joint.
Like forests robbed of their leaves by winter, Vala lamented for his cattle because of Bṛhaspati.
He performed an act that could not be imitated and was not to be repeated, since the sun and moon rise from each other in alternation.
The fathers adorned the sky with stars, as one adorns a dark horse with golden ornaments.
They placed darkness in the night and light in the day; Bṛhaspati split the mountain and found the cows.
We have performed this homage to the cloud-god, who roars repeatedly after many [days].
May Bṛhaspati bestow vital strength upon us with cattle, with horses, with heroes, and with men.
All my yearning thoughts, seeking the light of heaven, have sung in unison toward Indra.
They embrace him as wives embrace a husband, as they would a handsome youth, for the sake of his bounty and protection.

My mind indeed never turns away from you; in you alone, O much-invoked one, have I placed my desire. Like a king, O wondrous one, sit down upon the sacred grass; let there be a place for your drinking at this excellent soma.
Indra is the overcomer of distress and of hunger; he, the bounteous lord, rules over wealth and treasure.
For him, these seven rivers flowing down the slopes increase the vigor of the impetuous bull.
Like birds alighting upon a tree with beautiful foliage, the exhilarating Soma drops, seated in the bowls, have settled within Indra.
Their front ranks, flashing with power, have found the light of heaven for man—the Aryan light.
The gambler does not gather up what he has lost at play when Maghavan wins the sun as his prize.
No other, neither one of old, O Maghavan, nor one of recent times, can equal that heroic deed of yours.
Maghavan has gone about from tribe to tribe; the Bull has looked down upon the lowing of the people.
He at whose libations Śakra rejoices overcomes his assailants with potent Soma-draughts.
When the Soma-streams flow toward Indra like waters to the ocean or rivulets to a lake,
the inspired singers increase his greatness in the sacrificial hall, just as rain nourishes the barley with its heavenly bounty.
Like a bull enraged, he rushed through the dust, he who made these waters the wives of a noble lord.
That Maghavan found light for the man who presses the juice, for the one who gives quickly and offers oblations.
Let the axe spring up together with the light; let there be, as of old, a cow that yields the milk of Truth abundantly.
May the ruddy one shine forth with his brilliance, pure as the bright light of heaven; may the Lord of the Truth blaze like the radiant sun.
O Much-invoked One, may we cross over ill-will with cattle, and all hunger with grain.
May we, together with the kings, be the first to win wealth through our own heroic band.
May Bṛhaspati protect us from behind, and from above, and from below, from the one who intends evil. May Indra from the front and from the middle grant wide space for us, as a friend to his friends.
O Bṛhaspati and you, Indra, you two are the masters of celestial wealth and of that which is on earth.
Bestow wealth even upon the singer who praises you; protect us always with your blessings.
O Indra, we your friends, seeking you, call upon you for this purpose;
the Kaṇvas praise you with their hymns.
(20.18.2’) Indeed, nothing else has pleased me, O wielder of the thunderbolt, as much as this newest work of the skillful man; I have set my mind upon your hymn of praise.
(20.18.3’) The gods desire one who presses the soma; they do not long for sleep.
The unwearied ones proceed toward heedlessness. 3 O Indra, O Bull, we who long for you praise you aloud;
O Vasu, take note of this of ours! 4
Do not deliver us to reproach or to the words of the hostile enemy; for my mental power is centered in you.
You are our wide-spreading armor and our champion in the forefront, O slayer of Vṛtra.
I speak with you as my ally.
O Indra, we turn you toward us for the slaying of Vṛtra, for power, and for victory in battle.
O Śatakratu, may the worshippers turn your mind and your eye toward us,
O Indra.
We invoke all your names, O Śatakratu, with all our songs.
(20.19.3.c) O Indra, for the overcoming of adversaries!
(20.19.4’) With the hundred powers of the one praised by many, we magnify Indra, the sustainer of the people. (20.19.4.c) Of Indra, the upholder of the tribes. (20.19.4’) 4.
I invoke Indra, who is invoked by many, for the slaying of Vṛtra, and for the winning of booty in battles.
O Śatakratu, be victorious in the contests for booty; we pray to you.
O Indra, for the slaying of Vṛtra!
In glorious deeds, in the contest for booty, in battles, and in the winning of renown— O Indra, be victorious over those who harbor malice!
Drink for our protection the most powerful, glorious, and watchful Soma, O Indra, Lord of a hundred powers!
O Lord of a hundred powers, those vital energies of yours which exist among the five peoples—
(20.20.2.c) O Indra, those [powers] of yours I choose.
||2|| (20.20.3’) O Indra, you have attained great renown; bestow upon us invincible splendor. (20.20.3.c) We cause your strength to swell upward. ||3||
Come to us from nearby, O Śakra, and also from afar;
O wielder of the stone, come here from whatever world is yours, O Indra.
Indeed, Indra shall drive away even great fear that assails us.
For he is steadfast and active among the people.
(5) May Indra be gracious to us; may no evil reach us from behind.
May there be prosperity for us from the front. (6)
May Indra grant us freedom from fear from all directions;
he is the conqueror of enemies, the one who observes all people.
We bring forth our speech, we offer songs to the Great One, to Indra at the seat of Vivasvat.
(20.21.1.c) For never indeed have they found treasure as if among those who sleep; ill-praise is not commended among the bestowers of wealth.
(20.21.2’) You are the opener of the stall for horses, O Indra, the opener of the stall for cattle, the opener of the stall for barley—the powerful lord of riches.
Aid to men from of old, you who do not weary when unasked, a friend to friends—him indeed we praise here.
O powerful Indra, doer of many deeds, most resplendent one, this wealth all around you is known to be yours alone.
Therefore, O conqueror, gather it from there and bring it hither; do not let the desire of the singer who loves you remain unfulfilled.
With these days, with these drops of Soma, being well-disposed, drive away poverty with cattle and horses.
With the drops, may we, with Indra, rend the Dasyu; with our enmities stilled, may we be united with nourishment.

O Indra, may we be united with wealth, with nourishment, with spoils that are many-glittering and celestial. May we be united with divine providence, which is full of heroic vigor, preeminent in cattle, and rich in horses.

(20.21.6) Those exhilarations have gladdened you, those manly powers, O Lord of the Good, those Soma-draughts in the slayings of Vṛtra—when for the singer who spread the sacred grass, you, irresistible, struck down ten thousand Vṛtras.
(20.21.7) With boldness you go from battle to battle; you utterly destroy stronghold after stronghold with your might.
When, O Indra, through your friendship, you struck down the guileful one named Namuci in the far distance;
when you slew Karañja and Parṇaya with the most piercing path of Atithigva;
when you, unyielding, shattered the hundred fortresses of Vaṅgr̥da that were besieged by R̥jiśvan.

O you who are renowned, with your chariot wheel you struck down the ninety-nine thousand six hundred followers of Janarāja, who had come against you with his kinsman Suśravas— making them difficult to tread upon. O Indra, you protected Suśravas with your aids and Tūrvayāṇa with your protections.
(20.21.10.c) You subdued Kutsa, Atithigva, and Āyu for this great, youthful king who was to be served.

(20.21.11’) O Indra, may we be your most auspicious friends, protected by the gods at the height of our lives. Praising you, with you as our hero, may we attain an even longer and more extended span of life.
O Bull, at this pressing, I pour out the pressed juice for you to drink;
satisfy yourself and enjoy the exhilaration.
Let not the foolish, the greedy, nor those who mock you deceive you.
(20.22.2.c) Do not favor those who hate sacred knowledge.
(20.22.3’) Here, let these [soma-juices], rich in cattle, exhilarate you for great bounty;
drink like a wild bull at a lake.
Sing forth with song to Indra, the lord of cattle, as he is known— to him,
the son of truth, the protector of the righteous.
The bay horses have been let loose upon the ruddy sacrificial grass.
(20.22.5.c) Wherein we raise our voices together.
||5|| (20.22.6’) For Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the cows have yielded the milk-mixture, the honey-sweetness, (20.22.6.c) when he found it in his secret hiding place. ||6||
Come then to us, O Indra, being invoked toward me for the drinking of the Soma; come with your two bay horses, O wielder of the stone!
The Hotṛ has sat down according to the season; the sacrificial grass has been strewn in due order.

(20.23.2.c) The pressing-stones have yoked themselves at dawn. (20.23.3’) These prayers are being made, O you who are borne by prayer; sit upon the sacred grass. O Hero, partake of the sacrificial cake.
(20.23.3.c) Partake of the sacrificial cake, O Hero.
Rejoice in these libations of ours, O slayer of Vṛtra, in these hymns, O Indra, lover of songs!
(4) Our prayers caress the vast Lord of Might, the drinker of Soma. (5)
(20.23.5.c) As mothers [low for] their calf, [we low] for Indra. 5 (20.23.6’) So do you rejoice in the soma-juice for the sake of great bounty from your own body;
(20.23.6.c) do not deliver your praiser to reproach. 6
O Indra, we, seeking you and bearing oblations, sing your praises;
and you, O Vasu, are well-disposed toward us.
Do not release us to the enemy; come hither, O lover of the bay steeds.
(20.23.8.c) O Indra, self-dependent one, rejoice here!
8 (20.23.9’) O Indra, let the two long-maned horses, dripping with clarity, carry you hither on the easy chariot to sit upon the sacred grass. 9
Come to our pressed Soma, O Indra, mixed with milk— the one which, along with your two bay steeds,
seeks us. Come, O Indra, to that exhilarating drink, pressed by the stones upon the sacred grass.
(20.24.2.c) Will he not indeed satisfy us?
(20.24.3.a) Thus have my songs gone forth from here, sent toward Indra, (20.24.3.c) to turn him hither for the drinking of the soma.
We invoke Indra here with hymns for the drinking of the soma; will he not surely come at our songs of praise?
O Indra, these somas are pressed; take them up, O Lord of a hundred powers!
In your belly, O Lord of the prize-winning steeds!
(5) For we know you, O Sage, as the winner of wealth, bold in battles;
therefore, we seek your favor. (6)
O Indra, come with your bulls and drink this pressed juice of ours, mixed with milk and mixed with barley.
O Indra, in your own dwelling, I urge you to drink the Soma.
May this delight you in your heart.
8 We, the Kuśikas, seeking your aid, invoke you, O Indra, the ancient one, to drink of the pressed soma. 9
The mortal man who is well-protected by your aids, O Indra, goes first to the possession of horses and cattle.
You indeed fill him with even greater wealth, just as the conscious waters flow from all sides toward the ocean.
Like divine waters, they approach the place of the Hotṛ; having been brought down, they behold it spread out like the vast expanse of space.
(20.25.2.c) The gods lead the god-seeking man forward; they cherish him who loves sacred prayer like suitors.
(20.25.3’) You have bestowed the hymn-worthy word upon the two who, with uplifted ladles, serve as a pair.
Unrestrained, he dwells and prospers within your ordinance; a blessing is the power for the sacrificer who presses the soma.
Then the Aṅgirases first attained vital strength, they who had kindled the fires through their skillful work with the sacrificial post.
These heroes found all the wealth of Paṇi as food, consisting of horses, cattle, and livestock.
Atharvan was the first to stretch out the paths by means of sacrifices; from there, Sūrya, the guardian of the sacred law, was born as a seer.

(20.25.5.c) Uśanā Kāvya drove the cows hither; together we sacrifice to the immortal birth of Yama. (20.25.6’) When the sacrificial grass is strewn for the sake of good offspring, or when the hymn proclaims its song of
I offer a true draught for the bull’s drinking, for thee, O Lord of Bay Steeds, of the pressed juice, as thou goest forth.
Indra, rejoice here with our songs, being praised with all our prayers and with power.
In every endeavor, in every battle, we invoke the most mighty one.
(20.26.1.c) O friends, [call] Indra for our protection! (20.26.2’) May he indeed come, if he hears us, with his thousandfold aids, with spoils of war, to our invocation!
(20.26.2.c) [May he come] to our call with his strengths!
From the ancient dwelling, I call upon the hero of many defenses,
whom your father called upon of old.
They yoke the ruddy, bright one as he moves around those who stand still.
The luminous realms shine in heaven.
4 They yoke his two beloved bay horses to the chariot on either side—red, bold, and carrying the hero. 5
Making a signal for the signal-less, O men, making a form for the formless,
you were born together with the dawns.
O Indra, if I were the sole lord of wealth as you are!
(20.27.1.c) May my praiser be a possessor of cattle.
(20.27.2’) O Lord of Might, may I bestow upon this wise man and desire to give to him, were I to be a lord of cattle.
(20.27.2.c) Were I to be a lord of cattle.
O Indra, your bounty is like a cow for the sacrificer who presses the soma;
swelling with milk, she yields cattle and horses.
O Indra, there is no one to obstruct your gift, neither god nor mortal.
(20.27.4.c) Since you, when praised, desire to bestow wealth. (20.27.5.a) The sacrifice strengthened Indra when he spread out the earth,
(20.27.5.c) making for himself a diadem in the sky.
We choose for ourselves your aid, O Indra, you who have grown great and have won all treasures.
In the exhilaration of Soma, you extended across the mid-air and the luminous realms.
When Indra split Vala asunder,
he drove forth the cows for the Aṅgirases, making manifest those that were hidden in the cave;
he pushed Vala back and turned him toward us.
By Indra, the luminous realms of heaven were made firm and strengthened; they are steadfast, not to be driven away.
Like a joyous wave of waters, the hymn of praise hastens toward Indra with speed.

(20.28.4.c) Your exhilarations have shone forth. (20.29.1’) For you, O Indra, are the one who increases the *stoma*, the one who increases the *uktha*; you are the bringer of auspiciousness to those who praise you. (20.29.1.c) You are the maker of blessings for the singers. (20.29.1) 1. You, O Indra, are indeed the one who increases the *stoma* and the one who increases the *uktha*; you are the bringer of good fortune to those who offer praise. May the two long-maned bay steeds carry Indra to the drinking of the Soma,
to the sacrifice of the bounteous giver.
With the foam of the waters, O Indra, you struck off the head of Namuci.
When you conquered all rival hosts. 3 O Indra, the Dasyus who sought to escape by means of magic and attempted to scale up to heaven—you shook them down. 4
(20.29.5) O Indra, you have scattered the assembly of those who offer no libations in all directions, becoming the superior drinker of Soma.
5 (20.30.1) I shall proclaim your two bay steeds at the great sacrifice; I win for you, the conqueror, the desirable exhilaration. 1
(20.30.1.c) Like ghee, he who pours forth beauty with his bay steeds—may our songs enter you, whose form is golden.
(20.30.2’) For they have sung together toward the golden womb, urging on the two bay steeds as if to the celestial seat;
His is that golden, iron thunderbolt, desirable and golden, held within his two hands;
brilliant, fair-cheeked, with golden fury as its missile—golden forms have been infused into Indra.
Like a banner in heaven, the desirable one has been set up; the golden thunderbolt has expanded itself like a swift rush.
(20.30.4.c) The golden-jawed one struck the serpent; he of iron became possessed of a thousand flames, the bearer of the golden [light].
(20.30.5’) O Indra, golden-haired, you have always been delighted by the ancient sacrificers who offered praise.
You take delight [in the sacrifice]; all that is worthy of hymn is yours—your perfect, desirable bounty, O you who are born of the golden [light].
The two beloved bay steeds carry Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the exhilarated one worthy of praise, to the rapture [of the sacrifice].
For him, for Indra, the many libations are pleasing; the golden Soma-drops have flowed forth.
The bay steeds have been prepared sufficiently for his desire; the bay steeds, urging on the swift pair of bay steeds, hasten toward the steadfast one.
He who moves according to his pleasure with his bay coursers has attained his desire for the Lord of Bay Steeds.
He with the golden beard and golden hair, the iron-strong one, who grew mighty at the swift draught, he who drinks the golden juice;
he, the possessor of wealth, who with his bay coursers shall carry us across all difficulties.
Whose two tawny jaws, like two ladles, have flown apart as he shakes them for the sake of strength;
when, having drunk of the exhilarating, desirable juice, he polished his two tawny steeds over the prepared chalice.
And indeed, from the dwelling of the desirable one between the two worlds, the Lord of Bay Steeds has neighed like a courser toward the prize.
(20.31.5.c) For even the vast earth, the *dhiṣaṇā*, has been won by your might; you have assumed great vital power, O desirable one, even from that which was already desired.
(20.32.1’) Desiring both worlds with your greatness, you desire a thought ever new and dear to you.
O Asura, make the desirable dwelling of the cow manifest for the golden Sun.

(20.32.2) May the draft-horses of men bring you, the longing one with bay horses, O Indra, onto your chariot—so that you, delighting in the sacrifice at the communal feast where the ten fingers labor, may drink of the offered mead. (20.32.3) You have drunk of the pressed juices of former times, O Lord of Bay Horses; even so, this libation is yours alone.

(20.32.3.c) O Indra, drink the honeyed Soma; pour it all at once, like a bull, into your belly. (20.33.1’) O Lord of the Bay Steeds, drink here of the Soma washed in the waters, pressed by the men; fill your belly with it.
O Indra, you for whom the pressing-stones have shed [the juice], increase your exhilaration through them, for you are borne by the hymns.
I offer a true draught for drinking to you, the bull, of the pressed juice for your journey, O Lord of the Bay Steeds;
Indra, rejoice here with our songs, being praised by all our prayers and with power.
O Lord of Power, through your aid and your heroism, the eager ones who know the Eternal Order take on vital strength.
(20.33.3.c) O Indra, those who possess offspring have stood in the house, praising you as their companions at the feast.
(20.34.1’) He who, as soon as born, was the first wise god and encompassed the gods with his power;
he before whose breath the two worlds trembled through the greatness of his manly strength—he, O people, is Indra.
He who steadied the trembling earth, who set at rest the agitated mountains;
he who measured out the wide mid-air and propped up the sky—he, O people, is Indra.
He who, having slain the dragon, released the seven rivers, and who drove forth the cows by opening Vala’s enclosure.
(20.34.3.c) He who generated fire between two stones, the destroyer in battles—he, O people, is Indra.
(20.34.4’) He by whom all these things were made to tremble, who cast the Dāsa race down into hiding;
he who, like a gambler winning the stake, seized the riches of the enemy—he, O people, is Indra.
When they ask, "Where is that terrible one? they say of him, "He does not exist.
He destroys the prosperity of the nobleman like a gambler's stakes; have faith in him, for he, O people, is Indra.
He who is the inspirer of the weary, of the emaciated, of the priest who implores, and of the singer—
(20.34.6.c) He who is the protector of the one who has set the pressing-stones in motion, the fair-cheeked lord of the pressed soma—he, O people, is Indra.
(20.34.7’) He in whose direction are horses, in whose direction are cattle, in whose direction are villages, and in whose direction are all chariots;
he who begot the sun and the dawn, he who is the leader of the waters—he, O people, is Indra.
He whom the two contending armies, both the higher and the lower, invoke as their enemies;
he whom two men mounted upon the same chariot call upon separately—he, O people, is Indra.
Without whom the people do not conquer, and whom those engaged in battle invoke for protection—[he is Indra].
(20.34.9.c) He who became the counterpart of the universe, he who shook what was unshakable—he, O people, is Indra.
(20.34.10’) He who with his arrow struck down those who committed great sin against the many, yet did not think [of him as their foe];
he who does not yield to the arrogance of the defiant; he who is the slayer of the Dasyu—he, O people, is Indra.
He who discovered Śambhara dwelling among the mountains in the fortieth autumn;
he who slew the dragon Ahi as he displayed his power, the Dānu lying there—he, O people, is Indra. He who overran Śambhara with his spears, and who drank the pressed soma from the beautiful cup.
He who, amidst the mountains, overwhelmed the many people performing sacrifice—O men, he is Indra. He who, the bull of great power with seven reins, released the seven rivers to flow;
he who, thunderbolt-armed, struck down Rauhiṇa as he was scaling heaven—O men, he is Indra.
Even Heaven and Earth bow down before him; even the mountains tremble at his might.
He who is the Soma-drinker, whose arm is braced, who holds the thunderbolt in his hand—he, O people, is Indra.
He who protects with his aid the one who presses the juice, the one who cooks, the one who recites, and the one who exerts himself.
(20.34.15.c) He for whom there is the increase of the *brahman*, for whom there is Soma, and for whom there is this bounty—he, O people, is Indra.
(20.34.16’) As soon as he was born, he looked out from the lap of his parents; he knows not of any other progenitor than his own.
He who, being praised, observes the laws (*vratā*) of the gods—he, O people, is Indra.
He who desires the Soma, the lord of bay horses, the patron from whom all beings tremble;
he who slew Śambara and Śuṣṇa—he who is the sole hero, O people, he is Indra.
You who, even against the stubborn one, bestow strength upon him who presses and cooks [the offering]—you indeed are truly real.
(20.34.18.c) May we, O Indra, ever be dear to you; with brave sons, may we proclaim our wisdom at the assembly.

‖18‖ (20.35.1’) To him alone, the powerful and swift one, I offer this hymn like a refreshing draught, to the magnificent one; to the one who is worthy of praise, the irresistible Indra, I present these most excellent prayers. ‖1‖

To him indeed I extend this praise like an offering; I bring forth a hymn of laudation with skillful verse. For Indra, the ancient lord, they have polished their prayers with heart, mind, and inspired thought.
To him indeed I bring with my mouth this supreme, heaven-winning hymn of praise.

(20.35.3.c) With the most bountiful invocations of our thoughts and with well-fashioned hymns, we seek to magnify the patron, the lord. (20.35.4.a) For him alone I fashion this song of praise, as a carpenter fashions a chariot for its master;
(20.35.4.c) And songs with well-fashioned hymns for Indra, the bearer of songs, the all-impelling one, the wise.
For him indeed, for Indra, I fashion with the ladle a hymn like a prize-horse,
seeking glory— for him the hero who dwells in bounty, whom I shall praise, the shatterer of forts whose fame is celebrated.
For him indeed Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned the thunderbolt, most skillfully wrought, resounding, for the battle.

(20.35.6.c) By which he found even Vṛtra’s vital spot, striking him down—how great was he who, being the Lord, struck with his strike! (20.35.7’) Having at once drunk the draught from his mother’s libations, and having eaten the choice foods of the Great One, Viṣṇu, the more powerful, stole the cooked meal; he pierced the boar, shooting through the rock.
For him indeed, for Indra, even the divine wives, the consorts of the gods, wove a song of praise upon the slaying of the serpent.
He has encompassed the two wide worlds, heaven and earth; they have not attained the limit of his greatness.
His very greatness has exceeded the extent of heaven, earth, and the intermediate space.
(20.35.9.c) Indra, praised by all, the self-resounding and peerless one, has grown strong in his own home for the sake of battle.
(20.35.10’) By his very power, Indra cut Vṛtra to pieces with his thunderbolt as he was roaring;
like cows released from their pen, he set the rivers free, being intent on bestowing glory.
By his brilliance the rivers were stilled when he hemmed them in with his thunderbolt.
Acting as a lord, bestowing gifts upon the worshipper, the victorious one made a ford for Turvīti.
To him indeed, the powerful and far-reaching one, bring forth the thunderbolt with haste against Vṛtra!
Like a bull, he has rent asunder the joints; desiring to pierce them crosswise, he moves to flow through the floods of the waters.
(12) Proclaim with new hymns the ancient deeds of this swift one:
how, brandishing his weapons for battle, he, roaring in his fury, overcomes his enemies. (13)
Out of fear of him, even the firm mountains and heaven and earth tremble at his very birth.
Approaching the dwelling of the longing one, Nodhas instantly became ready for heroic deeds.
To him alone among them was that gift given, since he, being the sole lord, won much wealth.
Indra helped Pr̥itaśa, the Soma-presser, as he contended with Sūrya for the prize of the horse-race.
Thus have the Gotamas fashioned these well-wrought prayers for you, O Indra, joined with the two bay steeds;
bestow upon them a thought adorned with every beauty, and may he who is rich in prayer come quickly at dawn.

He alone is the one to whom the people must offer oblations; praise that Indra with these songs— he who rules as the bull, possessed of manly vigor, the true hero, full of many wondrous powers, and victorious.
Him indeed our ancient fathers, the Navagvas, the seven sages, impelled toward him, seeking strength.

(20.36.2.c) Him who strikes down the stars, the overcomer, who dwells upon the mountains, whose speech is guileless, and who is most mighty through our hymns—(20.36.3’) him we implore, Indra, for this wealth consisting of many heroes, full of men, and abundant in food; him who is unfailing, undecaying, and possessed of heaven—bring him hither, O Lord of Bay Steeds, so that we may rejoice! Tell us that, O Indra, whether your singers of old have indeed attained your favor.
What is your portion? What is your food, O fierce one, you who cause distress, you who are invoked by many and possess abundant wealth, O slayer of Asuras?
The trembling, eloquent voice of him whose song is now [sung] asks after Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, who stands upon his chariot.
(20.36.5.c) Toward the mighty one, the great-acting, the giver of strength, he goes for the sake of the path and for nourishment.

||5|| (20.36.6’) O self-strong one, with this very power, by means of the mountain swift as thought, you shattered even the unshakable, the firmly fixed, and the solid strongholds with boldness, O exuberant one. ||6||
With a new prayer, may we encompass him, the most powerful one, ancient as of old;
may that Indra, the faultless and excellent bearer, carry us across all difficult passages.
7 For the sake of the malicious people, you have set ablaze the earthly, celestial, and intermediate regions.
(20.36.8.c) O Bull, burn them from every side with your flame; scorch them for the hater of sacred prayer, the earth, and the waters.

(20.36.9’) You are the king of the divine folk and of the earthly world, O you of brilliant aspect. Take the thunderbolt in your right hand, O Indra; O undecaying one, you destroy all magical illusions.
(20.36.9.c) Take the thunderbolt in your right hand, O Indra; O undecaying one, you destroy all magical illusions.
O Indra, bestow upon us well-restrained, great, and unfailing prosperity for the overcoming of enemies— that prosperity by which you,
O wielder of the thunderbolt, make the Dāsa and Ārya foes, and the Nahuṣa tribes, easy to overcome.
O much-invoked Ordainer, worthy of sacrifice, come to us with your teams of horses that bring all desirable things.
Neither the godless nor the god shall restrain you; come quickly toward me with these [songs].

He who, like a fearsome bull with sharpened horns, alone causes all the peoples to tremble—he who is the one from whom you take away the wealth of every non-sacrificer, bestowing it upon the one who presses the soma.
O Indra, you indeed protected Kutsa, listening with your own body in the battle;
when you subdued the Dāsa Śuṣṇa and Kuyava for him, bestowing favor upon the son of Arjuni.
O bold one, with all your aids, you boldly protected Sudās, whose offerings were accepted.
(20.37.3.c) You protected Trasadasyu, the son of Purukutsa, and Pūru in the winning of land and in the slaying of Vṛtra.
(20.37.4’) O you of heroic mind, lord of bay horses, with your men you strike down many Vṛtras at the feast of the gods;
you sent the Dasyus Cumuri and Dhuni to sleep for the sake of Dabhīti, making them easy to slay.
These were your mighty deeds, O wielder of the thunderbolt, when you instantly [overthrew] ninety-nine forts;
you brought the hundredth to its end at Niveśana, and you slew Vṛtra and Namuci as well.
These, O Indra, are your ancient provisions for the liberal Sudās, who offers oblations and worships you.
(20.37.6.c) For you, the bull, I yoke the two bay stallions; may our prayers reach you, O you of many powers, for the sake of booty.

(20.37.7’) O powerful Lord of the Bay Steeds, let us not fall into misfortune or be cast away in this your conflict; protect us with your safe defenses, and may we remain dear to you among the patrons. (20.37.7.c) May we be beloved by you among the wise leaders.
O Maghavan, may we, your dear friends, rejoice under your protection in your favor. Subdue Turvaśa and Yadu; you who are worthy of praise, act for the sake of Atithigva.
Even now, O Maghavan, in your favor, the men who recite hymns proclaim their songs of praise.
(20.37.9.c) Those who, with their invocations, have failed to honor the Paṇis—choose us for that very alliance!
(20.37.10’) O most heroic among men, these hymns of praise are directed toward you, as they offer us wealth.
O Indra, be gracious to them in the slaying of Vṛtra; be the friend, the hero, and the protector of these men.
Now, O heroic Indra, being praised for your aid, strengthened by our prayer, grow mighty in your body!
Bestow upon us strength and grant us followers; do you gods protect us always with your blessings.

(20.38.1.c) This sacred grass is my seat.

(20.38.4.c) The voices have sung in praise of Indra.
(20.38.5’) Indra indeed, together with his two bay steeds, is mingled with the one yoked by speech; Indra is the wielder of the thunderbolt, the golden one.
(20.38.5.c) Indra is the wielder of the thunderbolt, the golden one.
Indra raised the sun high in heaven for far-reaching vision;
he split the mountain apart with his rays.
We invoke Indra from every side, away from all other people.
May he be ours alone.
Indra, in the exhilaration of Soma, extended across the mid-air and the luminous realms when he split Vala asunder.
He drove forth the cows for the Aṅgirases, making manifest those that were hidden;

By Indra, the luminous realms of heaven were made firm and strengthened.
(20.39.4.c) Firm, do not drive them away. (20.39.5’) Like a wave of water rejoicing, O Indra, the hymn of praise speeds swiftly;

For you shall be seen united with Indra, having come together with him who is fearless— both of you joyful, possessing equal splendor.
With those blameless ones who shine toward heaven, Makha worships mightily.
With the beloved hosts of Indra.
Then indeed, according to their own nature, they brought forth the state of being embryos again,
assuming a name worthy of sacrifice.
With the bones of Dadhyac, Indra, irresistible, struck down ninety-nine Vṛtras.
Seeking the horse’s head which was hidden away in the mountains—
He found that in Śaryaṇāvat.
There they recognized the secret name of Tvaṣṭṛ’s cow,
even so, in the house of the moon.
I have measured out my body from Indra— the eight-footed speech, nine-cornered, touching the eternal Order (*ṛta*).
Both worlds, heaven and earth, cried out after you as you roared.
(20.42.2.c) O Indra, when you became the slayer of the Dasyus.
(20.42.3.a) Rising up with vigor, having drunk, you shook your jaws;
(20.42.3.c) you drank the Soma pressed in the ladle, O Indra.
Shatter all enemies; strike down those who oppress us;
bring to us that desirable wealth.
Whatever was placed within the firm stronghold, O Indra, whatever is in the stable place, or whatever has been brought forth in the cavern—bring it to us.
(20.43.2.c) Bring that desirable wealth hither!
(20.43.3’) Of which abundant gift of yours all mankind shall take cognizance— Bring that desirable wealth hither!
Let the praiser extol with new songs Indra, the sovereign lord of the peoples,
the hero who overcomes men, the most bountiful.
He in whom all hymns of praise and all glorious deeds find delight.

Indra surpasses all enemies. (2) O Indra, as such, do you favor us with strengths; grant us both wealth and a path, and lead us toward happiness. (3)
We urge that Indra on for the great slaying of Vṛtra;
may he become the bull, the showerer of benefits.
That Indra has been prepared for the giving; he is most powerful, established in the exhilaration of the soma.
He is glorious, renowned, and worthy of Soma.
Like a thunderbolt fashioned by song, he is powerful and unshakable; lofty and invincible, he has grown great.
To Indra alone the singers have sung aloud; to Indra, with hymns, the chanters;
to Indra the voices have cried out.
Indra indeed is joined with the two bay steeds, mingled with them, yoked by a word.
(20.47.5.c) Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, is golden-hued.

Let your two long-maned bay horses, yoked by prayer, bring you hither, O Indra.
(20.47.8.c) Hear our sacred prayers!

Those who stand around harness the ruddy, flaming steed as he moves;
the luminous realms shine in heaven. They harness his two beloved bay horses, winged on either side, to the chariot.
